Ask Yourself Nicely.original:
When you want something from a stranger, you know you must be kind in making the ask. Of yourself, however, you demand instant performance. You lie awake at night, berating yourself: “Go back to sleep, you idiot!” Why not try what has worked flawlessly with other people for decades?
“Dear body, dear brain, might the two of you work together in helping me go back to sleep? That’d be awesome. Sleep is part of the solution, not the problem, you know? Worrying at night gets me nowhere, so if we could all pull together here, that would be amazing. Thank you so much!”
There’s no guarantee being kind to yourself will work, but it’s almost certain yelling at the mirror will not. Ask yourself nicely, and you may discover your subconscious was your ally all along.

“Dear me, I know you’re sad, but I’d love it if you could just get out of bed. The sun is waiting to greet you.”
When you’re your own best friend, you’ll treat yourself like one. And even if you don’t always succeed, at least you’ll always be nice.

“Come on. Just another 30 minutes. Please? Pretty please? You can do it. I know you can.” Suddenly, falling asleep becomes a favor you do for yourself. You’re no longer an angry manager, trying to get an employee to perform. You’re a friend, trying to help another friend. The shift in perspective is profound.
Treat yourself like you would treat others. You’re a stranger too, you know? A stranger you happen to know well — and therefore must treat extra kindly.

Silent Acknowledgement.original:
I can’t reply to every comment I get online. I can’t congratulate every friend on every LinkedIn update. These days, I sometimes can’t even answer every WhatsApp message.
But I can hit the button. I can like, clap, celebrate, heart, thumbs-up, or send any of the hundreds of possible emoji-reactions to a kind word, an awesome achievement, or a noteworthy statement.
Occasionally, I worry that an emoji-reaction is not enough. But personally, I find it refreshing to receive them. It’s nice to know there are no further words needed. Like a quiet nod among two people who aren’t in the same room. “Got it.” Or, “You’ve got this.” Conversation settled. Both clear to move on.
If I’m relieved to not get yet another message expecting a response, I’m sure others must feel the same. So I emoji-react and watch what happens. If more words are needed, I’ll certainly hear them sooner or later.
In a world that’s brimming with too much noise, silent acknowledgement isn’t just a remedy. It may actually stand out above the buzz.

I can’t reply to every comment I get online. I can’t congratulate every friend on every LinkedIn update. These days, I sometimes can’t even answer every WhatsApp message.
But I see them. I see all of them. And I acknowledge them. Silently. I don’t know whether this is enough, but it is something. Something I can do. I’m not ignoring you. I’m not indifferent to your success. I’m just busy. As busy as you are. As busy as we all are.
I’m not sure how much silent acknowledgement you’re receiving, but I hope you get some. I hope you’ll remember to send it to others. And I hope you’ll always find the time to give your loved ones the real thing.

Silent acknowledgement is a powerful form of respect. Don’t underestimate it.

The Backstory Is the Story.original:
Tolkien’s Silmarillion is a masterpiece. Not because of how well it is written, how coherent the story, or how illustrious its characters. It is a work of genius because Tolkien actually took the time, thought, and care to craft 5,000 years of backstory to his main works, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
5,000 years! Can you even imagine? That’s about as long as we’ve been recording our actual history as humans. Tolkien drew maps, family trees, even invented his own languages to give everything an original name yet one with a meaning we can comprehend.
Of course, like any human work, The Silmarillion is far from perfect. Compiled from endless of his father’s notes by Tolkien’s son Christopher, the book had to be whipped into shape. And of course, when you cover 5,000 years of history in 365 pages, not every character gets a full three-act treatment. Many have since been fleshed out in movies, TV shows, and fan fiction, starting from little more than the few sentences Tolkien originally dedicated to them.
But the fact that he devised not just a creation myth but an entire, five-millennia chronology for his work isn’t a fun piece of trivia. It’s a large part of the reason why what happens in the few years covered in his subsequent books resonates with millions of people around the world to this day.
When someone in The Lord of the Rings talks about the island kingdom of Númenor, the Balrogs of Morgoth, the first Dark Lord, or lembas, which is extra-nourishing Elven bread, all of those things mean something, and you can feel that meaning. You can look up each of those words and characters, and you’ll find more lore behind them—and regardless of whether you do so or not, the story itself hits different with all the weight of its backstory behind it.
Life is not just what we see. It’s also the invisible energy we put into what ultimately didn’t remain for the senses to witness. The backstory is the story—make sure you tend to it wherever you wish to tell a lasting tale.

Tolkien’s Silmarillion is a masterpiece. Not because of how well it is written, how coherent the story, or how illustrious its characters. It is a work of genius because Tolkien actually took the time, thought, and care to craft 5,000 years of backstory to his main works, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
5,000 years! That’s 1,000 years for every 100 pages of The Lord of the Rings. That’s 10 times the entire history of Western civilization. What Tolkien did was not just create a story. He created a world.
The Silmarillion is a book of legends, and it is exactly what makes the world of The Lord of the Rings feel so real. It’s the backdrop against which the main story unfolds. It’s the history, the culture, the beliefs, the values, the stories of the people. It’s the very air the characters breathe, and that’s why they feel so alive. It’s why we can feel them breathe too.
The Silmarillion is not just the backstory to The Lord of the Rings. It is the story. Without it, there’d be no story at all. Just a bunch of words on a page, no meaning, no context, no life.
The Silmarillion is the story because the backstory is always the story. What happened before is what makes what’s happening now interesting.
Your life is a story. It’s a story in the making, and every day, you get to decide what you’ll write. You get to decide what happens next. But what happens next is only as good as what happened before.
The backstory is the story. Never forget it.

It is a work of genius because Tolkien actually took the time, thought, and care to craft 5,000 years of backstory to his main works, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
The Silmarillion is the Bible of the Tolkien universe, and it’s not a book you read for fun. It’s a book you read to understand the world and the people in it a little better. To grasp the full meaning of the tales told in his other works.
It’s also a book you can read without ever having read or even heard of The Hobbit or The Lord of the Rings. That’s how good of a job Tolkien did. The backstory is a story in its own right.
Most of us don’t want to know the backstory. We want to know the result. We want the reward without the work. That’s why we turn on a movie on a Friday night, why we read a book in a weekend, and why we skim an article without ever giving it a proper read. We want the story without the backstory.
But the backstory is the story. That’s what the people who make things worth remembering know. They know that every piece of the puzzle matters, and that if you don’t put all the pieces in the right place, the puzzle will never come together. The picture will never form. And we, the audience, will never see the story that was meant to be.
It’s true that, often, the backstory will never be revealed. But that does not make it any less important. In fact, it makes it more important. If the backstory isn’t good, if it’s not coherent, if it doesn’t make sense, we will see right through it. We’ll know that the story is not a story at all, and we’ll toss it into the trash bin right then and there.
The backstory is the story. It is not optional. It is not something you can skip. The only question is whether you’ll tell it to us or not. But tell it to yourself? Craft it? Work on it? That you must do. You must do it for us. You must do it for yourself. And you must do it for the story that is meant to be.
If you don’t, no one else will do it for you. But if you do, you’ll give us a story worth remembering. You’ll give us a story that can last forever.

It\u2019s Okay If the Glass Breaks.original:
Donna Berzatto has been anything but a reliable mother to her three children. But when her only daughter Natalie, nicknamed “Sugar,” is about to give birth, the soon-to-be grandmother becomes an unexpected pillar of support.
With everyone else having turned off their phone during the family restaurant’s busy service hours, Donna and Nat end up at the hospital alone, and it makes for one heck of an episode of The Bear. Donna, brilliantly played by Jamie Lee Curtis, brings her daughter ice chips, shows her breathing exercises, and tells her stories to calm her down.
When Nat wants to know about the day of her own birth, Donna launches into “the fish tank dream.” She wasn’t due for a few days, Donna explains. One night, home alone, she climbed into bed at 8 PM and fell into a deep sleep. “And I had this…this really vivid dream, but—you know those kind of dreams where you’re just doing normal stuff, but things are, like, super detailed?” Sugar nods, and Donna continues.
She must have had the day off, Donna says, because in this “nothing-dream,” she was walking around the city. Not exactly her city—the city of Chicago—but some sort of hybrid between Chicago and New York. “And…and there was a fish tank.” “A fish tank?” “A big fish tank in the middle of the city. It was this giant fish tank, and I was the only one looking at it,” Donna says.
So there she was, standing in an all-grey city, all alone, looking at “a mega, like a dentist office kind of fish tank.” “And I remember the colors were…they were so sharp and vivid and neon, and I was the only one looking at it. It was beautiful.” But then, after “staring at it for the longest time,” something happened.
“And all of a sudden, I noticed that the glass started to come apart like it was gonna split,” Donna continues. “But I wasn’t worried, you know?” Somehow, even in her dream, she realized: “It wasn’t bad, because I knew that more people were gonna get to see these beautiful fish.” “And then?” “Then I woke up, and I was sweating, and my water had broke.”
Sometimes, we stare at a beautiful fish tank, and we don’t want the dream to end. Our son is acing his tests. We have the perfect week at the office. A stock just keeps going up. But sooner or later, the glass always cracks. It doesn’t have to be a bad thing, you know?
When you see the glass starting to come apart, don’t worry. Don’t think about the loss, or the shards, or the mess you’ll have to clean up later. Some short-term pain might follow, but that’s not the important part. Focus on what the break might set free for everyone, including you. Remember that more people will get to see these beautiful fish.
In order to discover the sea, we first must leave our aquarium. That’s why it’s okay if the glass breaks. As long as you keep swimming, it just might be good news.

With the baby’s father nowhere to be found, Sugar must make a tough decision: Will she give her child up for adoption? Or will she raise it on her own?
Donna is there to help her through it all. She even offers to move in with her daughter for a while. But when Sugar is finally ready to leave the hospital, she asks her mom to bring her a glass of water. Donna leaves the room, and on her way to the water fountain, she breaks the glass. She panics and runs away.
It’s a moment that perfectly encapsulates Donna’s life: She’s just about to get it right when everything falls apart. And while it’s a moment that’s easy to laugh off, it’s also one that’s easy to miss.
If you’ve ever dropped a glass of water, you know the feeling. It’s a small mistake, but it feels like a big one. It’s an accident that feels like a crime. “How could I be so stupid?” we ask ourselves. “How could I let this happen?”
But the truth is, it’s okay if the glass breaks. It’s okay if we make mistakes. It’s okay if we’re not perfect. It’s okay if we’re not always there for our children. It’s okay if we don’t always have the right words. It’s okay if we don’t always know what to do.
What matters is that we try. What matters is that we show up. What matters is that we’re there for our children when they need us. What matters is that we’re willing to learn from our mistakes. What matters is that we’re willing to change.
It’s okay if the glass breaks. It’s okay if we’re not perfect. What matters is that we keep trying. That we keep showing up. That we keep learning. That we keep changing.

 to-be mom, Donna says: “It’s okay if the glass breaks. You can always buy another one. And if you can’t, you can always drink from the cup.”
The glass Donna refers to is the one she smashed on the day of her own wedding. She was too nervous to go through with it, but her father reminded her that “the marriage is not the important part — it’s the wedding.”
Donna ran away and eloped with her fiancé, but on the day of the ceremony, she broke the glass tradition — a Jewish custom meant to symbolize the fragility of relationships — and thus managed to get everyone’s attention. It was her way of saying, “I’m not ready for this.”
Now, as her daughter is about to become a mother, Donna wants to make sure Sugar won’t make the same mistakes she did. “I don’t want you to feel trapped,” she tells her daughter. “You can always change your mind.”
When I started writing, I thought I would become a bestselling author within a year. When I started my first job, I thought I would be promoted within six months. And when I started my own business, I thought I’d make a million dollars within a year.
None of those things happened, and while I’m still working on all of them, I’ve learned that the glass always breaks sooner or later. The path to success is never a straight line, and so there’s no point in worrying about getting everything right the first time.
When you drop a glass, you can’t put it back together and use it as if nothing had happened. The pieces will never fit perfectly, and even if they do, the glass will never be as strong as it was before it broke. But even if you can’t use the same glass again, you can always buy another one. And if you can’t do that, you can always drink from the cup.
It’s okay if the glass breaks. Have the courage to admit when you’re wrong, and then find the strength to pick yourself up and try again.

Billion-Dollar Bullshit.original:
From 2014 to 2017, Juicero collected a whopping $120 million in funding from venture capitalists. The company then applied “the Silicon Valley formula” to its product, a juice dispenser. They made a sleek-looking machine that pressed juice made of fresh, local ingredients from specifically designed and verified packets. They charged $400 for that machine. They launched exclusively in California and only sold to customers via a subscription model. And a few months later, they shut down and failed.
It was a rare but gratifying example of Silicon Valley cutting its teeth on common sense—because there were so many obvious flaws in the product, an eight-year-old could have told you it wouldn’t work.
The dispenser couldn’t actually make juice out of fruits or vegetables you bought at the store. It had to be the packets. Those packets were not just expensive, they also expired after only seven days. And once they did, the machine wouldn’t press them. Oh, and to check that it shouldn’t press the bag, the Juicero Press had to be hooked up to the internet, too. No wi-fi, no party. But what ultimately did them in was a one-minute video from Bloomberg : A reporter pressed the bags by hand, and voilà, the juice still came out just fine. In fact, it was probably faster than using the machine. Less than five months after that video, Juicero announced they were quitting.
Just because something has millions, sometimes billions, of dollars behind it, that does not make it genius, useful, necessary, or even relevant. It can be billion-dollar bullshit. Don’t be impressed too easily—and whatever you buy into, make sure the juice is worth the squeeze.
Billion-Dollar Bullshit.ckpt_800:
From 2014 to 2017, Juicero collected a whopping $120 million in funding from venture capitalists. The company then applied “the Silicon Valley formula” to its product, a juice dispenser. They made a sleek-looking machine that pressed juice made of fresh, local ingredients from specifically designed and verified packets. They charged $400 for that machine. They launched exclusively in California and only sold to customers via a subscription model. And a few months later, they shut down and failed.
It’s easy to laugh at Juicero’s failure, but it’s also easy to see why investors were convinced: The team was strong. The product was high-tech. The branding was on point. And the business model was sound. It’s a classic case of “seemed like a good idea at the time,” and that’s what makes it so fascinating.
I don’t think Juicero was a scam. I think they were just trying to do what every startup tries to do: Make something that works and that people want. But sometimes, you don’t know what you’re doing. Sometimes, you can’t see what’s right in front of you. And sometimes, you’re just plain wrong.
The company’s founder, Doug Evans, had a vision: He wanted to make fresh juice available to everyone. He wanted to put a juicer in every home. He wanted to create a new standard for how we consume food. But in trying to do all that, he missed the forest for the trees. Juicero’s packets cost $5 to $8. That’s $5 to $8 for a single glass of juice. It’s more expensive than the juice you can buy in the store, and it’s more expensive than the juice you can make yourself.
Evans was so focused on his vision that he forgot to ask himself the most important question: Why would anyone buy this? And that’s why Juicero failed.
It’s easy to get caught up in the hype. It’s easy to get swept away by the momentum. But it’s important to remember that, at the end of the day, you’re still selling a product. And if that product doesn’t solve a problem for your customer, it’s not going to sell. No matter how much money you raise, no matter how much hype you generate, and no matter how much you believe in your vision.
In business, there’s a saying: “You can’t polish a turd.” It means that no matter how much you try to dress up a bad product, it’s still going to be a bad product. And that’s what Juicero was. A turd. A $120 million turd.
It’s a cautionary tale for all of us. A reminder that, no matter how much money we raise, no matter how much hype we generate, and no matter how much we believe in our vision, we still need to ask ourselves the most important question: Why would anyone buy this? And if we can’t answer that question, we’re just peddling billion-dollar bullshit.
Billion-Dollar Bullshit.ckpt_1628:
From 2014 to 2017, Juicero collected a whopping $120 million in funding from venture capitalists. The company then applied “the Silicon Valley formula” to its product, a juice dispenser. They made a sleek-looking machine that pressed juice made of fresh, local ingredients from specifically designed and verified packets. They charged $400 for that machine. They launched exclusively in California and only sold to customers via a subscription model. And a few months later, they shut down and failed.
What went wrong? Well, the packets were neither fresh nor local. They came from a factory in Los Angeles and had to be shipped all over the place. The juice was nothing special either. It tasted good, but so does any juice. The subscription model, meanwhile, meant you were paying $5-$7 per glass of juice, and the machine itself was, well, unnecessary.
The Juicero machine was a $400 device to press juice bags with the force of two shopping carts. You could do the same thing with your bare hands, and in fact, people did. When Bloomberg published a video of people squeezing Juicero bags by hand, the company was toast. They refunded customers for months, then tried to sell the machines for $200, and a few months later, they closed up shop.
The Juicero is the perfect example of billion-dollar bullshit. It’s a product that solves no problem whatsoever, created by a company that does nothing but generate more expensive waste while claiming to do the opposite. Juicero’s founder, Doug Evans, was a walking, talking pile of bullshit too. He claimed he was “the Steve Jobs of juice” and that he had “a gift for juicing.” He also said he was “a raw food and plant-based diet advocate,” yet was seen eating a cheeseburger at McDonald’s. He also threw a hissy fit when the Bloomberg video came out, and he was a notorious bully at work, even physically attacking people on multiple occasions.
The Juicero story is a cautionary tale for entrepreneurs, investors, and customers alike. Don’t fall for bullshit, and don’t spread bullshit either. Don’t invest in companies that create problems instead of solving them, and don’t throw your money at solutions to problems you don’t have. If something sounds too good to be true, it probably is. And if someone claims to have a gift for juicing, you should probably take your business elsewhere.

Pretend It\u2019s the Last Time.original:
My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
It can, however, also be a useful tool. In Creative Doing, my friend Herbert Lui writes: “Let go of your external expectations. Immerse yourself in the task at hand.” One way to do so? Pretend it’s the last time. Like Frank Sinatra did, at least according to his friend and fellow singer Bono : “Fully inhabiting the moment during that tiny dot of time after you’ve pressed ‘record’ is what makes it eternal. If, like Frank, you sing it like you’ll never sing it again. If, like Frank, you sing it like you never have before.”
“What if this was the last time?” The last time you’ll write. The last video you’ll shoot. The last slide you’ll ever make. Talk about going in with intention! “This philosophy is applicable to your craft,” Herbert writes. “You can pretend like it’s the last time you’re doing your work, the last chance you might be able to contribute to this piece of work. This immersion naturally lets expectations, hopes, and fears fade away; none of it matters.”
Whatever work you care about, the next time, pretend it’s the last time. Feel pressure, aspirations, and worry fall away, and then give it all you’ve got.

The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
It’s not that we should try to have it every day. It’s that we should try to have it more often than we do. We can’t always be nostalgic, but we can be nostalgic more often than we are. It’s a good habit to have. It’ll help us appreciate the present more and not take the people we love for granted.
The next time you see your dad, pretend it’s the last time. The next time you eat your favorite dish, pretend it’s the last time. The next time you talk to your best friend, pretend it’s the last time. You’ll feel more grateful and more motivated to make the most of your time together. You’ll also feel less sad if, one day, it actually is the last time.
Don’t miss the last times you know are coming. And don’t forget to pretend it’s the last time when you don’t know.

My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
What’s less obvious but perhaps even more important, however, is pretending “this is the last time” when you know it’s not going to be. When you’re not sick of your friend but tired of talking about the same old stuff. When you’re not sick of the food but tired of eating it every day. And when you’re not sick of your job but tired of doing the same task over and over again.
Pretend it’s the last time you can ask your friend the most interesting question you can think of. Pretend it’s the last time you can eat your favorite dish. And pretend it’s the last time you can submit a report with a new idea for a change. Watch what happens. How will you approach the situation? Which emotions come up? Is there a tinge of nostalgia? Some relief? And how do you act? Are you more curious? More thorough? More creative?
Sometimes, it’s important to realize what you’re about to lose before it’s gone. At other times, you must remember what makes something worth keeping while you still have it. Don’t wait for the last time. Make the most of today.

A Body Is Just a Shell.original:
When his son Dino died at just 24 years old, the great Enzo Ferrari learned that engineers can’t fix bodies. In the world of Alita: Battle Angel, the opposite is true: With most people being at least partially cyborg, Dr. Dyson Ido, played by Christoph Waltz, repairs bodies all day long.
When he finds a special soul, a mysterious teenage girl robot—or what’s left of her—in the scrapyard, he restores her completely. Now in a cyborg body that was reserved for Ido’s deceased daughter, Alita, the now-eponymous main character starts discovering who she is. Naturally, she completely wrecks her new frame in the process.
Thankfully, before returning to pieces, Alita found an old battle torso—the very kind she used to operate in her past life. So for a second time, Dr. Ido mends Alita’s body, and it is here that her journey comes to a crossroads. “Now you know who you are,” Ido tells her, pointing at the shiny nanotech covering Alita from head to toe. “But that’s just a shell. It’s not bad or good. That part’s up to you.” And sure enough, soon thereafter, Alita must choose how to use her newfound power —and choose wisely and fast.
Maybe one day, we, too, will be able to replace body parts as easily as we swap broken screens on our phones. Until then, however, our mortal forms will remain something even the most gifted engineer can’t fix—and yet, a body is just a shell. Why endlessly preserve a vessel with an expiry date if we don’t intend to put it to good use? However capable or limited your physical frame, make sure you fill it with good while you can—and don’t worry about a little wear around the edges.
A Body Is Just a Shell.ckpt_800:
When his son Dino died at just 24 years old, the great Enzo Ferrari learned that engineers can’t fix bodies. In the world of Alita: Battle Angel, the opposite is true: With most people being at least partially cyborg, Dr. Dyson Ido, played by Christoph Waltz, repairs bodies all day long.
When he finds the head and torso of a cyborg girl in a scrapyard, he gives her a new body, and Alita is born. Alita has no memories, and she must learn everything from scratch. In a way, she is like a child, and so Dr. Ido becomes her father.
As Alita grows into her new life, she discovers her body is more than just a shell. It is a powerful weapon, and she can use it to fight for what’s right. But she must also learn to protect her heart.
In a scene that mirrors the moment when Dino Ferrari was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Alita is told by her doctor that she has a “weak heart.” She can’t have a new one. She’ll have to make do with what she has. Just like Dino, Alita is told she can’t have the one thing she needs most. And just like Enzo, Dr. Ido is helpless in the face of his daughter’s pain.
But Alita is not Dino. She is a cyborg. And cyborgs can fix bodies. Alita may not be able to get a new heart, but she can get a new body. And she does.
In the end, Alita learns that a body is just a shell. It’s what’s inside that counts. And she uses her new body to fight for what she believes in.
Alita: Battle Angel is a story about identity, love, and loss. It’s a story about what it means to be human. And it’s a story about hope.
Hope that even when our bodies fail us, we can still find a way to fight for what’s right. Hope that even when we lose the people we love, we can still find a way to keep going. And hope that even when the world seems to be falling apart, we can still find a way to hold on to what’s important.
Alita: Battle Angel is a movie about finding hope in the darkest of times. And that’s why it’s a movie worth watching.

When his son Dino died at just 24 years old, the great Enzo Ferrari learned that engineers can’t fix bodies. In the world of Alita: Battle Angel, the opposite is true: With most people being at least partially cyborg, Dr. Dyson Ido, played by Christoph Waltz, repairs bodies all day long.
When Ido finds Alita, a fully cyborg girl with no memories, in a scrapyard, he initially wants to do the same. But the more he learns about her, the more he realizes that Alita is not just a body. She has a soul. A strong one. A soul that’s worth protecting.
Ido’s revelation is a powerful reminder: Bodies are just shells. We can swap them out. Replace them. Even abandon them. But our soul? That is ours to keep. We must protect it. Cherish it. And that’s why, when he first sees Alita’s head, hanging on a chain, Ido decides to help her. To give her a body. A shell. A new shell for a new life.
If you want to know what’s really important, look at the parts you can replace. Chances are, they’re not the ones that matter. Only once they’re gone will you see what’s left. What’s truly yours. And it’s probably a lot more than you imagined.

Zero Copies.original:
That’s how many I sold when I finally got my long-coveted Kindle Daily Deal.
On its Kindle store for ebooks, Amazon does both monthly and daily deals. They approach authors, and if they agree, their book will be discounted for a day or a month, and then Amazon will promote it.
Years ago, I read on a blog that Daily Deals worked much better than Monthly Deals. The idea was that if a book is only discounted for 24 hours, Amazon will push it much harder, and thus you should sell more copies. The article even showed some statistics to back this up!
My books have been out for three and two years, respectively. So far, all I’d ever gotten was the occasional Monthly Deal, and sure enough, they didn’t really move the needle. Ergo, when I recently got an invite to do a Daily Deal for Indian readers, I was thrilled! Finally I might see Amazon’s promotional powers on full display.
But the day came, and the day went, and I got zero sales. It’s not like I had high expectations. How and when you get picked for these events is arbitrary to begin with. Yet I was still underwhelmed.
In the end, the whole event turned out to be nothing more than a useful reminder: Getting picked is not all it’s cracked up to be—so never wait to get picked.
Zero Copies.ckpt_800:
That’s how many I sold when I finally got my long-coveted Kindle Daily Deal.
For the first 18 months of my book’s existence, I sold about 2,000 copies. Then, I got a Kindle Daily Deal. I sold 700 copies in a single day. I was ecstatic! Finally, my book would be a hit. Finally, I would get some momentum. Finally, the big break I had been waiting for!
Of course, the next day, sales went right back to zero. The day after, they went right back to zero. And the day after that, they went right back to zero.
It’s a great lesson to learn early: Nothing is a big break. You’re not entitled to a big break. And if you get one, you’ll still have to work for it. No one is coming to save you. No one will hand you a million dollars and say, “Here, go live your dream.” You have to do it yourself. You have to do it all yourself. And if you don’t, no one else will.
The Kindle Daily Deal was a great experience. It was a lot of fun. But it also showed me that, even if I got it every day, I’d still have to show up and write every day. I’d still have to do my best to make something good. And I’d still have to promote my work. That’s the only way it works. It’s the only way that lasts.
I’m not saying you shouldn’t take the big break if you get it. I’m saying you shouldn’t wait for it. You shouldn’t expect it. And you should never, ever take it for granted.
Zero Copies.ckpt_1628:
That’s how many I sold when I finally got my long-coveted Kindle Daily Deal.
After years of asking Amazon to promote my books, I finally got an email: “We would like to feature your book The 4 Minute Millionaire on October 15th, 2023.” I was thrilled! I set up the promotion, and I crossed my fingers.
Unfortunately, the deal didn’t go as I had imagined. Instead of being featured in the usual “Kindle Daily Deal” email, which goes out to millions of people, my book was tucked away on some remote page on Amazon, where only the most dedicated bargain hunters would ever find it. As a result, I sold zero copies.
It was a good reminder that, ultimately, your marketing is your responsibility. You can’t outsource it. You can’t hand it off to someone else and expect them to do a good job. You have to bring people to your work. You have to make them care. And you have to do it every day.
Sure, on some days, you’ll sell zero copies. But if you keep going, sooner or later, you’ll sell one — and that’s how it all begins.

It\u2019s Your Response-Ability.original:
Sometimes, a word transforms completely when you see it not for its dictionary entry but for its parts. Will Smith is a master at this. So was Bruce Lee. In Striking Thoughts, he notes that “response-ability” is one of several synonyms for “living in the now” and leaning into your creativity.
When we think about responsibility, whatever we imagine usually looks like work. “Ugh. Do I really have to? ” But what if responsibility is not an obligation but an opportunity? A chance to practice your ability to respond?
Life doesn’t force you to do anything. It just presents you with challenges. Whether you face them or walk away is up to you. But in every moment, you have the ability to respond, and how you respond is entirely up to you.
You can walk out singing the day you get fired. You can write a poem with a rhyming scheme no one’s ever used before. And instead of taking every word literally, you can pull them apart and infuse them with your own meaning.
Nothing is your fault, but everything is your responsibility —and when you use your response-ability, that word means “ freedom ” instead of “burden.”
It\u2019s Your Response-Ability.ckpt_800:

It’s a reminder that, yes, we are responsible for everything in our lives — but that responsibility is also a privilege. It’s our ability to respond. To make something new where there was nothing before.
What will you choose to respond to? What will you choose to respond with? These are the questions. Don’t let them become “How much can I get away with?”
When you respond, you are responsible. When you are responsible, you can respond. It’s a two-way street, and it’s a beautiful, endless loop of creativity. You’re not just making art. You’re making life.

We are not mere bystanders, Bruce wrote. We are actors. Participants. “Man is always a participant in the creative process, not by his mere existence, but by the nature of his reaction to the present.” It is our response-ability that makes us human. It is our ability to respond that makes us human.
It is not a duty. It is not a burden. It is a privilege. We have the ability to respond, and we can do so in infinite ways. We can choose to respond with anger. We can choose to respond with sadness. We can choose to respond with humor, with creativity, with kindness, with empathy, and with patience. We can choose to respond with a smile, with a nod, with a shrug, with a laugh, and with a hug. We can choose to respond with words, with silence, with a song, with a dance, and with a prayer. We can choose to respond with action, with waiting, with thinking, with learning, and with practicing.
Whatever the situation, the choice is ours. We can choose to respond to everything, to nothing, and to something in between. We can choose to respond now, to respond later, and to respond never. But we can always choose to respond. That is our response-ability, and it is ours to exercise as we see fit.
Life is not something that happens to us. We are not mere victims, floating down the river of time. We are paddlers in our own canoe. We are the ones steering the ship. The question is will we grab the oars? Will we take the wheel? Will we take responsibility for our response-ability?
The only way to find out is to ask us. You know where we are. We’re right here. Living in the now, exercising our response-ability. And we’ll do it again tomorrow. Care to join us?

Creativity as a Well.original:
Sometimes, I happen to draft article ideas during my meditation, and sometimes, all 15 minutes of endurance training go to that activity. That’s not ideal, but it, too, teaches me a lesson: If I spend as little as a quarter of an hour brainstorming, thinking through the past 24 hours, about what happened this week, and allowing my mind to resurface whichever thought it prefers, I have article ideas out the wazoo.
After 1,000 daily blogs, you’d think I’d start running out. The opposite is true. The hard part is not finding an idea to write about. It’s picking one out of many that is specific enough to hold meaning but that I can also get to the point of being shippable—perhaps not finished, but shippable—in a time frame that doesn’t swallow the rest of my day.
For all the difficulty the execution brings, the reminder that the creative mind never runs out is wonderful. Creativity is an infinite well: It will always, always fill your bucket—as long as you make the effort to go and fetch water.

After 15 minutes of reflection, I can write down a dozen ideas, and I can do that every day. I can’t write 12 articles every day, of course, but I can write one. And if I don’t, I can do it again tomorrow. I can do it again every day. I can do it again until the end of time, and that’s the magic of creativity: It’s not a well you can run dry.
The more you draw from it, the more it wants to give you. It’s a well of infinite water, and the only thing that can stop the flow is you. You can stop pulling water from the well. You can forget to take a drink. You can turn away from it and walk in a different direction. But as long as you’re there, standing next to the well, it will always provide for you.
It’s easy to forget this. It’s easy to think that, on any given day, you don’t have anything to say. But you do. You always have something to say. You always have something to write. You always have something to offer. The question is: Are you willing to pull it out? Are you willing to draw it from the well?
It’s not always easy, but it’s always worth it. It’s always worth the effort. And even if you only have 15 minutes to spend, you can still draw something from the well. You can still come up with a dozen ideas, or a single one. You can still write a sentence, or a paragraph, or an entire article. It’s always worth the effort.
So don’t forget the well. Don’t forget to drink from it. And don’t forget that it’s always there for you.

In other words, creativity is like a well: If you go to it every day, you’ll never run out of water. In fact, if you go every day, you’ll likely pull up more water than you can use. This applies to any kind of creative endeavor, be it writing, painting, making music, or building a business.
It’s easy to feel as if you’re being unproductive when you’re brainstorming, thinking, or staring at a blank canvas. Actually, you’re doing the most important work you can do: refilling your well. Keep visiting it daily, and you’ll never thirst for inspiration again.

Dust Walls.original:
A few weeks ago, I was scheduling dozens of posts from the blog to republish them elsewhere. Copy, paste, pick date, hit the button, repeat.
The scheduling interface allowed you to type in the publishing date manually, but once you clicked into it, it opened a full calendar view so you could select the date with your mouse. Eventually, I realized that for all dates beyond three months into the future, the calendar was grayed out. “Oh, I guess I can only schedule so far,” I thought. Then, I closed the tab and moved on, taking what I could get.
Yesterday, I went back to that interface. I looked at the calendar again. Then, I tried something sneaky: I manually typed in a future date that lay beyond the three-month mark…and voilà! As it turns out, you can schedule posts as far into the future as you like—you just have to type the date instead of select it from the calendar. Ironically, I’d been using this method all along. But when I saw that grayed out window…
Some walls are literally made of dust. They shine brick-red but give way at the faintest push. The opposite of invisible walls, these blockers barely exist at all. It is only once they make it past our perception that they seem as solid as concrete.
Don’t let dust walls keep you for too long. Whatever obstacle you are facing, poke the bricks before you take the long way around. They just might give way without making a fuss.

The process was simple, but it took a while. When I was done, I looked at the big calendar and saw the blue dots for each post. They looked like little dust particles on a wall, and I thought: “I just wiped the dust off this wall.”
Sometimes, you’ll have to clean the same wall twice. That’s okay. It’s part of the job. But it’s also nice to look at the wall once you’re done. To see the dust particles neatly lined up in front of you. “Look! I did this. I wiped the dust off this wall.”
The next time you have a repetitive task to do, remember: You’re not just cleaning a wall. You’re cleaning a wall made of dust. That’s worth something.

A few weeks ago, I was scheduling dozens of posts from the blog to republish them elsewhere. Copy, paste, pick date, hit the button, repeat.
After I had done maybe 40 or so, I looked at the list of posts still left to schedule. There were 60 more to go. My heart sank. “Ugh. This is gonna be a long slog.” I would have to do this same, boring task two and a half times more still to get it done.
But then I remembered: “Wait a minute. This is just a list of posts. Nothing more, nothing less. It’s just a piece of paper. And on that piece of paper, there are 100 items. So what?”
The only thing that made that list daunting was the invisible cloud of dust surrounding it. The “I don’t wanna do this” aura. But if I could clear away the dust, I’d see it for what it is: just another task, like any other. In fact, I might even enjoy it.
I took a deep breath, started on the next item, and — you could almost see it — the cloud of dust settled on the floor. Suddenly, the task was easy. Fun, even. I cruised right through those 60 items. It was a piece of cake.
The only walls we have in our lives are the ones we build out of dust. If you feel stuck, chances are, you’ve surrounded yourself with dirt. You’ve psyched yourself out of the very thing you want to do.
Clear away the dust. Wash the walls. And remember: What feels like a big obstacle is often just a tiny speck of sand.

Re-Set.original:
Every year, I choose a one-word theme. For 2025, it’s “Reset.”
When a ship traverses the sea for a long time, it’ll accumulate barnacles on its hull. For the tiny crustaceans, it doesn’t matter where they sit. They’ll attach to any surface, as long as it supplies them with the water from which they get their nutrients. For the ship, however, in time, they become a heavy burden—literally. And while the weight of the barnacles will rarely be enough to sink the vessel, it might slow it down or bring it out of balance.
2024 was the year I realized: After ten years of writing and working for myself, I’ve racked up too many barnacles. For the first half of those ten years, I was mostly learning, growing, finding myself as a writer, person, and entrepreneur. But from the pandemic onwards, everything was a blur. Financially, it was a rollercoaster, and the velocity of that ride kept me latching onto whatever next thing I could get a hold of. But in late 2023, there was nothing left to reach for, and my ship slowly started sinking.
It took me all year to process everything, to shed off my old identity, to rise from the ashes of a fire that had burned for a decade. And now that I’ve finally accepted change is in order, well, it’s time to scrape off some barnacles! Time to reset.
The word “reset” means to start over, of course. To shut down, erase, reboot, and begin anew with a clean slate. But it also means to adjust. To fiddle with just slightly, so that an imbalanced, misaligned object may once again slot into its proper place. That, too, is “re-setting.” Moving a piece of the puzzle for the big picture to make sense. I’ll need to do a lot of both, hence “Reset” as my theme for 2025.
My work will be reset. I’ve picked up a full-time job, and everything else will have to fit in around the edges. Four Minute Books will be reset. No more ads, affiliate revenue, or any form of monetization that is not me selling my own creations. Perhaps it’ll have to be merged into this blog or disappear altogether. My writing will be re-set. I’ll get a chance to realign on what I really want to write, but I’ll also have to adjust to make time to then do that writing.
It’s easy to reflect at the turn of the year, and I can only recommend picking an annual theme, but I also know this to be true: Reset buttons are everywhere. You can hit as many of them as you like at any time. Whether you need to re-set some planks or build a new ship altogether, don’t wait. You deserve smooth sailing at all times—and every removed barnacle counts.
Re-Set.ckpt_800:
Every year, I choose a one-word theme. For 2025, it’s “Reset.”
I don’t know what exactly I’ll reset. It could be my work. It could be my relationships. It could be my life as a whole. I’ll figure it out as I go.
What I do know is that the word “reset” feels like a relief. It’s a reminder to not be so hard on myself. To not take everything so seriously. To not get so worked up about every little detail. I can just hit reset, and start over.
I can reset my expectations. I can reset my perspective. I can reset my attitude, my mood, and my approach. I can reset my day, my week, and my year. I can reset my mind, my heart, and my spirit. I can even reset my entire life if I have to.
The point is that reset is always an option — and it’s never too late to press the button.
Re-Set.ckpt_1628:
Every year, I choose a one-word theme. For 2025, it’s “Reset.”
I picked the word because I felt I needed a break. After a big, all-consuming project, I want to get back to my roots. I want to reset my focus on writing, on business, and on life. I want to reset my health, my habits, and my reading list. I want to reset my relationships and how I spend my time.
But there’s also another kind of reset, and it’s one I find myself doing more and more frequently: the kind where you stop for a moment, breathe, and then re-set your mind in order to continue the same task. It might be a literal break, like standing up from your desk, walking to the window, and looking outside for a minute. It might be a mental shift, like dropping a train of thought that’s not going anywhere and picking up a new one. Or, it could be a simple, one-minute meditation where you close your eyes, reset your attention to the present moment, and then get back to your work.
The longer the task, the more resets you’ll need. When I write a long essay, I reset my thoughts many times. I take a break here, add a note there, and sometimes, I’ll even shut the laptop lid and come back the next day. If I want to work on something for eight hours in a day, I might take 15-minute breaks every two hours or so. I’ll reset my mind on the regular so that I can keep working on the same thing, not because I need a break from it.
There’s a balance between the two kinds of resets, and I think both are important. You can’t work on the same project all the time, and you can’t expect to breeze through a marathon without ever stopping to drink some water. The trick is to know which kind of reset you need when. When do you need a break, and when do you need to re-center your attention? Only you can answer those questions, but if you manage to do so correctly, you’ll flow through life with admirable poise.
Sometimes, you’ll need to reset your trajectory. Sometimes, you’ll need to re-set your mind. Know which one it is, and you’ll do just fine.

My First Job.original:
That’s an odd phrase to type when you’re 33 years old. But I guess it is. Outside of some internships, only one of which lasted five months instead of just a few weeks, I’ve never held a full-time job—until now. “Business Course Writer.” That’s my title. My responsibility will be to create materials that’ll help enterprise employees understand blockchain and its applications. Kinda cool, huh? I’m definitely not complaining. Storytelling all the way!
After ten years of self-employment, you’d think I’d have a lot of feelings about working for someone else. Resistance, perhaps. The belief that I had failed to keep my business running. Surprisingly, I don’t. New is just different. I feel some relief that my rent and expenses will be covered, although that’ll only fully kick in once my probation period is over. I’m grateful I’ve found a place that seems to be a good fit, with good people and a good mix of tasks in a field which interests me. But a few days into the job, it’s mostly “ wait and see,” yet when I look back, I have no urge to grind my teeth. Perhaps it’s a sign that I’ve made my decisions deliberately.
When I realized I’d need a new business model for the umpteenth time, I could have dug in my heels. I could have pushed and shoved and forced, and kind friends gave me plenty of ideas on how to do so. But I didn’t want to. Grinding hadn’t gotten me any closer to being an author in the last few years, so why not try a new angle? Why not write on the side, stop compromising in order to make money, and spend whatever time I can spare to make the art I actually want to make? “Let’s see if I can walk that road,” I thought. “Let’s find out where another path leads.” I didn’t choose to end up in front of this particular intersection in life, but once I arrived there, I chose to make less. To trade dollars for integrity and sacrifice time in favor of art. If anything, that felt empowering.
So here I am. Ready for new. Ready for different. Ready for a re-set. My name is Nik. I’m 33 years old. And I just started my first job.

Still Water Is a Mirror.original:
“Moving, be like water. Still, be like a mirror.” That’s one of Bruce Lee’s Striking Thoughts. When I read it, I realized that, actually, this is an encouragement to be like water, period.
When water is moving, it flows. But when water is still, it reflects—just like a mirror. If you want to reflect—about yourself, life, and the world—you first have to stop. You must allow the waves of your actions and emotions to calm down.
The time to think is when you’re not moving. Still your waters on occasion so you can see yourself for who you really are and reality for what’s actually in front of you.
Still Water Is a Mirror.ckpt_800:
“Moving, be like water. Still, be like a mirror.” That’s one of Bruce Lee’s Striking Thoughts. When I read it, I realized that, actually, this is an encouragement to be like water, period.
If you’ve ever seen a lake or pond in complete stillness, you’ll know: Still water is a mirror. It reflects the sky above it, the trees and bushes around it, and everything else that happens to be near it. If you throw a stone into the water, however, it ripples. It moves. It’s no longer a mirror. It’s a participant in what’s going on.
The point of being like water is to know when to move and when to be still. Sometimes, it is enough to observe. To watch. To reflect the world as it is. At other times, however, you must get involved. You must jump in. You must throw a stone into the water.
When you’re still, you can better sense which is which. You can feel whether it is time to act or time to wait. When you’re always moving, you’ll never know. You’ll be too busy to notice anything at all. So be still. Be like a mirror. Until it is time to move, be like water.
Still Water Is a Mirror.ckpt_1628:
“Moving, be like water. Still, be like a mirror.” That’s one of Bruce Lee’s Striking Thoughts. When I read it, I realized that, actually, this is an encouragement to be like water, period.
What does a mirror do? It reflects. It reacts to whatever is placed in front of it. The moment the object moves, the mirror changes. That’s what water does too. It adapts to whatever vessel it is poured into. It is always moving, changing, flowing from one state to another, from one place to another. But if you put it into a glass and let it sit, it will also just sit. It will wait until it is needed.
Still water is a mirror, and so are we. We are not meant to be moved by everything. Sometimes, the best thing we can do is to stay still. To wait and reflect. To be a mirror. Only when the right inputs come along can we mirror them back in the right direction. When we react to the wrong things, we’ll only send them right back from whence they came. That’s not helpful. It doesn’t move the energy along.
It takes time to learn what to reflect and what to absorb. To know when to stay still and when to move. But it is a skill worth learning. You are not a mirror. You are water. But when you are still, you are a mirror. It is a paradox, but it is one worth remembering.

Mapping the Terrain.original:
“Where does that door lead again?” Confusion arose in yesterday’s gaming session. My girlfriend held the controller for The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom. As part of her turn, she had stormed headlong into a new dungeon. I kept asking her to backtrack, but that was not her style. “No, no, no, just keep going!”
Once it was my turn, I did all the backtracking I had longed for—not because my girlfriend’s approach was wrong but for my own peace of mind. It was part gaming experience, part personality: I want to discover all of one area before moving on to the next. This helps me build context for what’s to come, and it also prevents landing in a room whose puzzle you can’t solve for lack of a tool you failed to pick up before.
In life as in games, there’s no one way to play them. If you want to charge, charge! Keep walking straight until you bump into an obstacle, then assemble your pole for vaulting over it on the spot. But when you feel unsure, cautious, and want to steel your nerves, map the terrain. Explore every nook and cranny before moving on, and mark each find as done and dusted.
Let your preparation give you confidence so you can step into the unknown with clear eyes. None of us know the future, but it often helps to remember which path we took to get there.

As part of her turn, she had stormed headlong into a new dungeon. I kept asking her to backtrack, but that was not her style. “No, no, no, just keep going!”
Once we were deep inside the maze, however, we had to backtrack. “Wait, was this the left or the right door? Which one did we come from?” After a few wrong turns, I finally pulled up the map. “Oh, yeah, we’re here.” With the terrain properly mapped, we could move forward once more.
The map is always there. We just have to remember to pull it up. It’s a good thing to do before you start a new quest, but it’s never too late to do it mid-adventure. Just remember to check the map, and you’ll always have a rough idea of where you’re going.
The map is not the territory, but it’s still a useful tool. Use it.

Remembering This.original:
In 2014, I was an intern at BMW M in Munich. I lived in a tiny apartment offered by the company that somehow still cost almost my entire below-minimum-wage salary. I was young, relatively broke, and single.
For the first three months, I had no internet. It was a deliberate choice so I’d go out, get to know the city, and meet people. But that also meant I couldn’t watch the very last episodes of How I Met Your Mother as they were released—and my single-self really needed that inspiration. So every once in a while, I went to a coffee shop, bummed their wifi, and downloaded the latest episode. Then, the introvert and romantic in me could watch it in the quiet comforts of his home whenever all the intern buzz became too much.
In one of those episodes, Ted and the love of his life, Tracy, finally go on their first date. Naturally, it’s awkward. The restaurant they’re supposed to eat at is noisy and has terrible food choices. They bump into Tracy’s ex and hide behind a car. By the time Ted is about to drop Tracy off at home, they both admit they’re probably not ready for a new relationship. But then, right as the thought, “I’ll never see her again,” forms in his head, for some reason, Tracy gives him a kiss. “Unless…do you want to walk around some more? It’s still early.”
Ted agrees and, as Tracy is standing three feet in front of him, holding out her hand, some cosmic intuition hits him. He doesn’t really realize it, but deep down, it clicks: “This is it. So for a moment that feels like an eternity, he just stands there, staring. Until Tracy asks: “What are you doing?” And to that, Ted can only offer the truth: “Remembering this”—because in his soul, he knows this is a once-in-a-lifetime event he will carry with him forever. And just as quickly, Tracy says, “Come on.” They join hands, start walking, and the moment is passed— lost but not gone.
I, too, will forever remember this scene. Not just the 10/10 storytelling from a great TV show, but myself, sitting in that tiny room without internet, watching it play out on screen—still single, still waiting for that special person, and, thanks to How I Met Your Mother, never losing faith that she is out there.
Love is not all we want out of life, but it sure is an image, isn’t it? Someone who holds out their hand to us and says, “Come on! We’ll walk together.” Just so we can stand there and say, “Okay. Yes. Thank you. I’ve waited a long time for this. But first, let me take a second to remember this moment.”
Whether it is love, work, friendship, art, beauty, pain, or inspiration that writes the next climactic scene in the movie of your life, be sure to take it in fully as it happens. Breathe deeply, listen to what your heart is telling you, and whenever the answer is, “This is it,” ask for some extra time to process. And if someone asks you what you’re doing, just tell them the truth: “Remembering this.”

At some point, I noticed a guy who was also alone. He had a drink in his hand, and he was just standing there, looking around. He didn’t seem to be having a good time. I thought: “Wow. This guy has no idea what he’s doing. He’s totally lost.”
But then, as I looked at him more closely, I realized: “Wait a minute. That’s me. I’m looking at myself in a mirror.” I had no idea how long I had been staring at my own reflection, but it was long enough to make some pretty harsh judgments about myself.
I laughed and decided to leave the club. I walked home alone, and on the way, I had a lot of time to think. I realized that, sometimes, it’s easy to forget that we’re all in the same boat. We’re all struggling with something, and we all have our own challenges to face.
It’s easy to look at someone and think, “Wow, that person has no idea what they’re doing.” But the truth is, we’re all just trying our best. We’re all lost sometimes. We all have moments when we feel like we’re not good enough, or that we don’t belong.
But the important thing is to remember that we’re not alone. We’re all in this together, and we all have the power to help each other. We can offer a kind word, a helping hand, or just a smile to someone who needs it.
So, the next time you find yourself judging someone, remember: you’re looking at yourself in a mirror. We’re all lost sometimes, but we’re all in this together. Let’s help each other find our way.

As I was walking to the door, I remembered something else. I remembered that, in 2009, I had taken a trip to London with some friends. One of them had bought a t-shirt at the Hard Rock Cafe. It cost 30 euros. I thought it was crazy. I had said: “I’ll never spend 30 euros on a t-shirt.”
Now, here I was, five years later, about to break that promise to myself. I went back, grabbed the t-shirt, and bought it. I still have it today. I still remember that moment. I’m proud of it.
Remembering this is worth more than $35.

The Silo is a dangerous place. 10,000 people cooped up in a 144-floor concrete pillar at all times, with no access to the outside? That’s a recipe for disaster even on the best of days. But once people start dying under mysterious circumstances, all bets are off.
Like Juliet’s boyfriend, George, who “fell down the stairs.” So when she miraculously gets the opportunity to become the new sheriff in town, of course Juliet agrees. Who wouldn’t want to investigate the murder of a loved one with appropriate resources? But naturally, Juliet soon has more enemies than she’s ever had friends. It’s hard, and for every question she answers, two new ones land on her desk.
One night, she discovers that even George wasn’t 100% straight with her. Talking to one of the few people in her corner, Juliet admits she is ready to call it quits : “I’m gonna turn in the badge and resign.” Her friend being a real one, she asks her if she took the job only for George or “because it was the right thing to do.”
And then, after a short lecture, the kind we all need at times, she leaves Juliet with a truly great piece of advice: “See, I don’t know what happened, but when you left here, love had you trying to do the right thing. And now anger is making you give up? That is a waste of time.”
When the next step feels like your shoes are, like the Silo, made of concrete, think back: Why did you pick this trail? Revenge, grief, anger—there are plenty of bad reasons to begin. But if you ventured out from a place filled with kindness and good intentions, why quit in frustration? Clearly, that’s not the same spirit, and though your mind might be the same, it likely isn’t as clear.
Don’t give up in anger what you started in love. The road only ends where your emotions run out, and most of the time, your last stop should mirror the one where your journey began.

There’s a lot to be said about the Silo, about fear, and about love. But right now, I’d just like to point out that, yes, it’s true: It’s easy to abandon things when we’re angry, even when we began them with the best intentions and the noblest of desires.
It’s easy to quit your job when your boss yells at you. It’s easy to break up with someone when they hurt your feelings. And it’s easy to throw the guitar into the closet when your fingers are sore from pressing strings. But what good will any of that do? What purpose does it ultimately serve?
Sometimes, the easiest thing is also the right thing. Most of the time, however, it is not. Usually, the easiest thing is only a distraction. A quick fix for a problem that requires a long-term solution. An immediate band-aid on a wound that needs to be healed with slow, careful treatment.
Don’t give up in anger what you started in love. Take a break. Cool off. Return to the problem with a clear head, and chances are, you’ll see it’s not as big as it looks. You’ll find a way to move forward. To keep the peace, solve the crime, and, most of all, maintain hope.

Driving a T-Rex.original:
I used to visit a friend’s house after school in the 90s. We played Need for Speed 2 on his computer. Thanks to a bunch of cheat codes, you could turn the game from a challenging car race into a completely ridiculous experience. I distinctly remember driving a T-rex around a Hollywood studios–inspired track at 200+ kilometers per hour. It was insane—but also insanely fun.
After finding the level and car on Youtube, one of the comments on the video stood out to me: “I miss the times when cheats made no sense and actually added a lot of fun to games.” My memory is a good example: I can barely recall any of the cars in the game, let alone the different tracks —but I can remember that T-rex-in-Hollywood experience any day of the week.
Sometimes, the things that make no sense are actually the few things that do. Don’t dismiss the quirky, fun, or seemingly irrelevant. One day, either of those qualities might be the only one that remains.

Because we’re used to it. Because we’re comfortable. Because it’s safe. But sooner or later, we’ll get bored. We’ll feel like we’re stuck in a loop. And then we’ll wonder why we’re not happy.
The truth is, there’s always another game to play. Another challenge to take on. Another adventure to go on. But we have to be willing to let go of the old game. To give up the comfort and safety of what we know. And that’s not easy. But it’s necessary if we want to keep growing.
So when you find yourself driving a T-rex, remember: There’s always another game to play. Don’t be afraid to let go of the old one.

There’s always someone pointing out what’s wrong with any experience, and they’ll do so in public. Often, they’ll get more attention than the people who had a positive experience and want to share it. That’s a shame, because if we only focus on what’s wrong, we’ll miss what’s right—and the right things are usually more important than the wrong ones.
When you see something cool, don’t hold your breath. Tell people. Don’t wait for the moment to pass. Don’t wait for someone else to do it. And don’t wait until you have a better story. You don’t need a funny anecdote. You don’t need a perfectly crafted tweet. You don’t need to be a car expert to say you enjoyed a car game.
When you see someone driving a T-rex, point at it and say: “Look! A T-rex!” You never know who might remember it 20 years later.

Big Waves Take Time.original:
Let’s say you’re starting a job after ten years of self-employment. That’s a big shift. As you look back on a decade of work, you realize what felt like a trip through the jungle was actually baking a layer cake, with many artifacts now remaining. But what will you do with them? All those websites and email signup forms and social profiles.
You could just leave them behind and allow them to catch dust. You could try maintaining it all, but that’s unrealistic. Chances are, you’ll want to curate some for future use, prep others for maintenance mode, and others still you may just delete altogether. But which shall be which, and when will you do all that work now that you’ve got a job?
A change in life seasons can feel like a massive wave coming at you. Before you’re done saying goodbye, you’re already knee-deep in new waters. That’s okay! Life is not a relay race, and even in those the handover can be messy. Switching waves rarely works as neatly as closing one book and opening another.
Whether it’s the old tide going out or the new one coming in, big waves take time. In fact, isn’t the opportunity to surf on them for longer the very best thing about them? But to do so, you must allow them to break slowly. Don’t rush transitions. There’ll be a time and a place for everything, and as long as you’re on the beach, you’re in the right place.

The next day, you realize: “Oh, I can’t just leave my email list alone.” So you start emailing them again. You tell them what you’re up to. You let them know about the new website. You send them a few more things. Maybe you’ll even start a new project. Or a new business. Who knows?
But the point is, you can’t just walk away from ten years of work. Not without feeling like you’ve left something behind. So you keep going. You keep working. You keep baking that layer cake.
And that’s the thing about big waves: They take time. You can’t just catch them and ride them. You have to wait for them. You have to paddle out and sit there. And sometimes, you’ll have to wait a long time. But eventually, the wave will come. And when it does, you’ll be ready.
So don’t give up. Don’t walk away. Keep baking that layer cake. Keep paddling out. And eventually, the big wave will come.

Flick It Again.original:
We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
To wrestle this unwieldy piece of cloth into a square, I take two of the corners, overlay them, and fold it in half. But then I’ve still got a long, if slightly narrower, sheet in front of me. So, to get the corners at the other end to overlay as well, I flick the blanket, and a big wave travels through the comforter. Hopefully, by the time it reaches the end, the two halves of the sheet will line up more closely. Often, they don’t—so I just flick it again.
Sometimes, it takes me three, four tries to get the edges to align, but sooner or later, I always get a layout I can work with. Then, it’s only a matter of lining up the side I’m holding with the other one, folding it over two more times, and voilà! A neatly folded, square cuddle blanket sits on the sofa, ready to open up again at night.
Life forces us through many a coin toss, but most of the time, there’s zero cost to giving the slot machine another spin. Randomness is everywhere, and while it’ll often obstruct your way forward, as soon as you give it another go, it might just as well clear a smooth path for you.
If anything could happen, there’s always reason to expect something good the next time. The only difference between a stony journey and a red carpet might be another coin toss—so whenever your blanket won’t fall into place, make sure you flick it again.

We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
’t fold it perfectly, of course. It’s a blanket, not a piece of origami. But I can fold it enough that it’s not a complete mess. Usually, I’ll have to flick the fabric a few times to get it to sit flat.
The first time I flick it, the blanket doesn’t move much. The second time, it moves a bit more. The third time, it moves a lot. But then, it stops moving. The blanket is in place. It’s ready to be folded again.
In the moment when the blanket stops moving, I can see the next flick coming. I can see myself flicking it again. I can see myself flicking it for the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh time — and I can see the blanket not moving at all. I can see myself wasting my time.
It’s a moment of truth: Do I flick it again? Or do I let it go? Will I take the next step that doesn’t matter? Or will I move on?
It’s a small moment, this flicking of the blanket. But it’s a moment that happens thousands of times. It’s a moment that, if you let it, can become a habit. A pattern. A pattern of doing what’s necessary and no more. A pattern of moving on to what matters. Of not getting stuck in the minutiae. Of doing what’s essential and then calling it a day.
Don’t flick the blanket again. Let it go. Let it be imperfect. And move on to what’s important.

Keep Pecking.original:
I’m sick for the umpteenth time this year. I have to change my travel plans, again. There’s a lot of work to be worked through, and yet once more here I sit, upright in bed, doing what I can but mostly resting and passing the time.
At least it’s a sunny day today. I can see the birds hopping around our garden. And you know what they do? The same thing they always do: pecking at the leaves. Just like I keep pecking at this keyboard—and like you should keep pecking at what’s important to you in this life.
A bird pecks because it wants to eat, but a bird also pecks because it’s a bird. We, too, need to do the former as well as the latter. It matters not whether you peck quickly and often or slowly and sporadically. Sometimes, you’ll be surprised at your own speed. Sometimes, you’ll only peck once for the day.
Regardless of your pace, just keep pecking—and whether it’s the weather, a difficult project, or your body, sooner or later, life will set itself right yet again.

When a woodpecker starts on a tree, it can’t tell you how many pecks it will take. All it knows is that, eventually, it will get to the bottom of it. When we’re sick, we can’t tell how many days it’ll take to get better. But we can keep pecking. Keep resting. Keep drinking tea. Keep watching movies. Keep eating soup. Keep taking our medicine.
In a way, it’s no different from when we’re healthy. We don’t know how many pecks it’ll take to write a book, make a million dollars, or get promoted. All we can do is keep pecking. Keep writing. Keep working. Keep practicing. Keep showing up.
The woodpecker knows that, sooner or later, it will break through. It’s not a question of if but when. So is life. When we’re sick, when we’re healthy, and when we’re sad. Keep pecking, and you’ll get there.

When you’re not at your best, keep pecking. You may not find a big meal, but you’re still part of the game, and you’ll be back in full force soon enough.

An Eternity for a Steppenwolf.original:
A “Steppenwolf” is a kind of wolfhound, half wild animal, half domesticated pet. In Hermann Hesse’s novel of the same name, protagonist Harry claims to be a specimen of this very variety, forever torn between a life outside society’s expectations and the comfort of hiding his lofty ideals in plain sight: among pubs, discussions about politics, and everything else mundane.
During a visit to an old friend’s house, Harry notices an embellished painting of Goethe, whom he adores,  but whose stylized icon he despises. Later, Goethe visits him in a dream only to tease him about his snobby attitude, eventually fading into darkness with “a still and soundless laughter that shook him to the depths with abysmal old-man’s humor.”
Much later in the book, Harry realizes what his dream was really about. It wasn’t an old man laughing at a deeply broken and depressed individual. It was an immortal being pointing the way to inner peace. Here’s my translation attempt from the original German:
“It was without object, this laughter. It was only light, only brightness, was that which remains when a real human has passed through the suffering, the vices, the errors, desires, and misunderstandings of humans and made it to eternity, to space. And eternity was nothing more than the salvation of time, was in a way its return to innocence, its reconversion into space.”
I didn’t really understand Hesse’s words. I don’t think Harry did either. Or that, really, anyone ever will. But I also kind of did, because after witnessing Harry’s story for 200 pages, as for him, Hesse’s imagery gave me a deep sense of peace. “Ahhh, eternity. What a great comfort to know we are but a speck of time in an infinite space. Why get worked up about the petty issues of existence? Why not just laugh about them?” That’s what the passage seems to say.
If you’re reading this blog, chances are, you, too, are a Steppenwolf. There’s the you that goes to work and cleans the sink and pays the bills and does all the things. But there’s also something deep inside, and it keeps scratching, scratching at all the surface-level stuff we call “living,” desperate, hoping, yearning for something more.
I don’t know where that “more” is for you. I don’t know if any of us will ever find it. But I know people like Hermann Hesse, the kind of people who write the kind of books like Der Steppenwolf, they all felt it too, and so when I read those books, I don’t feel alone. I feel connected. Quiet. Seeking yet satisfied. My inner wolf isn’t howling—and perhaps that’s all the eternity a Steppenwolf will ever need.
