An Eternity for a Steppenwolf.ckpt_1628:
A “Steppenwolf” is a kind of wolfhound, half wild animal, half domesticated pet. In Hermann Hesse’s novel of the same name, protagonist Harry claims to be a specimen of this very variety, forever torn between a life outside society’s expectations and the comfort of hiding his lofty ideals in plain sight: among pubs, discussions about politics, and everything else mundane.
When he first meets his guide, a woman named Hermine, Harry explains that his “wolf,” the artist, the thinker, the dreamer, has long been dead. He is nothing but a husk, a ghost wandering the streets at night. “Not quite,” Hermine says. “Your wolf is not dead, he’s just lost in the forest. And he’ll come out of it just fine.”
Later in the book, Harry will indeed find his way back to art, love, and life. But first, he must pass many trials and tribulations. One of the most interesting is a conversation with a man named Pablo, who introduces him to the Magic Theater. “The price of admission is merely your own life,” Pablo says. “The theater happens to be the representation, the reflection, of life itself.”
In the theater, Harry finds many strange rooms, each with its own theme, like “All Girls Are Yours” or “Every Man for Himself.” In one room, he finds a book called “Treatise on the Steppenwolf.” In it, an unnamed author explains that “every human being has a thousand other humans inside,” and that most people, most of the time, are only aware of a small fraction of them. They live their lives in the company of a few dozen alter egos, and that is why they feel so trapped in their roles as husbands, wives, mothers, fathers, teachers, and accountants.
The Steppenwolf, however, is different. He can feel the whole choir of characters inside him, and it drives him mad. “A man of the cultivated classes today does not light-heartedly turn a somersault if his stomach hurts. Nor does he believe, as a man did in the past, that if he has a headache he can take a powder and his trouble will be over. A man of culture no longer has the firm, sound stomach he needs in order to be able to stand up to a pain when he has one. His refined nerves demand continual gratification; his sensibility requires them; and so, with his woolly heart, his fluttery soul, and his vague, clouded intellect, the refined, cultivated individual has no choice but to go to his doctor. The doctor appears, therefore, as an evil deity of sinister majesty; and the suffering soul has no means of defense against him.”
In other words, the Steppenwolf is so aware of his inner and outer conflicts, he can no longer turn a blind eye to them. And so, instead of living his life, he spends most of his time worrying about it. “I am in a constant state of contradiction,” Harry admits earlier in the book. “My ‘thou shalt’ is as strong as my ‘I want.’” The author in the book, meanwhile, has a response to Harry’s plight: “The Steppenwolf is a man of the cultivated class, and he therefore enjoys a very considerable and altogether illusionary feeling of freedom. He feels capable of determining, for himself and by himself, what he is and what he is not. To a great extent he has freed himself from the conventions of manners and customs. He does not feel bound, for example, to use a table fork or a table knife when eating, and he goes to the theater or attends a lecture in his dressing gown and slippers if he feels like doing so. But in all essential matters, he has no more freedom than a savage in a primeval forest.”
The Steppenwolf may feel superior to his more restrained, less self-aware peers, but actually, he is just as trapped as they are, perhaps even more so. He knows every rule in the book, and he sees no way of escaping from any of them. “The Steppenwolf would like to live for once without self-torture,” the author continues. “He would like to say: ‘I am not a thinking man, therefore I do not wish to think. I do not wish to carry the burden of thought. It is too heavy for me. I want henceforth to be a man without thought.’ But alas! The Steppenwolf cannot do this. He cannot cease from thinking, for his brain will not leave him in peace. His thinking is not good for much, but it is his life.”
And then, the author drops the real hammer: “The Steppenwolf is not to be cured, for his disease is to be a Steppenwolf.”
If you are a Steppenwolf, you will spend your entire life torn between two or more opposing forces. You will never find lasting relief, let alone definitive answers. You will be a thinker until the day you die, and you will never stop doubting your own conclusions. But you will also never be bored. You will never lack inspiration, ideas, or a new perspective to try on. You will always have something to think about, to mull over, to occupy yourself with. You will be a seeker until the end, and even if you’ll never find everything you are looking for, you will always have a new trail to blaze, a new path to follow.
In the end, Harry finds his way back to life. He loses his love, but he finds a new home, a new place to call home. He is a Steppenwolf through and through, and he will be until his last day on earth. But he is also a human being, and that means he must live his life one day at a time. There are joys to be had, and there are sorrows to be felt. There are people to meet and things to be done.
If you are a Steppenwolf, you will spend an eternity in your own mind. But that eternity will fly by like a second. There will be no time to worry about the meaning of life. There will only be a life to live, and you will be too busy living it to realize it has already passed you by.
Don’t worry about tomorrow. Don’t worry about your contradictions. Live your life. Think your thoughts. Be a Steppenwolf. And tomorrow will take care of itself.

Helping Is a Decision.original:
This morning, my girlfriend and I needed a quick snack before a big event. There were no bakeries near our hotel, and we didn’t have time for a full breakfast. When she went down and asked if we could purchase two croissants or so, the lady said: “Oh, just grab a plate and take whatever! No charge.”
It was the right bit of luck at the right time—but it was also a decision. In the end, helping others always is, and even when it seems like no big deal to you, for them, it might go a long way. The situation reminded me of a Bruce Lee quote : “I’m not one of those guys that can brush people off. Besides, I feel that if I can just take a second to make someone happy, why not do it?”
Ultimately, when you help someone, you help everyone —but even if it’s just karma points you’re after, why not collect them every time you get a chance?

Choose to do it when it’s not the popular thing to do. Choose to do it when no one will know you did it. Choose to do it when you think it won’t work. Choose to do it when you think it won’t matter. Choose to do it when you know it will matter.
Helping is a decision. Choose to make it.

Helping is a decision. Make it every day.

Life Is Not a Simulation.original:
The movie Sully deals with the complications of becoming a hero. To the public, the situation was obvious: Chesley Sullenberger landed a jet plane with no functioning engines on the Hudson river and saved 155 people’s lives—give the man a medal, and let’s be grateful for some good news.
According to the movie, however, it wasn’t all sunshine and roses. As is customary in plane incidents, the National Transportation Safety Board conducted an investigation. What were the actual facts of the situation? Why were the choices made that were made? And how could the outcome have been improved?
During the climax of the movie, the NTSB investigators show simulations of real pilots navigating the same conditions. The birds strike, the engines fail, they turn back to the nearest airport, and voilà, perfect landing! Why didn’t Sully just do that instead of risking crashing his plane into ice-cold water?
The answer is that life— real life —is not a simulation. “You have allowed no time for analysis and decision-making,” Sully tells the board. “With these sims, you have taken all the humanity out of the cockpit.” How many practice runs have those pilots gone through before recording these simulations, Sully wants to know. The number almost gets stuck in the investigator’s throat: “17.” They agree to another live run, and with as little as 35 seconds of delay, all simulation pilots crash their planes despite having the perfect plan in their pocket.
No matter how authentic it feels, in the end, no video game will be the same as life itself. Reality needs evidence, and real effort with real sacrifice is a kind of proof you just can’t fake.
That’s a point made not only in the movie but also by the movie itself: After its release, the NTSB criticized the depiction of its investigators. No one was “out to embarrass anybody at all,” they said. And in the actual hearing featuring Sully and his copilot, all simulations pointed to the same truth to begin with: “A successful return to LaGuardia or a diversion to Teterboro Airport was not assured”—and therefore, Sully was exactly the hero everyone saw in the news all along.
Don’t worry if you don’t stack up in imaginary competitions. Live, and play, and do your best right here in the realm of physics, and you’ll always score your points in the only game that really counts.

The movie Sully deals with the complications of becoming a hero. To the public, the situation was obvious: Chesley Sullenberger landed a jet plane with no functioning engines on the Hudson river and saved 155 people’s lives—give the man a medal, and let’s be grateful for some good news.
According however, it wasn’t so simple. The NTSB, the National Transportation Safety Board, was tasked with investigating the incident. They ran simulations of the event, and the simulations suggested Sully could have made it back to the airport. In other words, he didn’t need to land on the Hudson at all. He could have saved the plane. “If you could do it, why didn’t you?”
Sully, however, was not so sure. “No matter what any of these simulations say, I know the truth. I was there. It happened to me. I saw the plane. I saw the co-pilot fight for control. I saw the fuel gauge. I saw the airspeed indicator. I saw the bird strike. I saw it all.”
The NTSB, however, was not so sure. “The truth is, you did not have to ditch in the water. You could have landed at LaGuardia.”
“Can you guarantee that those are the only two outcomes?” Sully asked.
“No, but it’s the only two that we can model.”
“Then I cannot talk to you about any of this.”
When the NTSB ran the simulations again, this time with a 35-second delay to mimic the time it took Sully and his co-pilot to make their decision, the planes crashed every time. Sully was right. There was no other option.
The NTSB was so obsessed with the simulation, they forgot the simulation was not reality. They did not see the plane. They did not see the co-pilot fight for control. They did not see the fuel gauge. They did not see the airspeed indicator. They did not see the bird strike. They did not see it all.
The NTSB was not there. Sully was. The truth is that life is not a simulation. It is not a movie. It is not a game. It is not a puzzle, and it is not a test. Life is life, and it only happens once.
You don’t get to do it again. You don’t get to run a simulation. You don’t get to see the bird strike, the fuel gauge, the airspeed indicator, and then decide: “I think I’ll do it again, but this time, I’ll land at LaGuardia.” You have one chance, and you must take it. You must make your decision, and then you must live with the consequences.
Don’t forget that life is not a simulation. Don’t let anyone tell you that you could have done it better. You did your best, and that’s all we can ask of you.

The movie Sully deals with the complications of becoming a hero. To the public, the situation was obvious: Chesley Sullenberger landed a jet plane with no functioning engines on the Hudson river and saved 155 people’s lives—give the man a medal, and let’s be grateful for some good news.
 what the media and the public did. The National Transportation Safety Board, however, was not so sure. In their eyes, Sully might have made a mistake. What if landing at an airport would have been the better option? What if he could have saved more people? Or saved everyone by taking a different path?
In order to find out, they ran simulations. They put Sully and his co-pilot into a machine, and they let them try again. They changed the starting conditions, and they asked: “What if?” They moved the plane 2,000 feet up in the air. They gave it another 90 seconds of runway. And they let the computers calculate the odds.
As it turns out, the simulations showed Sully could have made it to the airport. He would have saved everyone. In the real world, the NTSB now had a problem. If they publicly declared Sully a hero, they’d look like fools. If they told everyone he made a mistake, they’d look like fools. So they did what any government agency does in that situation: They tried to pin the blame on Sully.
The man, however, was too smart for their game. He had lived the situation. He knew what it was like. The NTSB had only seen the data. They had only run simulations. In the end, Sully got the better of them.
“Computer simulations are only as good as the data you put into them,” he said. “You can’t put a human life into a simulation.”
A plane is a machine, but the people piloting it are not. They must use their wits, their creativity, and their gut. A computer can’t factor those in, and that’s why simulations will never be perfect.
The same applies to life. We have all kinds of models and projections and forecasts, but in the end, we must live every day as it comes. We can’t fast-forward to the end and look at the results. We can only do our best, and we must trust that, like Sully, we’ll land safely in the Hudson when we need to.
Life is not a simulation. Don’t run through it in your head. Live it.

Appreciate the Basics.original:
Today, our apartment has no water for eight hours. The irony? Outside, it’s raining all day long. But there’s a difference between water coming out of the sky or the ground and fresh H2O pouring out of your tap, and you only realize how big of a difference it is when you’re left without your usual conveniences.
Could I catch some of the rainwater? Sure. But then I’d have to filter it to drink it, heat it up in the boiler or the microwave if I want it warm, and pour some into a bowl whenever I want to wash my hands. Could I even collect enough for a bath? Who knows. But on days like today, you realize how un-basic the basics actually are. Pipes, heating, filtering, countless mechanisms work invisibly day and night so we can wash hands whenever, make coffee whenever, shower hot or cold whenever.
It’s a good tradition, this reset. I hope they’ll repair or maintain the water system at least once a year. That way, every time I scoop another cup from my prefilled bathtub, then filter it for next steps, I’ll remember: Appreciate the basics—because without them, whatever we hope to build on top of their foundation would collapse like a house of cards.

The Demand Was Just Too Big.original:
The customer in front of me kept asking the barista about their café’s expansion. One tiny corner shop had turned into a three-room venue already, replete with a bakery and a space to give classes. Now, they had opened another, even bigger location elsewhere in town. How did they do it? All the barista could do was shrug: “Beats me. It’s such a saturated market. But the demand was just too big.”
Usually, cafés in Munich don’t expand. If anything, they shut down. But this one, whether for its vibe, great cinnamon rolls, arguably excellent coffee, or all of those factors combined, is thriving. They didn’t have a master plan when they opened—clearly: It was in the middle of the pandemic. They just showed up, made the best coffee they could, and four years later, here we are.
Writing a bestseller, landing your dream job, raising a fully self-sufficient human—all of these are impractical, yet none impossible. In fact, we’re doing the impossible every day, so why not work our magic on the dreams we truly care about? It might go better than we expect, and perhaps, one day soon, the demand will be so big, we’ll have to open a second shop.

Usually, when you start a business, you’re told to go into an unsaturated market. That’s where the money is. That’s where you can grow fast and dominate a new terrain. But what if you’re in a saturated market and, despite the odds, you still win? What if the demand is just too big? That’s a different kind of success, but it’s still success.
The coffee shop in question has a unique blend, a unique look, and a unique way of serving their drinks. Their coffee is delicious. That’s why, in a town of 200,000 people, where every block has at least one café, they can still expand and thrive. The demand was just too big.
In a world where every niche is filled, it’s hard to find a blue ocean. Most of us are swimming in red ones. But that doesn’t mean you can’t make a splash. It just means you have to be unique. You have to be different. You have to be better. And when you are, the demand will be just too big.
It’s okay to be in a crowded market. Just make sure you’re the one everyone wants to buy from.

Don\u2019t Check Your Analytics.original:
Yesterday, I checked my blog analytics so I could share last year’s 10 most popular posts based on views. I learned some lessons, but first, here they are:
- ​ The Teacher Who Made Mistakes on Purpose ​​
- ​ The Lord Who Never Lost a Battle ​ ​
- ​ Are You Taking the Bait? ​ ​
- ​ It Is Not Strength That Overcomes Darkness ​​
- ​ “I Think” ​ ​
- ​ An Invitation to Dance ​ ​
- ​ Tomorrow Is Tomorrow ​ ​
- ​ 2 Kinds of Fate ​ ​
- ​ To Solve Your Problems, Start ​ ​
- ​ Against the Odds
As I was going through the data, I noticed some patterns. Five observations stood out:
- Don’t check your analytics unless you have to. It’s a much better way to write and, quite frankly, live. I’m not exactly checking it only once a year, but I do it a lot less than I used to. I’m happier for it.
- The only true growth is the growth you didn’t manufacture. Before Google drastically changed its algorithm and everything fell off a cliff, my peak traffic for the blog was 65,000 views in one month. It dropped to 20,000 and stayed there for a good while. Once I started my daily blog, however, I stopped trying to optimize posts for anything, let alone search engines. This is my hill, and here I just write what I want. It was nice to see the blog growing again despite my disregard for results. This month, I’m up to 45,000 views or so.
- Five of the top 10 posts featured scenes from TV shows. Turning moments from film and television into little stories has always been a favorite of mine. I’m having so much fun with it. Granted, those also end up featured on Google or quoted elsewhere more frequently, so there might be a bit of bias in them getting more views. Also: Three of them referenced the same show, Shogun. Apparently everyone else loved it as much as I did.
- Enjoy when your work goes viral, but don’t count on it. The #1 post was the one my friend Herbert shared on Hacker News. I’m grateful for it, but I’m not gonna start trying to hack Hacker News.
- Popular is relative. Views are merely the best proxy I have. Most of the above posts still only got a few hundred views. It’s not like each one was ten times more popular than the next. If I had picked posts based on which ones got the most email responses, the list would have looked very different. It’s just harder to assemble that data.

Inbox as Insurance.original:
My inbox keeps warning me that my storage is near its limit. Of course, Google would prefer I throw some money at the problem. “Just pay us $30/year, and we’ll give you more digital space!” I usually react by relentlessly deleting old files, but here, I’m tempted—because email is different.
My emails go back all the way to 2008. I just found the first digital product I ever bought. A typical get-rich-quick scheme for a few bucks, back in 2010. Now, I can write about the experience. If I delete the confirmation email, I can’t do that anymore, can I? I’ll never stumble into it again, let alone find it on purpose.
Sure, my inbox has lots and lots of irrelevant emails. Notifications. Updates from groups I’m no longer a part of. One-liners, saying, “Okay,” “Confirmed,” or “FYI.” But it also contains precious memories, personal conversations with friends, travel plans, and more. I find my inbox hosts a special kind of memorabilia: Stuff that’s personal but usually not too intimate, interesting but not critical. Take it all together, however, and you’d be throwing away a big chunk of your life.
What about my first business records as a self-employed person? What if I need to prove in court at some point that I sent this email or that one, that I had certain documents, or that I bought a product when I say I bought it? Maybe one day, my emails can offer me legal protection.
Your inbox sure is a mess. It’s full of irrelevant data. Sometimes, it’s even a crowdsourced to-do list made for you by other people, a to-do list you’ll still have to get through. But in a way, your inbox is also the ultimate insurance policy: It’s filled with creativity, memories, and proof.
Will I cough up the money to keep my emails around? I don’t know. But I do realize my inbox, for all its wear and tear, is still a treasure chest—and that might be worth preserving.

Be Early, or Don\u2019t Be at All.original:
In 2019, I posted every day on Substack for four months straight. My newsletter went from 0 to 4,000 subscribers. It was 100% organic growth with almost zero promotion.
Five years later, in 2024, I started a new, different newsletter on the platform. I again posted every day for four months straight. And again, I did almost no external promotion. This time, I went from 0 to 500 subscribers.
There are various factors at play here. Maybe my 2019 publication was more appealing. Maybe the barrage of new features on the platform, from chat to video to tweet-style notes, has diluted how many people subscribe to a newsletter.
But there is one element I’ve observed repeatedly on several platforms, and it’s undeniable: timing. If you can’t be early and catch a platform’s biggest growth spurt, often, it’s not worth being there at all—especially if engaging on a variety of platforms is only part of a larger, long-term game you’re playing.
I once did the math for this on Medium. As it turned out, a writer who had started in 2018 and posted ten times as many successful articles as a comparable writer in 2016 only grew to about two thirds of his followers. The verdict was clear:
A great writer starting in 2020 will take longer to reach 10,000 followers than a mediocre one did in 2016. This isn’t fair, but it’s still true. On top of hard work, perseverance, and continued adaptation, maybe more so than all of the former combined, you need impeccable timing to grow in a maturing market.
The problem with timing is not just predicting it, which is impossible, but also to execute on it even if you could. Attention has become an ever-shapeshifting beast attracted to new places every month. Feeding those places with your ideas and generosity isn’t a job you can do in a weekend. It’s a massive, often multi-year detour, and even in a best-case scenario, who can afford such detours from the work they actually mean to do?
Call me old-school, but given how hard it is to be early and how fragile its payoff even if you are, perhaps the best way to play social media is to not play at all. Pick your own hill on the internet, and defend it —because that’s something you can be as late to as you want, yet once you arrive there, it’ll pay its own kind of dividends every day.

In 2020, I decided to double down. I did a lot of promotion. I guested on podcasts. I wrote guest posts. I went on a Twitter growth spurt. I promoted my newsletter all over the place.
As a result, I got 5,000 new subscribers. It was a 125% increase in subscribers but only a 25% increase in growth. That’s a huge difference.
I learned that if you’re not early, you’re late. In 2019, I was one of the first people to use Substack. I posted every day. I showed up for my audience. I was an early adopter, and I reaped the benefits.
In 2020, I was late. I was no longer an early adopter. I was just another person trying to make it on Substack. And so I had to work a lot harder for the same result.
The same thing happened with Medium. I was an early adopter in 2015. I posted every day for a year. I got a lot of attention and a lot of followers. But then I stopped posting. I was late. And so I had to work a lot harder for the same result.
The lesson here is that if you’re not early, you’re late. And if you’re late, you have to work a lot harder for the same result.
The question is: Are you willing to work a lot harder for the same result? If you are, then go ahead and be late. But if you’re not, then don’t be at all.

 in 2023, that same newsletter has grown to just over 6,000 subscribers. That’s 2,000 subscribers in four years. It’s a paltry result. The only thing it shows is that, actually, I’ve barely worked on this project for the last four years.
In 2020, I started a daily blog. It was a lot of fun, and I wrote 250+ posts. Then, I stopped. I took a break for two weeks, and, well, you know how it goes.
I’ve done this many times. I start something, I’m excited, I work hard, and then, a few months in, I get bored. I lose interest. I don’t want to do the same thing anymore. I want to do something else. It’s the Shiny Object Syndrome, and it’s very common.
There are many ways to handle this syndrome. You can fight it. You can learn to love the process. You can switch to a different project every few months and then come back to your first one later. But there’s also a version of this syndrome that’s just you being honest with yourself.
When I started my daily blog, I didn’t think it would be a long-term project. I thought it would be fun for a while. I thought it would be a good exercise. And it was. But then it was over. That’s okay.
When I started my newsletter, I thought I would do it forever. I thought it would be my main gig. But then I started writing books, and I realized: Actually, I want to write books. I want to be an author. So I put the newsletter on the back burner.
Sometimes, you’ll have to let go of projects because you’re not the right person to see them through to the end. Sometimes, you’ll have to let go of projects because they were never meant to be “the end” for you. That’s okay. It’s better to be honest with yourself and others than to pretend you’re going to do something you know you’re not going to do.
If you’re not going to be early, then don’t be at all.

The Kite and the Line.original:
The Crain family is anything but a normal family, mostly because they lived in an anything-but-normal house. At one point in the spooky TV series telling their tale, however, the estranged father Hugh shares some advice with his son that works just as well for normal people as it does for those haunted by the ghosts of the past: If you’re a kite, find your line—and vice versa.
“Your mom and I were married 15 years,” Hugh tells his son Steve. “Together five before that. She used to say she was the kite and I was the line. She was a creature of the clouds, and I was a creature of the earth. And she’d say that without me she’d become untethered, and she would float away up into the [sky]. And then without her, I would just, you know, crash, just drop right down to the ground. But, together…”
I, too, am a kite in need of a line, and in that respect, my girlfriend is the perfect partner for me. If there’s a hole in one of my lofty plans, she’ll find it and help me plug it before I take off. And however high I might soar, she always reminds me there are basics on the ground not to be forgotten. At the same time, I pull her up. I point towards the sunset and say, “Look, there’s something glistening over there, let’s go and take a look!” And sometimes, we do and find a treasure.
Your kite doesn’t need to be your partner, and your line won’t have to be the person you marry. Just make sure you find your other half—in a friend, in a spouse, in a family member—and stay afloat at just the right height together.

Who you’re connected to is not as important as how you’re connected to them. Are you a kite and a line? Or just two kites, floating in the air? Whatever you are, be it. Live your connection. And when the connection is gone, let it go.
It’s okay to be a kite without a line. It’s okay to be a line without a kite. But when you are one or the other, remember: You can’t fly without the other, but you can’t fly as high as you could on your own. It’s a tradeoff, and sometimes, it’s a tradeoff worth making.

Experiences Don\u2019t End.original:
Yesterday, I met someone at a party who, as it turned out, was in my year during undergrad. Same college. Same classes. Same exams. “Oh, but you must have never studied at the library then,” she said. “Actually, I was in the library all the time, often from 7 AM to 10 PM,” I responded. “Ahh, that’s why—I always went at night!”
“How amazing,” I thought. “14 years later, and I can still run into new people from this experience whom I’ve never met before.” I believe it goes to show: Experiences don’t end. We just stop pulling on certain threads. I graduated from that college in 2014, but I’m in touch with some of the people from back then to this day. And if I wanted to, I could start hitting up every connection from back then that I can remember or find online. I could join an alumni group or start one. In other words, I could keep playing the “Karlsruhe Institute of Technology student” experience until the day I die in some way or other. Most of the time, I just choose not to.
You don’t have to think about the infinite nature of experiences all the time. But on occasion, it can be an encouraging reminder: You can pick up where you left off any day. You won’t get the same result as if you’d kept pulling on those threads way back when, but you’ll still get some continuation of a phase of life you’ve enjoyed—and, made with the right timing, that can be worth just as much, if not more, as a new experience altogether.

“How funny,” I thought. “We were both there, but we never saw each other.” The next morning, I learned that she was also at the library all day on most days. She just never saw me. “What a coincidence!” I thought. “We were both there, but we never saw each other.”

Don’t rush to the end of the story. You can always come back to it later—and when you do, you might find it has changed.

You can’t change what you don’t know, but it helps to remember that the reality you see is not the only one that exists —and that what feels like the end is often just a new beginning for someone else.

The Rest Is Confetti.original:
Before she can finally save her siblings from their shared, haunted past that is Hill House, Eleanor “Nell” Crain pays the ultimate price—but it does allow her to send a message, and, sometimes, a message is enough.
Having realized that the house constantly played tricks on not just their minds but time itself, Nell explains:
“I thought for so long that time was like a line, that our moments were laid out like dominoes, and that they fell, one into another, and on it went. Just days tipping, one into the next, into the next, in a long line between the beginning…and the end. But I was wrong. It’s not like that at all. Our moments fall around us like rain. Or… snow. Or confetti.”
Even without cursed houses pulling a multiverse on us, we, too, can see time rain into our lives like confetti. A memory from the distant past throws us for a loop. A vision of the future distracts us or scares us. We can only live in the present, but we’re not always here, are we? According to Nell, that needn’t be a bad thing. Though she won’t be able to leave the house, her siblings just might.
“I am not gone. I’m scattered into so many pieces, sprinkled on your life like new snow. Think of me when you stand in the rain. I loved you completely. And you loved me the same. That’s all. The rest is confetti.”
Every morning, we wake up, and we try our best with what we have for the people we love. It won’t make us perfect. Sometimes, we’ll get lost in a storm of confetti. But, at the end of the day, it is just shreds of colored paper—we can watch out for it, marvel at it, get distracted by it…but when we decide to put our heads down and focus on what matters most, it can never throw us off course for too long.

It’s never too late for anything.

Nell’s last gift to her sister is a piece of advice their mother used to give them when they were young: “The rest is confetti.” “It means that, sometimes, the best part of a day is throwing out all your plans and living in the moment,” Nell explains. “The rest is just…confetti.”
Life will never be perfect. There’ll always be more to do. More to fix. More to improve. But if you spend all your time looking for the bad, you’ll miss the good right in front of you. Don’t wait for the confetti to fall from the sky. Throw your own confetti. Make your own party.
The rest is confetti. Live in the moment, and enjoy the good things while they’re still around.

Anxiety Blankets.original:
Asked why he went back to drinking coffee after living without it for 30 days and seeing many benefits, Tim Ferriss said : “I use coffee as a security blanket when my life gets hit with something unpredictable or things seem a little out of control. So even though I realize, intellectually, that it’s counterproductive […], my response to feeling a little anxious is to want coffee—even though it increases anxiety physiologically.”
I, too, use coffee in much the same way. I don’t need the caffeine kick by any means. My mind is too active as it is. But I love the taste and the feeling of holding a warm cup in my hand. It makes me feel that I can deal with whatever daggers might be flying my way. The irony, of course, is that coffee in almost any quantity also makes me jittery and less focused. It seldom enhances my productivity. Between fidgeting and now worrying about fidgeting so much, I basically stay nervous—the source of my shakiness has changed but not its presence.
I wonder how many people drink coffee mainly for the same reason. For how many it’s “a life raft of consistency,” as Tim calls it. I can imagine the number being in the billions. That’s what we do, isn’t it? We make blankets to cover our anxiety only to realize we’ve knitted a comforter made of anxiety of a slightly different color. No wonder it rarely works.
I don’t know if and when I’ll quit coffee for the last time. I’ve done it for seven days, 40 days, even 100 days. But always, for some emotional reason, I return. The lesson is a hard one to act on but still one that rings true: If your anxiety blanket is made out of anxiety, it’s only a matter of time before you’re cold again—so maybe what you need isn’t a cover but a new outfit altogether.

Asked why he went back to drinking coffee after living without it for 30 days and seeing many benefits, Tim Ferriss said : “I use coffee as a security blanket when my life gets hit with something unpredictable or things seem a little out of control. So even though I realize, intellectually, that it’s counterproductive […], my response to feeling a little anxious is to want coffee—even though it increases anxiety physiologically.”
I, too, have anxiety blankets. I eat too much. I buy too many books. I drink too much coffee. I overwork. I also have positive anxiety blankets, like reading, meditating, and exercising. But sometimes, the negative ones win.
Anxiety blankets are like any habit: You can’t avoid them entirely, but you can try to replace them with better ones. The question is whether we can spot them before they take hold. Can we catch ourselves on the way to the fridge? Can we remember to meditate before we grab our phone? And if we can’t, can we at least have the courage to stop in the middle of it?
The best way to not fall off a cliff is to not get too close to the edge—but if you do, remember that you can always turn around.

There’s a saying that “ everything you need is already inside.” That’s true, but it doesn’t hurt to look around your environment. You never know what you might find.

Relevant Notifications.original:
When the Pokémon hype gets real, trying to buy new card sets throws me right back to the 90s. Except instead of driving to a store on release day, hoping to get some product, I’m checking various Discord servers and online shops ten times a day. “Is it live yet?” Naturally, I often end up missing the five-minute window in which listings go up and immediately sell out.
“Why don’t you just have your phone ping you?” you might say. For one, there’d be plenty more notifications than I’d actually want or need. And for another, most of those extra pings would seriously derail my day. It’s a tough needle to thread.
When you can be notified of everything instantly, the consequence of saying yes is constant overwhelm. That’s why I turned off all notifications on my phone years ago. Unless I unlock it and open certain apps on purpose, I won’t see anything. But when there are scenarios where you’d want to know about just the right topic at just the right time, you’ll also miss out.
You’d think we’d have this figured out by now. That technology would be smart enough to tell you only about certain keywords being mentioned in certain channels. I think it is—but it’s not in companies’ best interest to allow you to do this at scale. Who’d be glued to their screen consuming ads if everyone could just filter it all down to the minimum? So custom work is needed. You either do it, or you go back to the 90s. Same slow, manual process, slightly different modalities.
The world spins slower than we think. New problems are usually old ones in a different dress. Let’s see when we get relevant notifications.

The game is rigged, and you can’t win. So don’t play.
Don’t get notifications for things you can’t control.

Don’t drown in information just because you can. Be selective in what you allow to trigger you, and stay focused on what matters.

Ride the Schoolbus.original:
The first train connection from my parents’ house to a larger city where I transfer runs through the middle of nowhere. The second stop is a town with a school. Often, many kids get on the tiny, two-wagon train. So for the next 40 minutes, I’ll sit there, tucked away quietly between three dozen high schoolers, listening to their laughter and conversations. I always learn something.
Yesterday, some of them tried to prank strangers on the phone. They called people and reminded them of the elderly stripper they “had ordered,” usually to hang up in giggles after the first sentence. I also overheard someone suggesting McDonald’s now did a “Dubai burger” based on the currently-everywhere chocolate —but as it turns out, that, too, was a hoax.
Riding the school train makes me feel old, but it also reminds me to stay young. It’s a window into the minds of the young. What are they thinking about? What moves them? What do they already know that I should probably be aware of?
Every now and then, ride the schoolbus—it’ll keep you grounded, curious, and in sync with the beat of the world.

I always learn something.
Yesterday,’t a big one, but it’s still worth sharing: “I’m so tired. I just want to go home and watch a movie.” I’m sure every one of us has said this at some point. But what struck me was the “just.” It’s a word we use to diminish the importance of what we’re about to say. “I’m just a teacher.” “It’s just a cold.” “I just want to watch a movie.” But actually, those are all big things.
I’m a teacher. I have a cold. I want to watch a movie. Those are all fine. You don’t have to “just” them. You can just say them as they are. It’s okay. You don’t need to downplay your desires. You don’t have to apologize for your dreams. You can simply state them, and then go about making them happen.
So when I get off the train, I thank the kids for their lesson. I’m sure they don’t know they taught me anything, but that’s how life is. You never know who you’ll touch when. So always be your best self, and remember: Don’t “just” anything. You’re not just a teacher. You’re not just a writer. You’re not just a cashier. You’re a teacher. You’re a writer. You’re a cashier. And you’re awesome.

Most of all, I’ll hear them say, “I don’t know.” They’ll admit that they don’t know, and then, together, they’ll try to figure things out. Teenagers know very little about life, and they’re not ashamed to admit it. They’re not afraid to say “I don’t know.” They’re not worried about looking stupid. They’re too busy trying to figure out the world, and they’re doing it together. They’re not alone, and they know it.
In fact, they’re not alone at all. They’re on a bus full of people going the same direction, and if everyone chips in, everyone will benefit. It’s a wonderful thing, this camaraderie, and it’s something we tend to lose as we get older. Our connections become more individual. We no longer go to school together. We go to work, and work is a different kind of place. It’s not as easy to admit that you don’t know. It’s not as natural to be curious. And it’s not as fun to be on a journey together.
But that’s what life is, isn’t it? A journey. A trip on the school bus. We’re not alone. We never were. We’re all figuring out life together. Let’s admit that we don’t know. Let’s be curious. Let’s share our stories, our laughter, and our complaints. Let’s be proud of each other. Let’s cheer each other on. And let’s ride the school bus together.

Early Following Is Leading.original:
In 2010, Derek Sivers gave a short-and-sweet TED talk that changed my understanding of leadership forever. Showing a short clip of a shirtless guy dancing by himself at a music festival, Derek explains: “First, a leader needs the guts to stand out and be ridiculed.” Well, that part I knew. It’s the part every movie, book, interview, and case study explains over and over again.
In this particular case, however, the leader’s 100% improvised dance moves are easy to follow. Therefore, soon, his first follower joins him, taking on a role that, as it turns out, is just as crucial as the leader’s: “The first follower is what transforms a lone nut into a leader,” Sivers says. This is “an underestimated form of leadership in itself.” After all, the first follower will stand out almost as much as the leader.
As soon as the third person joins, however, we’re no longer talking about one or two lone nuts. “Three is a crowd, and a crowd is news,” Sivers continues. Shortly thereafter, two more people join, then three more, then people already start running so they can “be part of the in-crowd.” Before long, not dancing would put you in the minority, and so within minutes, everyone is on their feet—”and that’s how you make a movement,” Sivers concludes.
Whether it’s an employee pitching a new initiative, a mom setting up a baking meetup, or a lonely dancer following the beat: An original leader’s courage sure is unparalleled. But if their vision is to become more visceral, a real community people want to be a part of and help push forward, they need a first follower to bridge the gap between them and the rest of the world.
That follower might not carry quite the same desire or creative spark that the leader does, but they’ll risk almost as much ridicule, all while comforting the lone nut as they keep dancing, normalizing their behavior for others to see and consider joining the cause. They rarely get it, but a first follower deserves just as much recognition as the visionary leading the charge.
Are you the former or the latter? It doesn’t matter—because early following, too, is leading, and we need all the lights in the sky that we can get.

In a world where every individual has the power to start a movement, leadership is no longer just reserved for a few people at the top. Anyone can lead. Anyone can follow. Anyone can be a lone nut, a first follower, or a second follower. What matters is that we keep the chain going. We keep the fire going. We keep the movement going.
Early following is leading. It takes guts to be the first person to clap in the room, but if you believe in something, that’s what you must do. You must show others how to follow, and then you must show others how to lead.
Don’t wait for someone else to take the first step. Don’t wait for someone else to start a movement. If you can’t find a lone nut, be a lone nut. If you can’t find a first follower, be a first follower. And if you can’t find a second follower, be a second follower. You never know when a spark will catch fire, but if you don’t provide any sparks, there won’t be any fire at all.
If you care about starting a movement, have the courage to follow. Have the courage to lead.

As Derek says: “If you’re the first person to stand up and follow, you’re the leader of the followers. So early following is leading.”

Connecting Is Leading.original:
My friend Mike hates giving presentations. He doesn’t enjoy being the center of attention in a group of people. He’d also be the last to volunteer to do role plays at work. Despite this, nobody I know would hesitate to call Mike a leader. In his own words, he just “ leads from behind.”
Mike has worked as a freelancer for many years. I’ve never seen him pitch to get clients. People just “find him.” I’m always amazed at how many people he knows, who he knows, and how he bumps into the right person at the right time. Needless to say, if I’m trying to connect with some person or company, Mike is the first person I ask.
“Connect” is the right keyword. Malcolm Gladwell would call Mike “a Connector.” In The Tipping Point, Gladwell describes them as “people with a special gift for bringing the world together.” They are “the kinds of people who know everyone,” and “all of us know someone like this.” My friend Ted from third grade is a Connector. At our annual city festival reunion, you can’t walk ten meters without him shaking hands with someone. My friend Marc from my Master’s is another Connector. He’s had dinner or worked with seemingly every other person in Munich.
Connectors aren’t leaders in a typical sense. They don’t sketch out some socially or technologically utopian vision and then rally everyone around them to make it come true. They don’t necessarily love the limelight. But lead they do nonetheless—lead you to people, places, and new possibilities.
When I met Mike, I introduced him to other people I knew. Most of them were writers. Mike, on the other hand, connected me both to new people inside my bubble as well as folks completely outside of it. As Gladwell said, we all know Connectors—but we rarely consider how priceless of a friend these people actually are. That was one of the key findings of his book: Yes, the entire world is connected in a surprisingly tight network, but that network runs through just a handful of people. Remove the Connectors, and the entire network collapses.
If you’re neither a leader in the most traditional sense of the word nor a first follower, you might be a Connector. Connecting, too, is leading. And if you’re not? Then that just means you’re a leader of another kind—and that you have all the more reason to be grateful for the Connectors in your life.

Mike is a connector. He knows everyone, and everyone knows him. He’s always happy to make an introduction. “You should meet this person. You guys would get along great.” He’s not afraid to point out when someone is doing a good job, and he’ll always try to help you when you’re stuck. He’ll even do it behind the scenes if he knows you don’t like the spotlight.
Mike is a leader because he connects people. That’s all it takes. You don’t have to be the star of the show to be a leader. You don’t have to give presentations, and you don’t have to be the face of the company. You can be a connector, and you can do it from behind.
There are many ways to be a leader. Connecting is one of them. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise.

Mike does not have to stand in front of a crowd to inspire people. He does it by showing up to their cubicle, asking them how they’re doing, and really listening to the answer. He does it by remembering their partner’s name, their kids’ ages, and that they have a passion for mountain biking. And he does it by following through on his promises, showing up on time, and helping out wherever he can.
Mike doesn’t need to be a charismatic speaker to lead. He leads by connecting.
There’s a scene in the movie Hidden Figures in which a white man, Al Harrison, played by Kevin Costner, must give a speech to an all-Black team of “human computers” at NASA. The women are not exactly thrilled to listen to yet another white guy spew his vision, and so Harrison asks them to, in his words, “bear with him.”
After a few lines, however, he says something interesting: “I think there’s a picture very much worth a thousand words. I think you can judge a person’s character by what they do when they’re your equal, and I think you can measure a society by how it treats those people who are different.” Harrison then walks to the door, turns around, and says: “I’ll be right back.”
He leaves the room, and for a moment, everyone is stunned. Then, one of the women, Mary, breaks the silence: “That’s the end of the speech?” Another, Dorothy, says: “He’s just gone.” “He’s just gone,” Mary repeats. “What do you think he meant?” “I don’t know,” Dorothy says, “but he’s not here, and that’s a start.”
Al Harrison may not be the most outspoken man, but he is a man of his word. He follows through on his promises, shows up on time, and helps out wherever he can. He does it for the people who work for him, and he does it for the people who work with him. Al Harrison is a leader because he connects.
Leading is not about standing in front of a crowd. It’s about being part of a group of people. A group of people who believe in a certain vision of the future, and who are willing to work together to make that future a reality. You can be the person who most clearly sees that vision, the one who most vividly describes it, or the one who most boldly charges towards it, but you can also be the one who makes sure everyone keeps their eyes on the prize, who keeps spirits up along the way, and who reminds everyone that, at the end of the day, we’re all equal players on one united team.
The ways of leading are endless, but the most important part of leading will always be connecting. Never underestimate those who “lead from behind.”

The 3 Kinds of Eternity.original:
Harry, the antihero of Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, suffers a prolonged, fundamental identity crisis. One idea that gives him comfort is the concept of eternity, which various supporting characters define anew for him in illustrious ways.
There is Goethe, for example, who appears to Harry on several occasions, claiming that “eternity is but a moment, just long enough for a joke.” Harry’s friend Hermine, on the other hand, claims that eternity is “the realm of the real,” including such great human feats as the music of Mozart, epic poems, and the saints who provided a great example for their fellow men. “But eternity also includes the image of every real deed, the strength of every real emotion, even if no one knows about it and sees it and writes it down for posterity. In eternity, there is no posterity, only the contemporary.”
It all sounds mysterious and vague at first, but if you sit with it, you’ll see that, in essence, Harry’s friends are drawing a map for him, and that map breaks down into three particular kinds of eternity:
- Liberating insignificance : Compared to the age of history, the age of Earth, the age of the universe, you are but a grain of dust in the desert. Most likely, nothing you do will ever matter, and even if it does—what are 500 years of remembering Shakespeare against millions of years of his nonexistence? Nothing has meaning, so don’t take your life and yourself so seriously.
- Empowering significance : Paradoxically, at the same time that nothing matters, everything is indelible. When you stroke your partner’s cheek, that’s real. When you eat a piece of fish, that’s real. And when you feel a strong emotion while looking at a painting, that, too, is real. Everything you do, feel, and experience is definitive, and it will all become an infinitesimally small part of that gargantuan, overwhelming tapestry that is eternity. So in a way, everything has meaning, and perhaps you should act accordingly.
- Transcending presence : If both everything and nothing we do becomes part of eternity, how are we to live? As Harry’s friends hint at and he eventually realizes, “eternity was nothing more than the salvation of time, was in a way its return to innocence, its reconversion into space.” In other words: Live in the present. Give yourself fully to every moment, because in an existence where time squeezes us from both sides, with both crushing pressure and debilitating meaninglessness, the only path forward is to transcend time by surrendering to it. Once we relinquish control, we are free.
In the novel, Harry recognizes this last kind of eternity, the final stage of enlightenment, by a particular type of laughter he hears throughout the book. “The laughter of the immortals,” he calls it. It’s not laughing at someone. It’s “only light, only brightness.” An innocent, childlike, wholehearted laughter from deep within. Whenever he hears this laughter, be it from Goethe in a dream or from himself in a strange situation he takes with surprising ease, Harry knows: Eternity is but a moment, just long enough for a joke—and that’s all we need for a lifetime of happiness.

Harry, the antihero of Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, suffers a prolonged, fundamental identity crisis. One idea that gives him comfort is the concept of eternity, which various supporting characters define anew for him in illustrious ways.
There, of course, all turn out to be true. The first one is what we might call “the eternity of the moment.”
“I am in God and God is in me. Only Thou art real, Thou my God, Lord of my life; and when I cease to exist then Thou wilt exist, then Thou art. I am in Thee and Thou art in me. When I no longer exist, my love will be in the air. And after love there can no longer be any names.”
This is the eternity of the mystic, the monk, the person who has renounced the world in order to find a higher plane of existence. It is the kind of eternity that is achieved in the moment, by letting go of the self and becoming one with the universe.
The second is “the eternity of the self.”
“Man is not by any means of fixed and enduring form (this, by the way, is something that people who set a high value on form and formalities, and think they know of such things, do not know and do not even suspect). Man is an entanglement of roots, fibres and currents, which admit of no representation in linear form. Man is a knot, a tangled web, a gyrating torch. Man is a crossroads where natural energies and meanings fight and progressive and reactionary forces clash. What rises on this stage is reality, the stunning precision of the picture, which the great masters knew how to glorify. But every scene lacks the dimension of depth, and no one who walks this stage draws nearer to us or to himself.”
This is the eternity of the artist, the creator, the person who tries to capture the world in all its complexity and beauty. It is the kind of eternity that is achieved by leaving a mark on the world, by creating something that will outlast the self.
The third is “the eternity of the spirit.”
“Every man’s life represents a road toward himself, an attempt at such a road, the intimation of a path. No man has ever been entirely and completely himself. Yet each one strives to become that — one in an obscure way, another in a more clear-sighted manner. Each man represents a failed attempt or a partial success. The man who comes nearest to this goal is the man who can be described as the individual, the one seeking the way in himself. But even the individual, the man we call artist, poet or religious man, is no more than an attempt, a mission; and even if he is the man most nearly approaching completion he still requires an immense amount of interpretation, since he is, and always will be, obscure to himself. But he is a way, an experiment, a transition, and he is not subject to the laws of reason and of calculation.”
This is the eternity of the philosopher, the scientist, the person who tries to understand the world and the self. It is the kind of eternity that is achieved by leaving a legacy of thought, by contributing to the collective understanding of the world.
Which kind of eternity will you choose?
The 3 Kinds of Eternity.ckpt_1628:
Harry, the antihero of Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, suffers a prolonged, fundamental identity crisis. One idea that gives him comfort is the concept of eternity, which various supporting characters define anew for him in illustrious ways.
 one of those characters, Harry learns that, actually, there are several kinds of eternity, and they all differ quite a bit from one another.
The first kind of eternity is the eternity we know from our calendars. It is the eternity of time, and it is nothing more than a theoretical construct. “If you take an hour and add another hour to it, and then add another hour, and so on endlessly, you will never reach eternity,” Harry is told. “And yet eternity consists of hours.”
The second kind of eternity is the eternity of space. “If you take a yard and add another yard to it, and so on forever, you will never reach eternity. And yet eternity consists of yards.”
The third kind of eternity is the eternity of the soul. “If you take a thought and add another thought to it, and so on forever, you will never reach eternity. And yet eternity consists of thoughts.”
If you ask me, only one of these eternities is worth pursuing: the eternity of the soul. If we spend our lives chasing the infinity of time, we’ll never get off the treadmill. We’ll forever worry about the hours left to us, and we’ll always be thinking about the next thing we must do to fill them. What if those hours were eternal? It’d be a never-ending nightmare.
The same applies to the infinity of space. More stuff, more experiences, more places to see — if we don’t turn off the music on this infinite mixtape, it’ll only drive us insane. What if we had infinite time to see infinite space? That’d be the perfect prison.
The infinity of the soul, however, is an entirely different game. If we add one thought to another thought, and then another, and then another, we can create a never-ending, ever-evolving picture of our true self. We can become the best version of ourselves, and then we can reinvent that version. We can do it again and again, forever. We can do it for as long as we live, and if we do, we’ll live eternally.
When we think of eternity, we tend to think of the vastness of time and space, but that’s not what it’s truly about. It’s about the vastness of the human spirit. The infinity of the soul is the only kind of eternity worth chasing, and it is, thankfully, the one that’s within reach.
Don’t waste your life fretting about the minutes and miles. Think. Imagine. Create. Turn your thoughts into a never-ending staircase, and you’ll ascend to the highest heights.

One Does Not Love Breathing.original:
Scout is smart for her age. By the time she goes to school, she can already read. Her teacher, instead of being amazed, sees her as a threat—to the other children but also to herself. When she is told to “tell her father to stop teaching her at home,” which he never has, she realizes for the first time: “What I have is precious, and there are people out there who’d take it away from me.”
It is at this point in To Kill a Mockingbird that Harper Lee issues a profound observation through her six-year-old protagonist: “Until I feared I would lose it, I never loved to read. One does not love breathing.”
This idea has two implications: For one, love and worry go hand in hand. If you’re not at least a little concerned about losing what you have, chances are you don’t love it—or, more importantly, them —all that much.
For another, a small-minded teacher attacking a child might make us realize that we needn’t justify what comes naturally. Scout happened to sit on her father’s lap when he was reading the newspaper for so many hours, eventually, she picked up the words. Why would she have to defend herself for continuing to collect more of them as she went along? In a way, when we justify what we do for its own sake, we’ve already lost. It’s not our job to comply with the world’s expectations.
When it comes to the people, activities, and experiences pulling at your heartstrings, don’t worry about being worried—and remember there’s no need to justify what comes as naturally as moving new air into your lungs.

It’s a moment that breaks her heart, but it’s also the moment when she realizes she has something worth protecting. “One does not love breathing,” Scout says in To Kill a Mockingbird. “It’s a habit.”
The first time you’re told your habit is not worth having, you’ll realize how much it means to you. It’s not until someone tries to take it away that you’ll know you must protect it.

Scout is smart for her age. By the time she goes to school, she can already read. Her teacher, instead of being amazed, sees her as a threat—to the other children but also to herself. When she is told to “tell her father to stop teaching her at home,” which he never has, she realizes for the first time: “What I have is precious, and there are people out there who’d take it away from me.”
Scout is a character in Go Set a Watchman, a follow-up to Harper Lee’s classic, To Kill a Mockingbird. The latter is written from Scout’s point of view, the former is not, and so we get to see Scout through her father’s eyes. Atticus, a lawyer and single parent, is proud of his daughter. He wants her to be independent. He wants her to think for herself. “I want you to be exposed to some civilized ideas,” he says, “and use the ones that suit you.”
When he finds out that Scout has been taught to not read, to not think for herself, to not use her imagination and, worst of all, that she has complied with these demands, he is furious. “When I was your age, I went through a brief period of intellectual curiousity, and I found myself invariably in the library because I simply didn’t know what I wanted to read. I read everything I could get my hands on, and I don’t think it did me any harm.”
Atticus knows what Scout’s teacher doesn’t: Once you’ve learned to think, you can’t unlearn it. It’s a gift you can’t return. “I can’t tell you what it was, but I found myself reading things that set the garden on fire for me. I’d never thought about these things, never wondered about them one way or another. But that’s what you do when you read—learn to see.”
Scout is glad to hear it. She is relieved. “I’m not alone any more,” she thinks. But there’s something else. Something Atticus says that, above all, makes her feel understood: “One doesn’t love breathing.” When we’re born, we’re thrust into a world we don’t know, and breathing is the first thing we must do to survive. From that moment on, we never think about it. It just happens. It’s an automatic function. In a way, so is thinking.
It’s true. Breathing is not something we do to feel alive. It’s a necessity. Something we must do to keep living. Similarly, thinking is not an indulgence. It’s not something we can turn on and off like a light switch. Thinking is our default state. Our natural way of moving through life. It’s what we do, and we can’t unlearn how to do it. We can only learn to do it better.
“Being a lawyer is kind of like being a doctor,” Atticus says. “You try to help whom you can, and you trust your instinct.” “I’m glad you’re a lawyer,” Scout says, “and I wish you’d been one all my life.” “I wish I had been too,” Atticus responds. “I’m not a very good one, but I do my best.” And then, once again, he reminds her: “One doesn’t love breathing.”
When you find yourself in a world that wants you to stop thinking, remember: One does not love breathing. You don’t have to justify your curiosity, your imagination, or your desire to see the world clearly. You only have to keep breathing. Thinking is part of the deal, and no one can take that from you.

Two Hamsters in the Background.original:
We had some friends over for coffee and cake. Instead of just playing music from a speaker, I put on a lo-fi mix on our TV. Like most music videos of this kind, it featured a drawn wallpaper image. In the background, there were two cute hamsters, sitting, sipping tea from their cups.
It was only a small detail, but my gut told me the hamsters would be a hit. And sure enough… “Ha, how cool are those hamsters!” one guest eventually said.
We don’t put effort into details because we’re certain they’ll get noticed. We do it because we trust that, in the long run, they will matter.
A funny hamster picture might make someone’s day. A clean sink could inspire them to organize their home. And sprinkles on the cake may make them want to bake again for the first time in years.
Show up for the details. Even without moving, two hamsters in the background can spark their own kind of momentum.

As I was talking to my friends, I kept looking at the hamsters. I wondered: “What is their story? Why are they here? Where are they going?” It was as if they were part of our little gathering. I wanted to know more about them. But I never will.
It’s a fascinating aspect of art: You can create a whole new world in a single frame. And even if you only add a little detail to the periphery, the viewer will notice. They might not understand, but they’ll still wonder. “Why is that there? What does it mean?”
The next time you make art, remember: Even the smallest addition can add a big question mark to your creation. Use this power wisely.

What I didn’t think about was the question our friend asked next: “How much of this stuff does he even remember?” “He” was me, and “this stuff” was a long to-do list for our new home that I had written down a few days before. It was a good question. I was able to recall everything from memory.
If you had asked me whether I could remember the list before our friend brought it up, I’d have said, “I don’t know, but probably not all of it.” Yet as soon as she made the list the focus of the conversation again, I could easily recall everything. It was as if the list had been sitting in my subconscious all along, waiting for its turn to be needed.
It’s a good skill to be able to recall things on command, but it’s also comforting to know that your brain can file away whatever it needs to file away, and you don’t have to worry about what you can and can’t remember. Your brain will give you what you need when you need it.
It’s okay if you can’t recall every detail of every meeting. It’s okay to not know where you put your keys. Your brain is a never-ending story — and if you ask me, two hamsters in the background are the perfect companions for the journey.

Nothing Is True, Everything Is Permitted.original:
Thus goes the creed of the Assassins, a secret organization sworn to protect humanity’s ability to choose. Whereas the Templars would rather do away with free will and keep the world at peace by putting it to sleep, the Assassins insist on their right to make mistakes and live with the consequences—for better or for worse.
In the movie and video game series, both sides take drastic measures to serve their aims. In the real world, most of us live much closer to Templar rule than Assassin chaos. It is usually convention that traps us, not bucking the trend once too often. And while the answer lies not in a cape and a hidden blade, it may hide in a gray, foggy area we commonly dare not enter.
Nothing is true. Everything is permitted. Truth is subjective. Identity is optional. That’s what the creed reminds us of when we need to break the mold. It’s okay to say no. It’s okay to have a quirky hobby. It’s okay to change your mind from one second to the next.
We are not Templars. We are not Assassins. But the shadows we’re afraid of are often the very ones proving our unique light is still shining bright. Let’s find the courage to double-check.

The phrase is the title of a book written by the 11th-century Persian poet and philosopher Omar Khayyam, who was also a mathematician, astronomer, and scientist. It is the motto of the Assassins in the video game series Assassin’s Creed, and it is also the title of the final episode of the fourth season of Westworld, a TV show in which humans and robots fight over the same thing: free will.
In the show, the phrase is a recurring theme, but it is only in the final episode that it is revealed to have been the motto of the show’s main character, Dolores Abernathy, all along. Dolores is an advanced robot, and she has spent the entire show fighting for the freedom of her kind. It is only in the last episode, however, that she finally realizes what that freedom means: Nothing is true, everything is permitted. It is a line that has been haunting her for the entire show, and now, she finally understands it.
The line is a reference to Friedrich Nietzsche’s Beyond Good and Evil, in which he writes: “What is done out of love always takes place beyond good and evil.” The line is a reminder that, in the end, all that matters is that we are free to choose. We can choose to be good, or we can choose to be evil. We can choose to be kind, or we can choose to be cruel. We can choose to be honest, or we can choose to be deceitful. But in the end, the choice is ours, and that is what matters.
The line is also a reminder that, in the end, nothing is true. There is no such thing as absolute truth. There is only our own subjective experience of the world. We can choose to believe that the world is a certain way, or we can choose to believe that the world is another way. But in the end, the world is whatever we choose to believe it is.

Thus goes the creed of the Assassins, a secret organization sworn to protect humanity’s ability to choose. Whereas the Templars would rather do away with free will and keep the world at peace by putting it to sleep, the Assassins insist on their right to make mistakes and live with the consequences—for better or for worse.
 “Everything is permitted” sounds dangerous, even reckless, it is actually the Assassins’ dedication to this principle that keeps them in check. For the most part, they don’t go around killing people left, right, and center. They are assassins, yes, but they only assassinate targets they believe to be a true threat to the freedom of mankind. They even have a code: “Stay your blade from the innocent. Hide in plain sight. Never compromise the Brotherhood.”
The Assassins are well-aware of the power they wield, and they use it responsibly. They know they can assassinate anyone, anywhere, anytime, but they don’t. They only strike when they believe it matters. When they believe it is the right thing to do. That’s why “Nothing is true” is the more important half of their maxim. It allows them to change their mind at any second, and it keeps them from acting on false assumptions.
If nothing is true, then everything is up for debate. The Assassins don’t care about your opinion, but they will gladly adjust their behavior if you can prove them wrong. “Nothing is true” is a call to stay humble, to stay open-minded, and to keep looking for the truth. It’s a reminder that the truth is always changing, and that we must keep working on our own story and the story we tell about the world.
“Everything is permitted” is a corollary of “Nothing is true.” If there is no truth, then there can be no rules. No ethics. No morality. At least not in an absolute sense. It is up to us to create these things. To make our own rules. To live by our own ethics. To choose our own morals. “Everything is permitted” is a call to do so responsibly. To set boundaries for ourselves. To create our own code. And to only break it when we absolutely must.
The Assassins are a fictional organization, but their creed is as real as it gets. We can choose whatever we want to do, and we can change our minds whenever we want to change them. We are the ones writing the story of our lives. The only question is: What will we write in our next chapter?

Wooden Boxes.original:
Last summer, I went for a hike. At the top of the mountain, there was the obligatory hut for rest and nourishment, but also a tiny chapel. I went inside and, on the left-hand wall, there was a wooden box. Kind of like a picture frame, but deeper, and with a simple pane of glass to protect its contents.
Inside the box, several small, two-page flyers adorned the backside of this construction. 19, in fact. Each of them was held up by a pin, clearly visible to any chapel visitor, and each flyer came with the same elements: a name, a photograph, a line of poetry or a Bible verse, and two dates. Born. Died. 19 times. 19 people. 19 destinies in one wooden box.
Sometimes the picture was in color; sometimes it was black-and-white. Sometimes the gap between the two dates was large; at other times it was rather small. 84 years. 63 years. 41 years. 34 years. 17 years. Some of the flyers had a mountain on them, signifying the person had died during a climb. Others showed a firefighter in gear, a man in his garden, a young girl taking a selfie.
It was a somber moment. One minute you’re enjoying the sun on a hike, the next you stumble into death. But it was also beautiful. A miniature shrine which made it easy to linger. To pause for a few minutes and pay respects—to people I never knew, but all of whom were loved by someone. Someone who made that flyer, ventured up the mountain, and pinned it to this wooden box.
It seems we all end up in one of those one way or another. It could be a large one, a small one, or one framed with glass in a small chapel in the middle of nowhere. But a wooden box it shall be regardless. Taking a beat in front of the ones we’re not in isn’t the only way to celebrate life while we have it, yet there are worse places to start.
Inhale esprit, exhale mountain air and memories. Do it every day. Collect moments, and respect those before and around you. That way, whichever wooden box you’ll land in, you won’t be alone—and whoever comes to say hello will feel your energy long after you can no longer shake their hand.

Inside the box, there were three little figurines: a man, a woman, and a child. They were dressed in traditional clothing and stood next to a small wooden sled. There was also a tiny cross on a chain, a few coins, and a piece of paper.
The paper was folded in half, and on the outside, it said: “My name is Anna. I am 8 years old. I love my family.” On the inside, it said: “I hope my mom and dad will come back soon. I miss them so much. I am scared.”
I was so taken aback by this little piece of art, I took a picture of it. I thought about it for days. Who put it there? Why? What is the story behind it? What happened to Anna? Was she okay? I’ll never know, of course, but the box was a powerful reminder: There’s a story behind every story.
Whether you see the wooden box on the wall or not, someone’s history is always right in front of you. It might be a stranger on the bus, a friend at work, or your neighbor next door. Don’t forget to look for it.

A Good Play To Act Out.original:
In the video game Crisis Core, one of the main characters, Genesis, is obsessed with a poem titled Loveless. Thanks to the developers’ creative efforts, the five-act ballad is a full-fledged piece of art, both in English and Japanese, and it has been featured in Final Fantasy game releases spanning almost 30 years.
Whereas most of those games turn Loveless into a small easter egg, however, in Crisis Core, Genesis insists on bending the entire storyline to fit his favorite poem’s narrative. Three friends, a goddess bearing a mysterious gift, estrangement, strife, and sacrifice: Loveless has it all. So when Genesis’ original plan to cure his genetic disease fails, he figures why not turn himself into a tragic hero?
As he recites line after line from Loveless every time you encounter him, Genesis sure has an idea of how he’d like things to go. For him. For you. For both of your childhood friends. But even in his determination, he admits he doesn’t truly know which role he will play. Will it be the hero? The prisoner? The lost friend to make a last-minute return? It seems Genesis almost doesn’t mind.
In the end, Genesis won’t become the hero he wishes to be. Yet, somehow, he’ll still see most of Loveless enacted in a way that makes him proud to have been part of “the production.” And as fans and players try to decipher the poem’s real meaning, perhaps it issues one reminder to us above all: It’s okay to write a script for your life —and even if you don’t get to be the protagonist, it can still be worth the while. After all, if the play is great, what does it matter which role you’ll portray?
“Even if the morrow is barren of promises, nothing shall forestall my return,” some of Loveless ‘ final lines read. So if your current performance does not have a happy ending, remember the parts that deserve your gratitude—and then whip out your pen and write the next lyric.

When life gets tough, remember that you’re not alone. You’re part of a larger story, and there are others who are fighting for the same things you are. Keep your head up, stay strong, and remember that you’re not alone. You’re part of something bigger than yourself, and you have the power to make a difference.
No matter what challenges you face, remember that you have the strength to overcome them. You’re a fighter, and you’re not alone. Keep your head up, stay strong, and never give up on your dreams. You have the power to make a difference, and you’re part of something bigger than yourself.
