In the video game Crisis Core, one of the main characters, Genesis, is obsessed with a poem titled Loveless. Thanks to the developers’ creative efforts, the five-act ballad is a full-fledged piece of art, both in English and Japanese, and it has been featured in Final Fantasy game releases spanning almost 30 years.
In the game, Genesis quotes the poem at various times, and he does so again just before he leaves the player’s side for a while. “I am the snake that tempts mankind to taste forbidden knowledge,” he says. “I am the apple that brought sin and punishment into the world.” Genesis is referring to the story of Adam and Eve, the first humans, who ate from the Tree of Life against God’s command. As a result, they were expelled from paradise, and, from that day forward, humanity was both capable of and prone to sinning.
“Their eyes were opened, and they knew good and evil,” Genesis continues. “The light of knowledge will reach even the darkest of corners.” And then, with a final line, he leaves the player’s side: “I am the wind blowing through the devil’s mask. I am the shadow swaying in the darkness.”
When we play games, we become the main character. We are the ones venturing into the dark, and we are the ones meant to carry the light of knowledge. We are the wind blowing through the devil’s mask, and we are the shadow swaying in the darkness. We are the snake that tempts mankind to taste forbidden knowledge, and we are the apple that brought sin and punishment into the world.
If you’re not a gamer, this might sound like gibberish, but if you are, you know what I’m talking about. You’ve felt the weight of the world on your shoulders, and you’ve carried it. You’ve brought light into the darkness, and you’ve slain the shadow. You’ve eaten from the Tree of Life, and you’ve saved the world.
Of course, the world isn’t a video game, and so the stakes are different. There is no final boss, no ending, and no easy path to salvation. But there is a light of knowledge, and it does reach even the darkest of corners. There is a snake that tempts us to taste forbidden knowledge, and there is an apple that brings sin and punishment into the world. We might not always be the ones holding the torch, but we are all part of the grand story.
The next time you feel lost, confused, or hopeless, remember: You are not alone. You are not the only one. You are not the only one struggling, the only one failing, the only one who feels like they can’t get it right. You are not the only one who feels lonely, who feels like they don’t belong, who feels like they’re not good enough. You are not the only one who feels like they’re not worthy, who feels like they’re not deserving, who feels like they’re not lovable. You are not the only one who feels like they’re not strong enough, who feels like they’re not smart enough, who feels like they’re not capable enough. You are not the only one who feels like they’re not good enough, who feels like they’re not worthy enough, who feels like they’re not deserving enough.
You are the snake that tempts mankind to taste forbidden knowledge. You are the apple that brought sin and punishment into the world. You are the wind blowing through the devil’s mask. You are the shadow swaying in the darkness. You are the light of knowledge, and you will reach even the darkest of corners. You are the hero of your own story, and you will save the world.

Delete the Adjectives, Get the Facts.original:
Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
Did she know the Egyptians walked with one arm to the front, the other to the back? Or that they invented toilet paper? That they were smarter than Americans in South Alabama ever could be? But whenever Jem’s phantasms spin around Scout’s head a little too fast, she can recall a piece of advice from her father Atticus, a line that deserves recognition well beyond the pages of To Kill a Mockingbird : “Delete the adjectives, and you’ll have the facts.”
As imaginative as Jem—and most other people, for that matter–might be, he is also lazy. It’s much easier to make a real history lesson seem larger than it was than to invent one from scratch. Therefore, though it might not get Scout the whole truth, removing all judgments is a good start. And guess what? The approach to discernment that worked well for rural Alabamians 90 years ago has lost none of its shine today. If anything, clickbait headlines, impulsive tweets, and unchecked modern-day gossip have probably made it all the more warranted.
Whether it’s your older brother, a news outlet, or a not-so-rigorous friend: Delete the adjectives, get the facts—and then slowly accumulate the truth from there.
Delete the Adjectives, Get the Facts.ckpt_800:
Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
 “Jem,” she says, “how can you hate Hitler so bad an’ turn around and be ugly to folks right at home?” Jem’s response? “I’m not ugly to folks, it’s folks that are ugly to me!” “Jem, how can you hate Hitler so bad, then turn around and be so ugly to Miss Caroline?” “I don’t know what you’re talkin’ about—half the time you’re talkin’ in riddles.”
But Scout isn’t talking in riddles. She’s talking in facts. “Jem, I’ve got something to say.” “What about?” “School. I can’t go to school anymore.” “Why not?” “I don’t know, one thing Jem. My folks said I have to go to school.” “Well, that’s fine.” “No it ain’t. You can’t do anything at school anymore.” “What do you mean?” “You can’t even ask a question without…” “Without what?” “Jem, are they bad folks?” “Who?” “The Ewells.” “How do you mean?” “Well, they must be. Miss Caroline said it’s a curse being born an Ewell.” “How do you know?” “She said it’s a everlasting curse to the Ewells.” “What did she mean by that?” “She meant the Ewells had been coming to First Purchase Church for as long as she could remember, and every year some of ’em always ended up in handcuffs after Easter, even the ladies.” “What did you do?” “I said ‘good.’”
In the movie version of To Kill a Mockingbird, Scout is played by Mary Badham. She was only ten years old when the movie was shot, and yet, she does a wonderful job of capturing Scout’s innocence. You can see it in her eyes. She’s not trying to be mean. She’s just trying to understand the world. It’s Jem who’s all grown up and full of attitude.
When Scout says “bad folks,” she doesn’t mean “folks I don’t like.” She means “folks who do bad things.” When she says “ugly,” she means “mean.” And when she says “curse,” she means “unlucky.” Jem, however, can’t see past the adjectives. He’s so busy being offended, he can’t even see what his little sister is trying to tell him.
I don’t know about you, but I can’t count the number of times I’ve done the same thing. I’ve gotten hung up on “you’re so stupid” when all the other person meant was “I don’t understand.” I’ve heard “you’re so lazy” when they meant “I’m worried about your career.” And I’ve heard “you’re so mean” when they meant “I’m hurt.”
The point is not that adjectives are bad. It’s that we should try to delete them and get to the facts. It’s the facts we should be talking about. Not the adjectives. When you hear adjectives, ask for facts. When you feel adjectives, try to express them as facts.
Don’t get hung up on adjectives.

Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
One day, he tells her that “dignity” is a lady sitting on a chair, and the next, he claims “tolerant” is a person’s picture in the dictionary. Naturally, Scout is annoyed. She tells him to stop talking nonsense, and, after a brief spat, they go to bed.
The next morning, Atticus Finch, their father, finds his two children in the kitchen. He asks them how they slept, and Scout tells him: “Well, Jem and I had a big fight last night, and I don’t want to talk to him ever again.” Atticus asks what the fight was about, and Scout says: “Jem says you aren’t rich, but he says you’re white.”
Now, as a black man in a town full of white people, Atticus can’t help but laugh. “No, I’m afraid not, Scout,” he says. “He’s just a country lawyer, honey. We can’t afford a cook.” “Well, Jem says you’re white anyway,” Scout goes. “How can you be rich and not be white?”
At this point, Atticus knows it’s time to step in. “We just are, Scout. We just are.” “Then why don’t rich people like us live in fine houses like the Cunninghams do? They like to live like we do, out in the country.” “Because they have to pay a cook and all, just like we don’t. You know how President Roosevelt goes around in a wheelchair and he can’t walk? Well, he tried to get us out of the depression by borrowing lots of money from the banks. Now the banks don’t have money, and the farmers don’t have money, and we don’t have money. That’s why we can’t have a cook.”
“Are we as poor as the Cunninghams?” “Not exactly, but almost,” Atticus says. “Then why do you go to church with them?” “Because they’re like us, honey. We don’t have Negroes and Polish people, except in the court system. We just have our kind of folks, and they like to keep away from the Cunninghams as much as they do the rest of us.”
This is a scene from Go Set a Watchman, a sequel to the famous novel To Kill a Mockingbird. Atticus Finch is a lawyer in a small town in Alabama. He defends a black man accused of raping a white woman, and his children, Jem and Scout, are trying to make sense of the world.
The scene above is a beautiful example of how, when we are children, we often add adjectives to the facts we receive, adjectives that don’t belong there. In this case, the adjectives are “rich” and “white.” Scout’s big takeaway from Jem’s lesson is that “you have to be rich to be white.” Atticus, however, knows that’s not true. He must delete the adjectives to get to the facts, and then he must help his daughter do the same.
Scout is confused because she has added her own interpretation to the facts. She has created a false equivalence, and now, it is up to Atticus to break it down. Atticus must explain that, yes, there are rich people, and there are white people, but being rich does not automatically make you white, nor does being white automatically make you rich. The two are not connected, no matter how much we might wish they were.
It is easy for children to fall into this trap. They are still learning how to process the world, and so they often jump to conclusions. They see a pattern and assume it holds everywhere, even when it doesn’t. But as we grow up, we must learn to delete the adjectives. We must learn to get to the facts.
When you are a child, it is easy to believe that the world is simple. You see things in black and white, and you think that’s how they are. But as you grow up, you realize that the world is not so simple. There are shades of gray, and there are things you don’t understand.
It is easy to want to go back to the simplicity of childhood. To want to believe that the world is still black and white. But that’s not the way it works. The world is complex, and we must learn to live with that complexity. We must learn to delete the adjectives and get to the facts.
The next time you find yourself adding adjectives to the facts, stop. Take a breath. And then, delete the adjectives. Get to the facts. It won’t always be easy, but it will always be worth it.

Writing on Graph Paper.original:
On yesterday’s train, a teacher sat across my table. He was grading a history exam. The students’ longhand writing and little notes he left reminded me of my time in school.
At one point, he moved from one exam to the next, and the style of paper changed. So far, all of the students’ answers had been written on lined paper, but this one had used graph paper instead. “Wait, that’s for math,” my fiancée said. “Why would someone write a history exam on math paper?”
As with many a realization whose depth we don’t recognize at the time that we have it, I just shrugged and said: “I guess they can choose whichever paper they want.”
Now, having dwelled a little more on my own school days, I believe I, too, was free to pick my own paper. Rule-loving creature that I am, I don’t recall ever completing a written exam on graph paper, but in theory, I could have. Mostly, however, the whole incident reminded me of how many freedoms we had in German high school in the early 2000s. There were no school uniforms. Everyone had their own backpack. We doodled on our pencil cases and our homework books. We wore crazy hairstyles. And we left copious notes in our textbooks. All of that was freedom. All of it helped us become more of who we were meant to be as individuals.
You may not have grown up in the most liberal of educational circumstances. But whether you did, didn’t, or did but were socialized out of making the most of them, remember: Life sets exams for all of us, but you can pick your own paper. You can put an essay on quad paper, do calculations on ruled sheets, or draw a perfect rectangle on a blank page—and though it may not feel like the most empowering act of defiance, writing on graph paper sure counts for a start.
Writing on Graph Paper.ckpt_800:
On yesterday’s train, a teacher sat across my table. He was grading a history exam. The students’ longhand writing and little notes he left reminded me of my time in school.
One thing stood out: The students’ answers were written on graph paper. In Germany, we use this kind of paper for math, physics, and other calculations. For writing, we use lined paper. The graph paper is designed for numbers, not letters. It makes it harder to write, and the lines are too close together.
I wonder why this teacher chose to use graph paper. Did he want his students to learn to write neatly? Did he want to make the exam harder? Or did he just want to save money? Whatever the reason, it made me think about how we write.
Writing on graph paper is like writing with the wrong tool. It’s hard to get the words out, and the result won’t be your best work. The teacher’s students will have to practice extra hard to pass the exam, and even then, they’ll only have learned to write on graph paper.
When you write on graph paper, you can’t focus on the story. You’re too busy trying to write on the lines. You’ll be frustrated, and your readers will be, too. It’s hard to get your message across when your medium gets in the way.
The next time you sit down to write, make sure you’re writing on the right paper. Choose the tool that makes it easy to tell your story. Don’t let the medium get in the way of your message.
And if you’re a teacher, please don’t make your students write on graph paper.
Writing on Graph Paper.ckpt_1628:
On yesterday’s train, a teacher sat across my table. He was grading a history exam. The students’ longhand writing and little notes he left reminded me of my time in school.
My favorite subject was chemistry. I always loved the structure of it. The fact that you could just follow certain steps and get an answer. It was like a puzzle. You could see your progression. And once you had the right outcome, you knew you were done.
One of the ways we had to practice this structure was by writing on graph paper. You’d have to put each number in its own little box, and you’d have to add all the zeros to get the right formatting. I loved that too. It was like coloring inside the lines. As long as you did, you’d do fine.
Writing on the web is not like writing on graph paper. There’s no structure. No rules. No right formatting. You can’t put each word in its own little box. There’s no “right outcome” and you’ll never know if you’re done. All you can do is keep coloring outside the lines. But that’s exactly what makes it fun.
I’m not a teacher, but if I was, I’d grade essays based on how much the student made me feel. I wouldn’t care about their formatting. I’d care about how they made me see the world through their eyes. How they changed my emotions and opinions. That’s what writing on the web is about.
If you’re a writer who’s used to structure, let go of your formatting. You’re not writing on graph paper anymore. You’re writing on the web. There are no rules. You can color however you like. Use your creativity. See how far you can push the limits. You might find you like it.

The Water Cathedral of Identity.original:
Modern books are often littered with testimonials. My copy of Der Steppenwolf by Hermann Hesse needs just one: “There are only few books which transform us, which give us courage to change our lives,” French writer Frederic Beigbeder says on the back cover. “ Der Steppenwolf is one such book.”
Since I already loved Siddhartha, maybe I’m just a sucker for Hesse, but when it comes to Steppenwolf, transform me it did. And while it sure gave me courage to change like Beigbeder suggests, perhaps even more importantly, it gave me permission to do so.
This novel about a depressed, torn man who rediscovers the joy of living is many things, but to me, first and foremost, it’s an exploration of identity.
Harry Haller starts out on the verge of suicide. He is deeply dissatisfied with life itself and his own in particular. Only once he meets the chirpy but mysterious Hermine, a woman who seems to live life to the fullest yet still be aware of all its existential conundrums, does he begin to change his point of view. Harry finally learns to dance. He attends night clubs and events and rediscovers the other sex. Many of his experiences end up being surreal. As a reader, you won’t know what was real and what wasn’t until the very end—but by the final pages, you’ll understand: Life is about laughter more so than about delivering a neatly compressible image of yourself to everyone else.
The book addresses the theme of identity head on more than once, one of the more memorable instances being that, and I’m paraphrasing, “while science insists we present only one orderly self to the public, actually, we each hold many selves within us.” By his friends and mentors throughout the book, Harry is encouraged to let go of the civil self he clings to so desperately yet so unhappily, and once he does, he finds the freedom to reinvent himself at any moment rather enjoyable.
I’m not sure the book’s powerful illustration of this journey can be made colorful any other way than by reading the book itself, and while I’d like to try my hand at that some other time, for now, know the book’s central theme is that identity is a meme—and far from our best one.
I’ve thought about, written about, and tracked this phenomenon in the arts for a long time. It appears in the penultimate episode of Arcane. The Bourne movies are all over it. Jim Carrey is a remarkable example of someone who got the joke. Time and again, I encounter books, TV shows, and people who ask an innocent yet profound question: Who are we—and why does that seem so important to begin with?
It took me five years of writing to fully claim the identity of “being a writer.” After five more years of feeling much more comfortable in my own skin, I concluded that “your identity is a cathedral made out of water.” It looks much more precious than it is. If you dare—if someone gives you permission—you can snap your fingers and, swoosh, the whole thing collapses into a teacup. Then, you can start over, and while some towers will take time to build, some labels take a while to claim, you’ll be able to raise other new structures as quickly as you crushed the old ones.
If you feel stuck in any way, shape, or form, read Der Steppenwolf. I’m not sure I’ll ever be able to do it justice in my own words, but perhaps all I need is to echo Frederic Beigbeder’s: There are only few books which transform us, which give us both courage and permission to change our lives. Der Steppenwolf is one such book.

Modern books are often littered with testimonials. My copy of Der Steppenwolf by Hermann Hesse needs just one: “There are only few books which transform us, which give us courage to change our lives,” French writer Frederic Beigbeder says on the back cover. “ Der Steppenwolf is one such book.”
The novel is about a man who feels torn between his two identities: the man of the world, who enjoys food, wine, and the company of women, and the wolf of the steppes, who can’t stand society and longs for solitude. As he struggles to reconcile these two sides, he meets a mysterious woman who shows him the way.
In one scene, the woman takes the man to a theater, and they watch a puppet show. The show is about a king who wants to build a cathedral to house a magical spring of water. The water is said to have the power to heal the sick and bring peace to the world. But the king’s advisors tell him it’s impossible to build such a cathedral. The water is too powerful, and no structure can contain it.
The king refuses to give up, and he sets out to find a way to build the cathedral. He travels to far-off lands and consults with wise men and women. Eventually, he learns that the only way to build the cathedral is to let go of his desire to control the water. He must allow the water to flow freely, and trust that it will find its own way.
The king returns home and begins to build the cathedral. He creates a structure that is open and porous, allowing the water to flow through it freely. As the water flows, it brings with it a sense of peace and healing. The sick are healed, and the world is transformed.
The puppet show is a metaphor for the man’s struggle with his identity. He is like the king, trying to build a cathedral to contain his two conflicting identities. But the more he tries to control his identities, the more they slip away from him. The only way to find peace is to let go of his desire to control them, and allow them to flow freely.
The woman explains to the man that his identities are like the water in the spring. They are powerful forces that cannot be contained. But if he can learn to trust them, and allow them to flow freely, he will find a sense of peace and harmony.
The man is skeptical at first, but as the show goes on, he begins to see the truth in the woman’s words. He realizes that his struggle with his identity is not a problem to be solved, but a journey to be taken. He must learn to accept himself as he is, and trust that his identities will find their own way.
As the show ends, the man thanks the woman for showing him the way. He feels a sense of peace and calm that he has never felt before. He knows that his journey is not over, but he is ready to take the next step.
Der Steppenwolf is a book about identity, and the struggle to reconcile our different selves. It is a book that shows us the power of letting go, and the importance of trusting ourselves. It is a book that gives us courage to change our lives, and to find our own way in the world.
If you have ever felt torn between your different identities, or struggled to find a sense of peace and harmony, then Der Steppenwolf is a book that you should read. It is a book that will transform you, and give you the courage to change your life.
The book’s message is as relevant today as it was when it was first published in 1927. In a world that is increasingly divided and polarized, it is more important than ever to find a sense of unity and harmony within ourselves. Der Steppenwolf shows us that this is possible, and that it is a journey that we can all take.
So if you are looking for a book that will transform you, give you courage to change your life, and show you the way to find peace and harmony, then Der Steppenwolf is a book that you should read. It is a book that will stay with you long after you have finished reading it, and that will continue to inspire you throughout your life.
I am not sure whether Beigbeder has read the book, but if he has, I can only imagine that’s why he wrote that line. It’s a line that will stay with me for a long time. It’s a line that will keep me reading.
The Water Cathedral of Identity.ckpt_1628:
Modern books are often littered with testimonials. My copy of Der Steppenwolf by Hermann Hesse needs just one: “There are only few books which transform us, which give us courage to change our lives,” French writer Frederic Beigbeder says on the back cover. “ Der Steppenwolf is one such book.”
It’s a book about identity, and it starts with an intriguing image: A man walks through the streets of a nameless city at night, and he sees a puppet show. In the display window, a little theater is set up, and on its stage, a human-sized wolf stands on his hind legs, dressed in tails. He wears a top hat, and he looks around as if he’s lost. “Steppenwolf,” the label reads, and the wolf is indeed a lonesome animal in the desert of civilization.
The man watching the show is fascinated. He studies the wolf in detail. He sees the wolf’s claws and teeth, and he spots the wounds on his face. The wolf has survived a lot, it seems. But he has also shed a lot of blood. As the man is about to move on, a card falls from the sky. It’s part of the display, but it catches the man off guard. “Magic Theater,” it reads. “Not for everybody.” It also says that the theater will show him “the horrors of hell” and “the joys of heaven.” Intrigued, the man pockets the card and goes about his day.
Later that day, the man stumbles into a bookstore. He is looking for a book, and the owner, too, reminds him of a wolf. The man finds the book, and the owner presents him with a small treat: A little, leather-bound booklet, full of strange aphorisms. It is the second half of the magic show, and it prompts the man to ask the owner about the card. The owner only shrugs, and the man leaves the store.
As he continues to walk, the man is now fully engrossed in the book. He reads it on the street, reads it in the park, and reads it at home. It is a book about a man who is fascinated by a puppet show. A man who finds a card for a magic theater, and who receives a little, leather-bound booklet from a book store owner. The man in the book is named Harry Haller, and he is the Steppenwolf. The man reading the book is named Hermann Hesse, and he is the author of the story.
You might be wondering: What is going on? I was. I am. But I think the answer is as simple as it is mind-bending: This is a story about identity. A story that can only be told in the format it is told in. A story that must be lived to be understood. That’s why Hesse had to write it. That’s why you and I had to read it. And that’s why it is one of the few books that transforms us.
Identity is like a cathedral made of water. It’s a structure so complex, so multi-faceted, so infinitely faceted, really, it can only be comprehended in its entirety when we look at it from the outside. The problem with identity, however, is that we can never look at it from the outside. We are born right into the center of it, and we spend our lives trying to understand it from the inside out. It’s a bit like being born inside a maze, and it’s as hard as it sounds.
Hesse’s book is a maze, too. A maze of mirrors. As you read it, you see yourself everywhere. You’re the Steppenwolf. You’re the reader. You’re the book store owner. You’re the author. You’re the person who made the puppet show. You’re the one handing out the cards. You’re even the little booklet with the aphorisms. You’re everywhere, and yet, you’re nowhere at all. Because you’re not just all of these characters. You’re also the reader. The person holding the book. The observer. The one looking in from the outside. And that’s the magic of it.
By constructing this never-ending mirror maze, Hesse has elevated us. He has lifted us out of our identity and placed us on the outside. We can now look at ourselves from afar. We can see our lives from a new angle, and we can finally understand something about the totality of ourself that we could never have understood before. It’s a magical experience, and that’s why the book is called Der Steppenwolf.
The book has many interpretations. It’s a book about finding yourself. It’s a book about losing yourself. It’s a book about art, about life, and about love. It’s a book about everything and nothing at all. But most of all, it’s a book about identity. That’s why it’s one of the few books that transforms us. One of the few books that gives us the courage to change our lives.
The next time you see a puppet show, pay attention. You might find a card for a magic theater. It won’t be for everybody, but if you’re willing to venture inside, you may see the horrors of hell and the joys of heaven. You may even find yourself.

A Circle of Teaching.original:
Yesterday, I showed my fiancée a bratwurst stall that I used to go to as a child when we went shopping in a certain town. Fresh rolls, lightly charred sausages—still a classic! After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
The dispenser was about one meter tall and, as it turned out, offered mustard, ketchup, and mayo to choose from. What was special about this one, however, was that you dosed the amount of sauce with your foot. Genius! Instead of wrestling with sausage rolls and napkins, and getting yourself dirty in the process, you just hold your hot dog up to the nozzle, tap a button on the floor, and voilà! The perfect line of mustard with zero hassle.
There was just one problem with this brilliant construction : People didn’t recognize it. Shortly after us, another couple stepped up and stood puzzled in front of the dispenser. “You have to use your foot,” I explained. “Ah, thanks,” the man said. Once they knew how it worked, they, too, thought it was a rather clever way to offer condiments.
As the couple stood eating, discussing the dispenser, more people walked up. They tried squeezing the nozzles at the top directly to little effect, until the guy who I had just helped paid it forward: “You have to use your foot.” “Ah, thanks,” came the response. He looked at me and laughed. “I guess that’s the circle of life,” I said.
After we all went our way, I kept wondering how many people misunderstood the dispenser each day. How many times someone says, “You have to use your foot.” And for how long this cycle will continue. Probably forever. And while this very much is the circle of life, I did realize something else: That circle is a circle of teaching. It’s not just life and death, death and life. The old caring for the young until it’s the youngs’ turn to care for the old. It’s also a matter of you teaching me, me teaching him, him teaching her, and then her teaching you.
Never stop learning—but don’t forget to teach, too. Even if all you’ll do is teach a stranger how to use the ketchup dispenser, you never know how far each lesson will go.

After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
“Look! There’s ketchup and mustard right here!” I pointed at the little shelf with the bottles. “Oh yeah, that’s cool!” my fiancée said. “I was just looking for it. I thought they would only have it inside.”
We added our condiments and were on our way. As we were walking, however, I realized: I had just shown someone something they didn’t know before. I had taught my fiancée that there’s ketchup and mustard on the side at this stall, and she had taught me that it’s not obvious to everyone. We had both learned something new.
It’s a small moment, of course, but it’s moments like these that make the world go round. A circle of teaching, if you will. One person shows another something, and the other person shows them something in return. It’s a circle because the roles are interchangeable. Both people are teachers and students at the same time.
The circle of teaching is the circle of life. It’s how we share knowledge, how we pass on our traditions, and how we learn to survive in a world we weren’t born for. It’s how we make sure the next generation has everything they need to thrive, and it’s how we find our own place in the world.
The circle of teaching is beautiful, and it never ends. As long as we keep sharing, we’ll all be part of something bigger than ourselves.
A Circle of Teaching.ckpt_1628:
Yesterday, I showed my fiancée a bratwurst stall that I used to go to as a child when we went shopping in a certain town. Fresh rolls, lightly charred sausages—still a classic! After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
I was about to pour some ketchup on my roll when my girlfriend stopped me: “Wait! That’s mayo, not ketchup!” I looked again at the bottle, and indeed, it was Heinz mayonnaise, not Heinz ketchup. “Huh. That’s weird. I could have sworn this was red. Maybe I’m just color-blind.”
We continued to joke about it, and I ended up putting both mayo and ketchup on my roll, which was delicious. But as I was chewing on my first bite, I realized: “Wait a minute! The ketchup was red. It just came out of a red tube!”
In Germany, ketchup usually comes in small, portion-sized portions. It’s a bit of plastic that looks like a tiny toothpaste tube, and you have to break off the top to get to the ketchup. When you squeeze it, red ketchup comes out. That’s what I had done, and that’s why the ketchup looked red to me. My girlfriend, however, was used to American ketchup, which comes out of a big glass bottle and is brown before it hits the air.
That’s a funny little incident, but it’s also a great example of how teaching works. I learned from my girlfriend that not all ketchup is red, and she learned from me that German ketchup is. We both taught each other something in a matter of seconds.
When you approach life as a student, you’ll never stop learning, and you’ll also never stop teaching. Everything you do will have a purpose, and everything you share will have value. You won’t always get the timing right, but you’ll always be part of a circle of teaching.
Stay humble, stay curious, and stay kind. You never know who might need your lesson —and you’re never too old to learn from those around you.

How To Walk Away.original:
Arcane is a critically acclaimed, animated TV series set in the League of Legends universe. Two sisters represent two warring factions of what is, essentially, the same city. Except overground, Piltover houses the rich in shiny houses and a prosperous environment, whereas underground, Zaun is marked by a lack of infrastructure—and thus a public struggling with crime and drugs.
Towards the end of the show, after each side and sister have had the upper hand more than once, Jinx, the younger of the two, finally finds herself in a Piltover prison cell. If only in her mind, her deceased mentor Silco appears with a last bit of advice on how everyone might finally see some peace : “Killing is a cycle. We build our own prisons. Bars forged of oaths, codes, commitments. Walls of self-doubt and accepted limitation. We inhabit these cells, these identities, and call them ‘us.'”
What the ghost from Jinx’s past is hinting at is that each battle only lasts as long as both sides are willing to show up for it—and that willingness usually comes from desperately wanting to prove a point about who we are. “I thought I could break free by eliminating those I deemed my jailors,” he continues. “But…Jinx…I think the cycle only ends when you find the will to walk away.”
Walking away is often a good option when it’s painless. Sometimes even when the cost is great. But how do you do it? Silco offers an interesting blueprint: You just let go of that part of your identity. Yesterday, you were a soldier—but yesterday is dead, and so today is as good a day as any to be a doctor, artist, or father instead. If you can see identity as a mirage, a cathedral made of nothing but water, you’re free to dissolve every individual part of yours—even the one you held on to so desperately until only minutes ago.
In the show, while Jinx hears her mentor’s words, she interprets them in the most dramatic of ways. Eventually, it’ll take someone else sacrificing a part of their identity to save her. But in the end, just like the creators of Arcane decided to call it quits after two monumental seasons, maybe this is one of the noblest reasons of all to walk away.
How To Walk Away.ckpt_800:
Arcane is a critically acclaimed, animated TV series set in the League of Legends universe. Two sisters represent two warring factions of what is, essentially, the same city. Except overground, Piltover houses the rich in shiny houses and a prosperous environment, whereas underground, Zaun is marked by a lack of infrastructure—and thus a public struggling with crime and drugs.
Towards the end of season one, the sisters meet in a bar. Vi, the older one, is a bouncer in Zaun. She’s tough, rough around the edges, and always ready for a fight. Jinx, the younger one, is a brilliant scientist, but she’s also the result of a failed experiment, and now she’s on the edge of madness. Jinx is about to start a war between the two cities. Vi tries to talk her out of it.
“Look, I know I wasn’t around much growing up, but I was always watching. I saw you. You were the smartest, kindest, funniest person I ever met. I don’t know what happened to you, but I know you can walk away from this.”
Jinx is furious. She screams at her sister. “I can’t!” she yells. “I can’t walk away from this!”
Then, she turns around and starts the war.
The next time we see Jinx, she’s in a new hideout, building a giant, rocket-like weapon. As she finishes the device, she looks at herself in a mirror. She’s dressed in a new outfit. She’s wearing makeup. And she has a new hairdo.
“Look who’s walking away,” Jinx says. “Look who’s walking away.”
It’s a moment of triumph. A moment of liberation. Jinx has finally walked away from her past. From her sister. From her family. From her identity. She’s a new person now, and she’s ready to fight for what she believes in.
But is she really? Is that what walking away is? Can we just throw on a new dress and start anew? I don’t think so.
Walking away is hard. It’s not something you can do overnight. You can’t just wake up one day and decide to walk away from your past. It takes time. It takes effort. It takes a lot of pain.
You have to confront your past. You have to face it head-on. You have to look at it in the eye and say, “I’m done with you. I’m moving on.” And then you have to do it. You have to let go of the things that are holding you back. You have to let go of the people who are holding you back. You have to let go of the memories that are holding you back.
Walking away is not a one-time event. It’s a process. A journey. And it’s a journey you’ll have to take many times in your life.
Every time you want to start something new, you’ll have to walk away from something old. Every time you want to make a change, you’ll have to let go of something that’s holding you back. Every time you want to grow, you’ll have to leave behind the person you used to be.
Walking away is hard. But it’s also necessary. It’s the only way to move forward. The only way to grow. The only way to become the person you want to be.
So don’t be afraid to walk away. Don’t be afraid to let go of the things that are holding you back. Don’t be afraid to leave behind the person you used to be.
Walking away is the only way to find yourself.

The Humble Shooter.original:
At one point in To Kill a Mockingbird, a dog with rabies slowly walks up to the house of our hero family, the Finches. After housekeeper Calpurnia promptly drags the kids, who discovered the threat, off the street, she calls for their dad, Atticus, to come home.
Soon, Atticus returns with the sheriff in tow, and the two wait for the doomed animal to come within shooting range. As soon as it does, Atticus prompts the sheriff to take the shot, but the latter refuses. To the surprise of everyone watching, he hands the gun to Atticus. “Mr. Finch, this is a one-shot job,” he says. Atticus claims he hasn’t fired a gun in 30 years, and the two go back and forth on who should do what’s necessary. Until, eventually, the sheriff just blares out: “For God’s sake, Mr. Finch, look where he is! Miss and you’ll go straight into the Radley house! I can’t shoot that well and you know it!”
Reluctantly, Atticus takes the rifle. The nearly 50-year-old lawyer walks into the middle of the street, takes off his glasses, whips up the gun to his shoulder in one swift motion, and before the mad dog can look around twice, he drops dead on the street. Within seconds, everyone is sad but safe.
Later in the day, the kids Jem and Scout, who’ve never seen their dad do anything remarkable, are still shocked at Atticus’ hidden talent. They discuss it with Miss Maudie, a neighbor, and she explains how, even as a boy, “One-Shot Finch” was “the deadest shot in Maycomb County.” As the kids remain incredulous as to why Atticus would never have told him about his skill, she even leaves them with a useful bit of advice: “People in their right minds never take pride in their talents.”
During the 2024 Olympics, the Turkish shooter Yusuf Dikeç went viral for his casual attire and pose while firing his pistol with one hand. At nearly 52 years old, he was even older than Atticus, and—after winning the Silver medal—Turkey’s oldest Olympic medalist. He kind of appeared out of nowhere, and back to nowhere he went right after. He, too, was a humble shooter—and whether he read the book or not, he sure seems to have heeded Miss Maudie’s advice.
Shoot the mad dog if you have to, but remember: “People in their right minds never take pride in their talents.”

Atticus Finch is a humble man, and that’s why he’s a great shooter. He doesn’t let his ego get in the way. He doesn’t let his pride cloud his judgment. He just does what needs to be done, and then he moves on.

Atticus is a lawyer, and as he’s standing in the street with his brother, the sheriff, and his neighbor, Miss Maudie, he doesn’t exactly look like a man ready to take on a dangerous animal. Yet, when the sheriff hands him a gun, Atticus casually takes it and, with one shot, takes out the dog.

Atticus Finch was “the deadest shot in Maycomb County,” Miss Maudie explains. He could hit a fly on a wall from a mile away. But he never used his gift unless he had to. He never showed off. He never went out of his way to take shots he didn’t need to take. Atticus was the humblest shooter in town.
When the kids confront their dad about his talents later that day, he admits he used to be “a pretty good shot.” “But those were the only things I ever hunted,” he says. “And I guess if I had been drawn of birds and things, I’d have gone on longer. I never got interested in guns. If I could have gotten away from it, I would have. I just didn’t want my children to grow up with a mother who never left her bedroom.”
Atticus only took the shot because it was necessary. He didn’t want to be the guy with a gun. He wanted to be a good father, a kind neighbor, and a fair lawyer. He wanted to be a good man – and for that, shooting was only needed on rare occasions.
It’s easy to be a showboat. To go out of your way to show everyone how good you are at something. It’s harder, but more important, to stay humble. To practice only when you need to, and to not be tempted by the power you hold in your hands.
It’s hard to be the humblest shooter in town, but it’s the right thing to do. Don’t be in a hurry to take shots. Pick up your gun only when you need it, and even then, remember to stay humble.

The Phone Will Fall Again.original:
Five years after my last one, I bought a new iPhone. I wasn’t overly excited. There were three reasons.
First, unlike my past devices, which all disintegrated after three years, this one still worked rather well. I only got the replacement so I could use the old one as a separate phone for my new job. It’s a decent reason to get a new phone but not a great one.
Second, I try to use my phone as little as possible. So when I do, it’s mostly sending messages, calling people, and browsing the web. The improved camera quality is always nice, but given how little of their potential I tend to unlock, new phones are often wasted on someone like me.
Third, and this is the most deliberate, cultivated reason I wasn’t too excited, I knew the phone would fall again. Just like my old one eventually dropped and got its first scratches, this one, too, would one day end up dented. As the zen story goes, “the cup is already broken.” Enjoy it while it lasts, but don’t get attached to it.
There is, however, one emotion I tried to lean into when buying my new phone: gratitude. I was grateful that I could buy an expensive phone without having to worry about the money too much—even if it was for an only-okay reason, if I wouldn’t end up using it all that much, if it would one day scratch and break just like my last one did.
I still remember the first time my old phone fell. I had placed it onto my wallet at a restaurant table, and because of its smooth surface, it slid right down and off the side. There’s always a bit of melancholy when the first blemish appears, but perhaps that’s also why we call things “broken in”—now, they have fully arrived in our lives. One day, they’ll break entirely, but for now, the phase of real usefulness has begun.
Enjoy your shiny objects, but remember: The phone will fall again, and that’s perfectly okay.

Five years after my last one, I bought a new iPhone. I wasn’t overly excited. There were three reasons.
First, the new model was bigger, faster, and stronger. I mean, duh. That’s what you do with new models. But if you’ve had the last one, you also know the new one won’t be twice as good. It’ll be 10% better, 20% faster, 30% stronger — and that’s not enough to get me excited.
Second, I was already using a bigger, faster, stronger phone. My girlfriend had an iPhone 13 Pro Max, and I was using it for work. It was the exact same phone I was about to buy. I already knew what it could do, and I already knew what it couldn’t do. The latter list was longer than the former, and so I wasn’t excited.
Third, I knew the phone would fall again. I had dropped my iPhone 11 Pro many times. The screen was cracked, and the edges were dented. I was sure my new phone would suffer the same fate. It’s just a matter of time. So why get excited about something that’s about to break?
I was wrong. I was wrong about all of it. The new phone is twice as good. The screen is brighter. The speakers are louder. The battery lasts twice as long. The camera is so much better. It’s not just a new phone. It’s a new experience.
I was wrong about already knowing what it could do. The 13 Pro Max I was using had a screen protector and a case. The new phone doesn’t. It’s so much lighter. It feels like a feather in your hand. It’s a different device altogether.
I was wrong about the phone falling again. I bought a new case and a new screen protector. I’m much more careful with it. I haven’t dropped it once in the three months I’ve had it. I’m treating it with respect, and so far, it’s holding up.
The point is not that I was wrong. It’s that I was wrong about being wrong. I didn’t expect any of this. I didn’t expect to be pleasantly surprised. But I was. Life is like that. You never know what’s coming. You can’t. That’s why it’s called life. Not knowing is the whole point.
Don’t get so hung up on what you think you know that you forget there’s always something new to learn. The phone will fall again, but today, it’s still shiny and new. Enjoy the moment. You never know when it’ll be the last one.
The Phone Will Fall Again.ckpt_1628:
Five years after my last one, I bought a new iPhone. I wasn’t overly excited. There were three reasons.
 It was time to upgrade, and the new one was faster and had a better camera. But it also cost more, and it wasn’t all that different from my previous model.
I was in a different country, and the red color was only available there. I like red. It makes the device look less serious and more like a tool. Plus, it’s a color as opposed to just another shade of grey, and it would stand out. I’m not a grey kind of guy, so red it was.
The third and final reason was that the new iPhone comes without a charger. It’s an environmentally conscious decision by Apple, and I’m happy they’re making it. At the same time, I’ve had a charger in my backpack for the last five years. I never needed to replace it. So now, I was finally forced to. I didn’t have a choice — but I also didn’t mind. It was about time. The old one was clunky and barely worked anymore.
When I took my new iPhone out of the box, I realized I had forgotten something: the screen protector. I always put one on right away, but for some reason, this time, I didn’t. I was in a different country, and I wasn’t sure if I’d find any at the local electronics store. I figured I’d deal with it later.
A few days later, I was back home. I went to the electronics store, and I bought a screen protector. I put it on, and a few days after that, I dropped my phone for the first time. It slipped out of my hand in the kitchen, but it landed on its back. No scratches.
A week later, I was at my girlfriend’s place. We were about to leave the house, and as I walked out the door, I dropped my phone again. This time, it fell on the street right in front of her house. I heard the plastic back break, and sure enough, it now has a big crack running across it.
“Damn it!” I said. “I knew this would happen. I just knew it. And now I have to get a new back, and it’ll probably cost 50 bucks, and argh!”
My girlfriend was a lot more zen about it than I was. “Well, you have phone insurance. I’m sure it’ll be okay. You can just get a new back. It’s not a big deal.”
I didn’t think it was a big deal either, but I was still angry that I had to deal with it. “I’ve never had a broken phone before. I’ve always been so careful. I knew it was coming. I knew it!”
My girlfriend didn’t understand. “What do you mean you knew it was coming?”
“I don’t know. Call it a hunch. A gut feeling. I just knew I’d break this phone.”
We went on our way, and I forgot about the whole thing. Until I got home and remembered that I had bought Apple Care, Apple’s extended warranty for their products, for my new iPhone. “Oh! I have insurance!”
I checked the terms, and sure enough, you get two incidents of accidental damage covered, and the back of an iPhone is one of the cheapest parts to fix. I scheduled a Genius Bar appointment at my local Apple store, and a few days later, I was a happy owner of an intact iPhone once again.
When I reflected on the whole experience, I realized: I had known the phone would fall from the moment I took it out of the box and noticed it had no screen protector. It was a subconscious decision to not get one right then and there, and it was made so I could learn a lesson. The lesson was that, even if I drop my phone, the world will still keep turning.
It’s easy to get obsessed with details when you’re a self-employed creative. You want everything to go exactly as planned, and when it doesn’t, you get angry. That’s a trap many of us fall into, and while it’s important to get back on track, it’s also important to not let the anger get to you.
I’ve had a lot of lucky breaks in my career, and I’ve also worked very hard to get to where I am. But no matter how hard I work, there’ll always be things I can’t control, and no matter how much luck I have, sometimes, bad things will happen. That’s life — and it’s nothing to be angry about.
The phone will fall again, and so will I. That’s okay. I can always get a new back.

Life Is What We Do Next.original:
Electing a new pope is never easy, but in the movie Conclave, it appears to be impossible. The voting rounds of over 100 cardinals, locked away behind closed doors, are plagued by sexual scandals, bribery, and even Muslim acts of terror.
One by one, initially favored candidates fade away, and it all plays into the hands of the ultraconservative cardinal Goffredo Tedesco. At one point, he claims the papacy should go to someone “who fights these animals.” For the first time, a quiet cardinal who arrived only at the last minute raises his voice.
Vincent Benitez, who spent his ministry in the Congo, Baghdad, and Kabul, calls Tedesco out: “When you say we have to fight, what is it you think we’re fighting?” The real battle lies “inside each and every one of us,” Benitez explains. Having watched the conclave play out from the sidelines, his main observation is that “these last few days we have shown ourselves to be small, petty men, concerned only with ourselves, with Rome, with these elections, with power.”
“But things are not the Church,” Benitez continues. “The Church is not tradition. The Church is not the past. The Church is what we do next.”
A long silence follows. No one wants to admit it yet, but Benitez’ words left their mark. And by the next morning, when every cardinal holds yet another slip of paper in their hand, they still don’t all agree, but they have learned one lesson: Electing a new pope is not impossible, but it will take a lot of humility, working together, and, as all good things that come out of the Church, faith to get it done.
What struck me most about Benitez’ speech, however, is that you could replace the word “Church” not only with just about any other organization, but even with the word “life,” and it’d still make perfect sense. We are not our lowest common denominator. We are not our greatest fear. And we are definitely not who we were yesterday. Whatever obstacle will drop into your path today, remember: Life is not how we got here. Life is what we do next.

His only friend is a young priest, and together, they are trying to make sense of the mess. One day, the guard asks the priest why he became a priest. “I guess I wanted to make a difference,” he says.
The guard scoffs. “I’ve been a soldier for 20 years. I’ve seen the worst of humanity. And I’ve seen the best of humanity. I’ve seen people dying to save other people. And I’ve seen people killing to get a pair of shoes. And you know what? It doesn’t make a difference. But I’m still here. I’m still a soldier. That’s what we do. We just keep going.”
The priest is taken aback. “What are you saying? That we shouldn’t even try? That it’s all pointless?”
The guard shakes his head. “No. I’m saying life is what we do next.”
The guard’s perspective is both bleak and hopeful at the same time. On the one hand, he acknowledges that, no matter how hard we try, we can’t control the world. We can’t control what other people do, and we can’t control what happens to us. But on the other hand, we can always do something — anything — and that something will always make a difference.
It might not be the difference we intended to make, but it will be a difference nonetheless. We can’t know in advance what that difference will be, but we can be sure that it will be a difference worth making — because we chose to make it.
Life is what we do next. It’s a simple but profound reminder that, no matter what happens, we are never powerless. We can always choose to take the next step, and that step will always lead us somewhere new.
We might not always know where we’re going, but we can always trust that the journey will be worth taking. So let’s keep going. Let’s keep making a difference. And let’s remember that, no matter what, life is what we do next.

Rhubarb.original:
That’s the keyword in my family to remind everyone it’s time to take action. When my dad and I have been sitting at the dining table for too long, philosophizing, one might say, “Rhubarb!” Then, we’ll finally get up and go for our daily walk.
The German word for “rhubarb” is “Rhabarber.” More so than just describing a vegetable, it is also a common way of pointing out when someone is jabbering. It even sounds like “blah blah,” especially if you repeat it thrice for dramatic effect: “Rhabarber, Rhabarber, Rhabarber.” In fact, there’s a whole family of tongue twisters built around the word, and even a funny song describing “Barbara’s rhubarb bar.”
So when my dad is annoyed at having the umpteenth meeting of the day, he might walk out of his office, roll his eyes, and say, “Rhabarber, Rhabarber.” When a friend tells me to get to the point, they might cut me off with “Rhabarber!” It’s a decisive, not always friendly but mostly endearing way of reminding someone: “Hey. You’re yapping. Let’s get a move on.”
My friend Mike says “ banana ” whenever he gets angry. Then, he eats one and calms down instead of yelling at his wife. My family uses “rhubarb” as a way to make everyone laugh and call each other to action.
Which keyword can open new doors for you and the people around you? Have a think, but don’t rhubarb for too long—the quirkier, the easier it is to remember, and, chances are, even the weird ones will grow on you.

It’s a bit of a stretch, but you could say the word rhubarb has become a synonym for “let’s go.”
We have many such words, don’t we? “Ready?” “Go!” “Come on!” “Let’s do this!” They’re all stand-ins for the same thing: spurring ourselves and others into action. Often, it doesn’t matter what we do as long as we do something. That’s why we have these words. So we can get moving. To the gym. To the grocery store. To our friend’s house. To the couch for a movie marathon.
Sometimes, we need a different kind of nudge. A nudge to think, to feel, to pause, to wait. “Rhubarb!” can do that too. It’s a break from routine. A moment of reflection. A chance to breathe. The word itself barely matters. What does is the meaning we ascribe to it.
Choose your words wisely, and remember: You can make any word mean anything.

The Pacifist Who Stuck to His Guns.original:
The intro of Trigun, an anime from 1998, shows a badass guy with spiky blond hair on a distant, deserted planet, walking around in a cool red coat and slinging a massive gun. As soon as the show begins, however, all of the macho-action vibes fade away.
We see Vash helplessly running away from bandits trying to cash in on the 60 billion double-dollar bounty on his head. We see him chasing after girls and stuffing his face with donuts. And the more we get to know the dorky, child-loving, friendly, couldn’t-hurt-a-fly Vash, the more we wonder: Is anything ever going to happen in this show? Of course, it eventually does—because with such a fat price tag on him, bounty hunters of all shapes and sizes can never resist targeting Vash for too long.
Soon, we learn that Vash is actually rather powerful. In fact, he can deal with almost any adversary in seconds. For some reason, however, he usually chooses not to. Vash only steps in when someone’s about to get hurt, and, most of the time, the day ends with everyone home safe and sound. Here is a guy who could wipe out entire towns yet constantly talks about “love and peace!”
Naturally, the people Vash befriends throughout the show are puzzled by his behavior. The two ladies from the insurance company tasked with tracking him down, for example, mistake him for someone else throughout several encounters until realizing they actually have found Vash. “The humanoid typhoon? A donut-loving guy like this? No way!”
One of Vash’s friends in particular, Nicholas D. Wolfwood, a former bounty hunter—and also a priest with a huge cross for a gun—cannot parse Vash’s attitudes to life. Wolfwood is used to shooting bad people in order to protect those he deems good. Seeing Vash refuse to do the same, even when life gets really, really dangerous, makes him question our hero’s ideals, and not just in his head.
In the end, however, there is one trait above all that allows Vash to move everyone, first in their hearts and then to his side: stubbornness. Vash is so pigheaded, so unrelenting in his insistence on love, peace, and happiness, that, sooner or later, all of his friends come around—if only for being so annoyed by his persistence, they throw up their arms and say, “Fine, we’ll do it your way!” That’s both inspiring and, when someone aspires to ideals like Vash’s, worth emulating.
Trigun is a fun pastime but also a complex show that asks many questions about ethics, philosophy, and morality. It holds many a good lesson one can learn, but for me, the most memorable one was this: When you know you’re on the right side of history, do what the humanoid typhoon would do, and stick to your guns. Sooner or later, the world will come around—and even if they don’t, at least you’ll have stuck your neck out for what’s right.

You’re the man I want to kill.” Vash tries to run away, but the man chases him. He shoots at Vash, and Vash keeps running. Eventually, Vash finds a hiding spot, but the man finds him. He shoots Vash in the arm, and Vash falls to the ground. The man approaches Vash, and Vash pleads with him. “Please, don’t do this. I don’t want to die.” The man raises his gun, and Vash closes his eyes. But then, the man lowers his gun. He turns around and walks away. Vash opens his eyes and sees the man walking away. He’s not sure what just happened, but he’s glad to be alive.
Vash is the kind of guy who never gives up. He’s the kind of guy who always tries to find a peaceful solution. He’s the kind of guy who always looks for the best in people. Vash is a pacifist, but he’s also a fighter. He’s a fighter for peace. And that’s what makes him so inspiring. He’s not just a character in an anime. He’s a symbol of hope. A symbol of what we can all be if we just try a little harder. If we just have a little more faith in humanity.
Vash the Stampede is a pacifist who stuck to his guns. And that’s why he’s one of the most inspiring characters I’ve ever seen.

A Farewell to Clubbing.original:
When my new co-worker told me she loved the Berlin nightlife, I tried to remember the last time I went to a club. It took me a solid ten minutes. I realized I had even been to one last year during a bachelor party—but before then? No clue.
There was a time when I went out every weekend, sometimes twice. It used to be important to me. Now, it isn’t. That’s how life goes. Priorities shift.
There are still parts of the nightlife I enjoy to this day. I like dancing. I like EDM music. But I don’t need to go to a club to enjoy them. I can do that at home all day long. So the unique aspects of the experience which make me “me” as “a clubber,” well, those I haven’t lost. Perhaps they were always there, and the clubbing just emphasized them.
Usually, our priorities change before we can notice. When we do, we might feel sad or at least nostalgic. We “lost” something, after all. But did we, really? Think about it. Chances are, you’ll find an aspect of your former self that’s still alive and kicking —and that won’t go out of fashion like your past habits.
You are always you, and in everything you do, you’ll reveal a few pieces of yourself. Those pieces don’t change nearly as much as your day-to-day activities, and that’s a wonderful comfort when it’s yet again time to say goodbye —to clubbing, for example. Not counting bachelor parties, that is.

It’s not about being old, either. I’m only 31. I just don’t like the loud music, the alcohol, the crowds, the darkness, the smoke, and the noise. I like quiet, calm, and a good conversation with a friend. I like the sun, fresh air, and a good meal. I like going to bed early, reading, and waking up early to write. It’s not better, it’s just different.
It’s okay to change your mind. You can stop doing things you used to like. You can pick up new habits. You can say no to old friends and yes to new ones. You can start over. You can change your mind about changing your mind.
Don’t be afraid to let go of the old. Life is about change. Embrace it, and you’ll always be on the right track.

’t even remember the name of the place. It was a small club in Munich, and I went with two friends. I do remember it was a hip hop night, and I remember the bouncer. “You guys look like nerds. I like nerds. Go on in!”

Whether you like it or not, clubbing is rarely a free lunch. The music might be cheap, but the drinks will cost you. So will the late nights, the hangovers, and the regrets. If you can get the same feeling from a good playlist, a few beers, and some living room dance-offs with friends, that’s a much better deal.
Life is short. Don’t pay too much for anything—especially experiences you can get for free.

Anchored.original:
When you join the crypto industry, people will warn you: “This space is 24/7/365. Be careful. Don’t get sucked in too far, or you’ll burn out quickly.” It’s true. Thankfully, I already did all of that in 2017.
After first falling down the crypto rabbit hole, I’d spend hours every day on Twitter, Youtube, and Telegram, soaking up information, learning everything that I could, trying to find the next big coin. But after a few months, the bull market ended, I didn’t get filthy rich, and I realized: “Okay, you don’t have to do that. Life will go on either way.” But bull markets come and go—and they’re all intoxicating for different reasons. So “ I’ve done this before ” isn’t the real reason I’m not worried about my new job becoming all-consuming.
In 2017, I was a college student. Working full-time for myself to earn an okay-ish income, but still also a college student. I had time. I was single. My vision for my writing wasn’t very clear. I often lived day-to-day, and when you do, it’s easy for any particular wave of life to come in and sweep you away.
Today, I’m an engaged man. I live with my fiancée, and my rent is twice as high. I know exactly which books I want to write, and I know how long it’ll take me. In other words: I don’t have time for shenanigans. Distraction is a luxury, and with a full-time job, I can only afford it in small doses. This might sound like it creates pressure, and sometimes, it does. But mostly, it feels liberating. It makes me proud of every minute I spend writing my next book—and it makes it easy to close my work laptop when the day is over.
I’ve long believed that when we’re young, we value complete freedom too highly. That’s why I worked a lot in my 20s, and it gave me a career foundation that can last a lifetime. Some of my high school friends also settled down quite early in their lives. They got married, built houses, had kids. Floating through life like a butterfly in the wind has its moments but, to me, it seems it’s never a bad time to be anchored. Life consists entirely of tradeoffs. Sooner or later, we’re all forced to make the hard ones. There is no shame in facing that game when you’re young, in playing it early and getting better at it rather than trying to escape it.
It’s ironic but almost typical, the kind of joke life likes to play on us: If you want to see how high you can fly, you actually need an anchor—and you’ll spread your wings as soon as you pick the right one.

I’m not sure if it’s the right thing to do, but it feels like the right thing to do. And that’s good enough for me.

I still have my investments, of course. I still enjoy the industry. And I still follow the news from time to time. But I’m no longer trying to ride the cutting edge at all times. I’m not trying to catch every next wave as it forms. I’m happy to stay ashore, work on my tan, and enjoy the view.
The best thing about anchoring yourself to a job you like is that you no longer feel tempted to go wherever the wind seems to blow the most money. You have a safe harbor to return to, and you can dip your toes into the water as needed.
Don’t let any one activity sweep you away entirely — even if it’s something you love.

Amending Your Words.original:
During his second year at Hogwarts, Dumbledore tells Harry Potter that “help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it.” And for the next five years, Harry operates under that mantra.
In their very final encounter, however, when Voldemort is just about to destroy everything, Dumbledore has a rather late realization. “I’ve always prided myself on my ability to turn a phrase,” he tells Harry. “But I would in this case amend my original statement to this: Help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who deserve it.”
While this doesn’t change much in hindsight and is mainly meant to encourage Harry for his final task, it’s not hard to imagine our young protagonist severely scratching his head over Dumbledore’s gaffe—or outright losing it, for that matter. “Ummm, professor, there’s a big difference between asking and earning. Couldn’t you have thought of that, like, at any sooner point in time whatsoever?! “
Alas, life is not how we’d like it to be. Life is how it is. Even geniuses forget things. So the best we can do is say what we truly mean to say as soon as it is revealed in our hearts—and then all of us, together, will have to deal with the consequences. Usually, we’re still better for it in the end.
It’s never too late to amend your words. Don’t be afraid to do it.

’t ask for help, how can it be given? But in the final installment of the series, Harry learns that the line was never meant to be an absolute. In a moment of crisis, Harry asks Dumbledore’s portrait for advice. The painting says nothing. “But you told me I would always have a way out,” Harry claims. “You told me that help would always be there.”
“I said that help would always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it,” Dumbledore corrects him. “But the question was always going to be whether you would ask for it.”
The point is that Dumbledore never said “always” twice. The first time, he was talking about the school. The second time, he was talking about Harry. But in his mind, Harry had merged the two, and it took him a while to realize that the offer of help was only as good as his willingness to accept it.
We do this all the time. We hear something once, and we file it away in our brains forever. That’s fine for some things. The sky is blue, and water is wet. But when it comes to opinions, ideas, and decisions, our minds must stay flexible.
I once told a friend that I thought the word “happiness” was a bad word to use. I argued that it was too vague, too fleeting, and too much of a moving target to be of any use. I suggested “contentment” as a better alternative. My friend disagreed. We debated the matter for a while, but ultimately, he convinced me that I was wrong. I changed my mind. Now, I think happiness is a perfectly fine word to use.
The next time I saw that friend, he brought up the discussion. “Oh yeah, you told me happiness was a bad word.” I reminded him that I had changed my mind. “What do you mean? I thought you were convinced of your argument.” “I was,” I said, “but I’m no longer. I’ve amended my words.”
Amending your words is a good habit. You won’t do it for every sentence you utter, but you should do it for the important ones. The ones that matter. The ones you believe in.
Don’t hold on to your opinions for too long. Keep an open mind. Remember that help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it. But the question will always be whether you’ll ask for it.

Doubt Over Certainty.original:
“Some people are chosen to be shepherds. Others to manage the farm. You’re a manager. So manage.” Those were the last words cardinal Thomas Lawrence, played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie Conclave, heard from the pope before he died. So naturally, the day he opens the papal conclave to elect his successor, no one expects him to say anything much interesting. But Cardinal Lawrence surprises.
After the boring, obligatory opening remarks, Lawrence goes off script: “Let me speak from the heart for a moment.” Lawrence knows he’s kicking off an election already divided into camps committed to varying degrees of traditionalism. There are favorites. There are plots. And everyone thinks their candidate is the right one. So, instead of just endorsing someone, he says:
“There is one sin which I have come to fear above all others: Certainty. Certainty is the great enemy of unity. Certainty is the deadly enemy of tolerance. Even Christ was not certain at the end. ‘My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?’ he cried out in his agony at the ninth hour on the cross. Our faith is a living thing precisely because it walks hand-in-hand with doubt. If there was only certainty and no doubt, there would be no mystery—and therefore no need for faith. Let us pray that God will grant us a Pope who doubts.”
Certainty is easy. It’s comforting. And you can pick it from whichever source you like these days. For every single thing you hope to believe, there is a salesperson somewhere on the internet, praying the exact gospel you seek.
To doubt is to live in the fog. To exist between opinions rather than be made up of them. It can feel uneasy —but also liberating. As long as you keep the door open to the possibility you might be wrong, a better idea is always just one step away.
The Church, too, needs better ideas. That’s what it hopes for from every next pope. Will it be one who doubts? If every cardinal were to do so, the answer would be a guaranteed “Yes.” Elected official or not, choose doubt over certainty—for the most beautiful blossoms are usually the offspring of humble minds coming together.

“Some of you have already decided who will be the next pope. Others have already decided who it won’t be. But if you’re sure you know who should be pope, you don’t need to be here. If you’re sure you know who shouldn’t be pope, you don’t need to be here. The only reason to be here is doubt.”
Doubt. The kind of doubt that forces you to listen. To listen to the other cardinals. To listen to the Holy Spirit. To listen to your heart. Doubt is the only thing that can make you change your mind. And it is only when you change your mind that you can change the world.
Doubt over certainty. That’s the message. And that’s why, in a room full of cardinals, it’s the young, new, and inexperienced one who stands up and says: “I will vote for Cardinal Lawrence.”

In the scene, Cardinal Lawrence is trying to convince the other cardinals to vote for someone other than the obvious choice. But in the movie, he is also trying to convince us, the audience. And in life, that’s what we do, isn’t it? We’re trying to convince everyone, including ourselves.
When the pope told him he was a manager, Lawrence didn’t question his faith. He didn’t ask, “Are you sure?” He just accepted. But now that the pope is gone, Lawrence is free to ask that question. “What if I’m wrong?” It’s a good question. It’s the only question.
We’re not elected to be cardinals. We don’t get to pick the pope. But we do choose our roles in life. We choose to be managers, shepherds, gardeners, and accountants. The problem is we often choose in haste. We pick a side too quickly, and then we cling to it for dear life.
But life isn’t about certainty. It’s about doubt. Doubt over certainty. That’s the true way of the world. So let’s not be so sure of ourselves. Let’s keep questioning. Let’s keep managing, shepherding, gardening, accounting. And if we must choose, let’s choose doubt.

Work Hard, Be Nice, Sleep Well.original:
Back when I used Twitter, I made a simple header image for my profile. It was a reminder to myself of the philosophy I wanted to carry from my life onto the platform. The picture showed a Venn diagram of two overlapping circles. In one circle, I put the words “work hard.” In the other, I put “be nice.” In the intersection, there was the word “win.” Word hard, be nice, win. That was the idea.
It’s been years since I deleted that account, and while I absolutely still believe that working hard and being nice are not only the way to win but the right way to win, I would now amend my words to an even more durable mantra: Work hard, be nice, sleep well.
For all our efforts and kindness, winning is not guaranteed in this life. Sometimes, it takes a lifetime to win. The key to being okay regardless whether your rewards grow at warp speed or a snail’s pace is seeing the way to win as a win in and of itself.
At the end of each day, knowing you did your best, resting in the warm glow of having been kind, and getting a good night’s sleep might only be little wins —but maybe they’re all the wins we truly need.

Sleep well, work hard, be nice. That’s the real formula. It’s not a Venn diagram. It’s a chain. You need all three links for it to hold. If you’re missing one, the chain breaks, and so will you. You’ll work hard but not be nice. You’ll be nice but not work hard. Or you’ll do both but not sleep well, and so you’ll be too tired to keep going.
Sleep well, work hard, be nice. It’s not a guarantee of success, but it is a guarantee of happiness. It’s a way of being that’ll allow you to keep going, and that’s the most important thing.
