The only reason to make calculated moves in business is to save time and money. If you know you can save 20% on a deal by approaching the seller through a back channel, that’s a smart move. If you want to get someone to buy your product, however, the only way to do it is to show up and say: “Hey! I made this. I think it’s great, and I hope you will too. Do you want to buy it?” That’s it. There’s no other way. Everything else is a detour, and if you take too many of those, you’ll never reach your goal.
If you want to sell something, sell it. If you want to collaborate, suggest a collaboration. And if you want to get to know someone, just say hi. There’s nothing wrong with being professional, but if professionalism means you can’t be authentic, you’re doing it wrong. Don’t make calculated moves when life requires an honest approach.

Squeezing Too Early.original:
It’s possible to write a daily blog in 15 minutes. Even ten. Even five. The question is how many minutes went into it before you started typing?
Sometimes, the very spontaneous, off the cuff, almost-stream-of-consciousness pieces turn out amazing. Most of the time, they don’t. If nothing went in, how can anything come out?
When you press a dry sponge, it releases no water. First, you must soak it. Continuing to fill an already-filled sponge merely changes the composition of the output. Squeeze too early, however, and you won’t get any output at all.
Don’t be afraid to keep inhaling.

I know people who can write a blog post in five minutes, but it’s only because they’ve been thinking about that post for the last three weeks. They’ve been living it. Living the idea. Then, once it’s ripe, they can sit down and squeeze it out. That’s what we’re doing here. Squeezing ideas.
You can’t squeeze too early. If you do, you’ll only get a few drops. If you wait until the fruit is ripe, however, you’ll get a full glass of juice. Don’t squeeze too early.

In some days, I write multiple drafts, sit with them for hours, and then decide to publish none of them. That doesn’t mean those days were wasted. I can still use those drafts later. I can rework them. Or I can let them add up.
The more drafts I have sitting around, the more I’ve practiced. The more I’ve practiced, the higher the chance the next thing I write will be good. It’s as if I can “squeeze” more quality out of what I’ve previously written. I’m compressing it, and some of the juice ends up in my latest post.
If I squeeze my creative past too early, however, there won’t be any juice left. If I publish everything I write, I’ll run out of things to say. If I don’t save some of my best ideas for later, I won’t have any great ideas left for later.
It’s okay to compress. To squeeze the sponge and see what comes out. But make sure you have something to squeeze in the first place.

Nourishing in Increments.original:
One theme in Samurai Champloo is hunger. The protagonist, a teenage girl named Fuu, and her companions—two bickering swordsmen—are mainly trying to make it from meal to meal in feudal Japan.
In one episode, they discover a bag of gold in a river. Thrilled with their good fortune, they instantly treat themselves to a massive meal. As she does several times in the show, Fuu tries to eat in advance for the whole week. While it’s funny to see the anime character triple in size, we can guess where it’s going. By the time the episode’s adventure ends the next day, Fuu sits under a tree, looking slim as ever. With a big sigh, she goes: “I’m hungry.”
Some things, you can only nourish in increments. Humans. Love. Art. It’s nice to finally find a gap in the calendar for a big project—a trip with the family, shooting a short film—but it’s rarely needed and, sometimes, an outright excuse to not get started.
No tank can be filled to the point where it’ll never run out. The only way to not go hungry is to eat a little every day. Nourish the big things in increments.

One theme in Samurai Champloo is hunger. The protagonist, a teenage girl named Fuu, and her companions—two bickering swordsmen—are mainly trying to make it from meal to meal in feudal Japan.
They’re always broke, always hungry, and so they’re always looking for the next gig that’ll get them their next meal. When they’re not, they’re fighting for their lives, often against the very people who hired them. It’s a hard life, and it’s not one they chose. They just ended up in it, and now they must survive.
What I learned from Fuu and her friends is that, sometimes, you can only nourish yourself in increments. A little rice here, a little tea there. A few coins now, a new job later. It’s not the best situation, but it’s a situation you can work with.
The next time you feel like you’re starving, remember: A little nourishment is better than none at all, and a little nourishment is always available.

 but also “hunger,” Fuu will often say. “I’m hungry,” “he’s hungry,” “we’re all hungry.” It’s a running joke in the show, but it’s also a theme that permeates the whole story.
When the trio first meets, Fuu is starving. She’s a waitress in a tea house, and her boss won’t let her eat. When she does, she eats in increments. One stolen onigiri here, a few leftover scraps there. It’s only after she runs away with the two samurai that she gets to eat a proper meal.
The same applies to her dream of finding “the samurai who smells of sunflowers.” She can’t accomplish it in a day. She must do it one step at a time. And even though they don’t always get along, her two new friends also seem to be hungry for something. A home. A purpose. A sense of meaning. And so the three of them travel together.
Sometimes, the gang will have a lucky streak. They’ll find a kind merchant who feeds them, or they’ll earn some coin doing odd jobs. But they never get too far before their pockets and bellies are empty again. In one episode, they even win a huge amount of money, but it gets stolen before they can enjoy it.
When I started my first job, I thought I’d finally be set. I was so sick of being a broke college student. I would spend my weekends working at a call center, and I’d spend the money on a 2-euro slice of pizza. It was a far cry from the lifestyle I wanted to have. But even though my salary was 60x what I made in that call center, it still didn’t last very long. I could pay my rent, sure, but I couldn’t buy a car, nor could I travel the world. I was still hungry.
In a way, we are all hungry. Not just for food or money but for meaning, connection, and impact. These things, too, we can only attain in increments. A great meal won’t last you a week, and a big payday won’t last you a lifetime. In the same vein, a single painting won’t make you feel like a great artist, and neither will a single compliment from a fan.
It’s hard to accept that we’ll always be hungry. That there’ll always be something more to want, more to attain, more to feel, understand, and experience. But it’s also comforting. There’s always another meal to be had, another trip to be taken, another person to meet. We’ll never be done, but we’ll also never be bored.
Life is about nourishing yourself in increments. Some days you’ll have a feast, and on others you’ll be starving. Enjoy the former when you can, and endure the latter until it changes. After all, you’re not alone. We’re all hungry—but we’re also all in it together.

The Painter Who Couldn\u2019t See.original:
There once was a painter who couldn’t see. He wasn’t born blind. In fact, he enjoyed the gift of vision for the first 68 years of his life. Once he developed cataracts, however, the sense he relied most on to make his art began to darken—and so did his paintings.
The painter had lived a slow life in the countryside since his 40s. His favorite subjects were the plants in his garden. By the time his vision began to fade, he had been painting the same themes for a decade. On some days, despair caught hold of him. “Useless old fool!” he denounced himself as he slashed, painted over, and burned some of his works. Yet, on most days, he simply continued painting.
As the years went by, his sight ebbed and flowed. Near his 80s, he received a final request from his government: Paint your flowers on large canvases, so we may install them in large halls for the world to see. He painted some. He destroyed some. But in the end, he furnished over 40 large paintings of lilies swimming in the water.
By the time the painter closed his eyes for the last time, he was 86 years old. He had painted the same subject, water lilies, more than 250 times over the course of 30 years—and those marked just 10% of his body of work. He had also painted people, train stations, and hay stacks.
After his death, the government exhibited some of his works. People from all over the world marveled at the beautiful flowers on the walls. He had been a prolific artist, no doubt. But the water lilies—they stuck. Was it the 30 years of dedication? Or the struggle against his waning eyesight?
Whatever it was, even 100 years after his passing, anyone who witnesses his art can feel it: Via the indelible intention of his life, Claude Monet, the painter who couldn’t see, proved a fellow French artist right: “It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.”

The painter was Claude Monet, and by the time he was 82 years old, he could no longer see the world in anything but a blur. His paintings became less and less realistic, and more and more abstract. Monet’s final series, a collection of murals depicting his own garden, was completed when he was 86 years old. It was a series of water lilies, and the paintings were all in blue.
In his last years, Monet had a new lens on the world. His vision was different, but it was still a vision—and so he kept painting. In 2022, one of his water lilies sold for $50.3 million. It was the most expensive impressionist painting ever sold at auction. That’s how much a man’s vision is worth, even when it’s not perfect.
Sometimes, you’ll be the painter who can’t see. You won’t know what you’re doing, and you’ll have to work in the dark. But you’ll still be the painter, and so you must keep painting. You may not be able to see the big picture, but you can still add to it. Just keep showing up, and trust that, one day, the light will return.

There once was a painter who couldn’t see. He wasn’t born blind. In fact, he enjoyed the gift of vision for the first 68 years of his life. Once he developed cataracts, however, the sense he relied most on to make his art began to darken—and so did his paintings.
James McNeill Whistler was an American expat who spent most of his life in the UK. He was known for his moody paintings and witty, often provocative remarks. “The vast majority of English folk,” he said, “cannot and will not consider a picture as a picture, apart from any story it may be supposed to tell.” Whistler demanded people view art for its own sake, not as a means to an end.
After his mother died in 1881, Whistler’s paintings grew darker still. He painted a lot of seascapes, nocturnes, and cityscapes shrouded in fog. He received many awards for his work, including an honorary membership in the Royal Academy of Arts, which he declined.
In 1903, Whistler died in London. He was 69 years old. His eyesight had been deteriorating for years, but his last painting was finished only a few months before his death. It was a seascape, of course. A dark painting made by a painter who couldn’t see.

It\u2019s Not Time To Worry Yet.original:
When lawyer Atticus Finch is tasked with defending a Black man in 1933 Alabama, for the first time, the single dad to two preteens is forced to put his children through something they won’t understand. For months, they’ll have to endure the misgiving looks and hateful comments from all around town. Never mind the fact that the defendant is innocent. People believe what they want to believe.
Naturally, the central case in To Kill a Mockingbird dampens the mood around the Finches’ home. But through the many dark days, Atticus repeats one line again and again: “It’s not time to worry yet.”
When Jem, Atticus’ son, destroys an old lady’s flowerbed because she ridicules his dad, his sister Scout fears the consequences. “It’s not time to worry yet,” Atticus tells her. And sure enough, Jem survives his apology to Mrs. Dubose.
After Atticus loses the case, his family is outraged. How could the town do this to an innocent man? “It’s not time to worry yet,” Atticus goes. There’s an appeal to be held, and his client is far from dead.
To the book’s characters, each next challenge seems to be worse than the last, but for them as for us, it’s empowering to tack on one little word to a sentence that might otherwise be nothing more than outright denial: “It’s not time to worry yet.”
Don’t ignore harsh realities, but don’t lose your head either. Chances are, you’re not stuck in a guillotine—and it’s not time to worry yet.

For months, they’ll have to endure the misgiving looks and hateful comments from all around town. Never mind the fact that the defendant is innocent. People believe what they want to believe.
Naturally, Atticus’ son Jem is worried. He knows the situation is serious. He knows it’s not going to be easy. But he’s not sure how much he can take. “I’m not going to be able to take it,” he tells his father. “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Atticus says. “The way everybody’s talking about you and about us. I don’t know what they mean half the time.” “I don’t either, sometimes,” Atticus admits.
“Why don’t people like us any more?” Jem asks. “They do. They just don’t know us. I think they’re afraid of us a little.” “But why?” “Well, I think that’s because they don’t know us. They don’t know what we do in here. They don’t understand how we live. They don’t understand how and why we live the way we do because they don’t know us.”
“Is that why you’re doing it?” Jem asks. “Part of it,” Atticus says. “But there’s so much more to it than that.” “I don’t understand it,” Jem says. “Of course you don’t. Sometimes, I don’t either. And sometimes, I have to explain things twice, three times just to my own brother. You’re very young, Jem. You’ve had experiences in your life, but no real depth to them. You’ve never been challenged the way you’re being challenged now.”
“Is that why you’re doing it?” Jem asks again. “No,” Atticus says. “The main reason I’m taking this case is because if I didn’t, I couldn’t hold my head up in town. I couldn’t even tell you or Scout not to do something again.” “You mean it’s because you’re afraid?” Jem asks. “No,” Atticus says. “It’s not that. It’s because I’m afraid I won’t.”
When Jem asks him why he’s doing it again, Atticus says: “I want to be like you, even if it’s only for a moment. I want to be like you, somehow.” “It’s never for a moment, is it?” Jem says. “No,” Atticus admits. “It gets to you. It stays with you. It’s in you. Forever.” “How do you get rid of it?” Jem asks. “You don’t,” Atticus says. “Let it pass over you. Through you. And you let the words become just that: words.”
“Is that all they are?” Jem asks. “No,” Atticus says. “They could be a whole lot more. But if you let them, if you let it, that’s all they are.” “Is it always like that?” Jem asks. “No,” Atticus says. “Sometimes, you have to do things just because they’re right.” “Why?” Jem asks. “Because it’s the right thing to do,” Atticus says.
“Even when people hate you for it?” Jem asks. “Especially then,” Atticus says. “Am I going to hate you for it?” Jem asks. “I don’t know,” Atticus says. “I hope not.” “But it’s going to be hard, isn’t it?” Jem asks. “Yes, it is,” Atticus says. “Is it always going to be like this?” Jem asks. “I don’t know,” Atticus says. “I hope not.”
“Why?” Jem asks. “Because I don’t want you to have to go through this,” Atticus says. “I don’t want you to have to feel this.” “But I do,” Jem says. “I do. And I’m scared.” “I know you are,” Atticus says. “But it’s not time to worry yet. It’s not time to be afraid. Not yet. Not now. Not today. Not tomorrow. Not for a long time.”
“Why?” Jem asks. “Because I’m here,” Atticus says. “I’m here. And I’m not going anywhere. Not today. Not tomorrow. Not for a long time. I’m here. And I’m not going anywhere. Not today. Not tomorrow. Not for a long time.”
“Promise?” Jem asks. “I promise,” Atticus says. “I promise.”

When lawyer Atticus Finch is tasked with defending a Black man in 1933 Alabama, for the first time, the single dad to two preteens is forced to put his children through something they won’t understand. For months, they’ll have to endure the misgiving looks and hateful comments from all around town. Never mind the fact that the defendant is innocent. People believe what they want to believe.
“Do you really think there’s a chance, Atticus?” his daughter Scout asks him. “Well, if I didn’t, I couldn’t live in this town,” he responds. “I couldn’t hold my head up.” “Do you think they’ll take Tom Robinson’s life?” “I don’t know, Scout.” And then, as if he was talking to himself, Atticus goes on: “I don’t know, but I gotta do it. I couldn’t go to church and worship God if I didn’t try to help that man.”
As the trial gets underway, Atticus is called “nigger-lover” in the street. His children are beaten up by their school friends. It’s all very stressful, but through it all, Atticus maintains a kind yet stern face. “I’m not worried yet,” he tells his brother. “I want to keep this in perspective.” And when his daughter tells him she’s not sure she can take any more of the insults, he simply reminds her: “You just hold your head high, and keep those fists down.”
It’s easy to let our troubles get to us. To worry about the worry before the worry has even begun. But Atticus Finch reminds us that it’s not time to worry yet. There’s no need to get worked up over a future that might not happen. Only time will tell, and time is something we all have as long as we’re alive.
Stay in the moment. Keep your head high, and your fists down. There’s always a chance tomorrow will be a good day — and until it’s over, so are you.

The Eternity Mindset.original:
I’m writing this blog in 23 minutes, but I try to believe I have all the time in the world.
The other day, I was watching a TV show with my mom. Three renowned, German chefs travel across the US and Canada in a mobile home. At one point, the oldest of the guys reminds them that he’s almost 60. “I’ll be lucky if I see another 25 summers.” Ali, who’s ten years younger, gets visibly emotional on camera. “We really don’t have that much time!”
It’s true. There are only so many hours in this life, and if we don’t grab a good chunk of them and dedicate them to the things we truly care about, they’ll be gone before we now it. Hence, this blog. Every morning.
That said, over the years, I have discovered urgency only helps on one time frame: the 24 hours you are on right now. Beyond that, short-sighted thinking and mid-term pressure have done nothing for me. I discovered I mainly wanted to write books in 2021. All of the detours I took since then to make money, they feel like distractions. And many of them didn’t work out regardless.
You’d think writing books is an extreme example of goals which take a long time, but is it? Writing great songs. Being an exemplary parent. Building a local community. None of that happens in a year or two.
I don’t know what it was about Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, but that book showed me the eternity mindset : Put in a little work every day, but pretend you have endless lifetimes to accomplish what counts. Will it yield better books, sounder choices, a happier life? I’m too young to know—but I guess I have all the time in the world to find out.

I’m writing this blog in 23 minutes, but I try to believe I have all the time in the world. That’s what it feels like when you have a mission. You’re not worried about the details. You’re not worried about the timeline. You know you’ll get there eventually, so you just keep driving.
You don’t need a map. You don’t need directions. You don’t need to know how you’ll navigate the next turn. You just need to keep going. You need to keep driving. The path will unfold in front of you. You’ll know the next exit to take when you get there.
The only way to waste your time is to stop driving. To throw your hands up in the air and say, “I don’t know what to do.” That’s a lie. You always know what to do. You always know the next step. The next step might be a wrong turn, but even that will lead you somewhere. You can always come back. You can always try something else. You can always U-turn and take a different exit.
What you can’t do is stop driving. You can’t let the car sit idle. You can’t drift along at one mile per hour. You need to keep driving. You need to go fast. You need to go fast so you can take the turns. You need to go fast so you can go far. You need to go fast so you can take wrong turns, U-turn, and find the right path. You need to go fast so you can have a real mission. So you can feel like you have all the time in the world.
The only way to waste your time is to stop driving. Don’t stop driving.

No Time To Explain.original:
In July 2010, someone on the BitcoinTalk forum challenged Satoshi Nakamoto on the scalability of his experimental, peer-to-peer payment network. After several users discussed the issue, Satoshi eventually weighed in, addressing some assumptions and pointing to a prior post for more of his thoughts on the topic. He ended his entry with a line that has been making the rounds in the crypto community ever since: “If you don’t believe me or don’t get it, I don’t have time to try to convince you, sorry.”
You are on your own journey. At times, you, too, won’t have time to explain yourself to everyone. The people who are meant to get it will, and of those who don’t, plenty will accept it without blinking twice. The rest? They’ll have to come to their own conclusions.
Having good answers ready is useful and worth working for. But at a number of crossroads, the only way forward is to be okay with leaving some questions unanswered. Sometimes, there’s just no time to explain.

The Inside View.original:
I’ve been surprised at my own observations since taking a full-time job. Having been self-employed for a decade before, I guessed my views would be different than most people’s, and they are, but not in the way I expected.
Everything is still new, sure, yet I barely feel “stuck in the everyday humdrum,” even when attending lots of meetings. I seem to have more energy, not less, and even the additional work of writing in the mornings comes surprisingly naturally. I also barely spend time on company politics or industry news, and, so far, it doesn’t affect my work negatively at all.
It’s also been funny to observe my friends’ observations. “That sounds hellish,” one commented on my schedule. If you had told me about it before the job, I probably would have thought the same. But now that I’m in it, it actually feels fine.
“It must not light your inner fire, but at least it pays the bills,” another said. It’s true that the subject matter is not the end-all, be-all for me, but I do find every day at work interesting, and, ironically, I spend more time on my next book than I did before.
“I hope you’re getting the coffee orders right!” Okay, that one was mostly a joke, but again: To my own surprise as much as anyone else’s, I’ve been working on important projects from day one. I’ve even got my own major initiative to carry.
The inside view is always different. You’ll never see life from the exact same vantage point as anyone else, and even the most common of sense often doesn’t apply. The best you can do? Withhold judgment where you’re able, and offer it loosely held where you can’t. Turn opinions into questions, allow yourself to frequently update your perspective, and wherever you’re the one seeing what no one else can see, be grateful for the inside view.

Finally, I’ve realized that even if you’re not the boss, you can still make a difference. I’ve never had more of a say in what I’m doing than I have now, and I’ve never felt more empowered to try and change things for the better. It’s a different kind of empowerment than being your own boss, but it’s still empowering.
I’m not sure how long I’ll stay in my current role, but I’m glad I took it. It’s always good to get a new perspective, and sometimes, the only way to do that is to literally sit in a new chair.

I don’t mind if it takes up most of my time and energy. In fact, I think it’s a good thing. It’s nice to have a singular focus. To feel like I’m doing something bigger than myself. It’s a welcome break from constantly fretting about how to pay for everything, and it’s nice to have a team you can go to when you’re stuck.
Finally, I thought I’d be more worried about my autonomy. “What if they want me to do something I don’t like? What if I don’t control my vacation days?” Surprisingly, I find the lack of autonomy rather soothing. It’s nice to not have to think about certain things. I can just do my work, then go home and not think about work at all. If I don’t want to take two weeks off in August, I don’t have to. I can just keep working, and that’s fine too. There’s a lot of peace to be found in letting go of control.
The point is that no matter how much you think you know about something, you’ll always discover new things once you get the inside view. You can’t judge a book by its cover, and you can’t know what it’s like to be a bee without flying with one. If you’re not sure about something, try it! You might be surprised at how much you’ll learn — and how much you’ll like it.

There’s the timeline you’d like to be on and the one life chooses for you. Know when to pause your diet, and remember: Every now and then, it’s okay to put pleasure before work.

Important Ideas Will Come Back.original:
I used to regret not writing down ideas for posts that came to me at night. I wanted to hold on to every flash of insight. Even back then, rationally, I knew most of my ideas wouldn’t be great, but I thought, “Hey, if I don’t ship all of them, how will I ever find out which ones resonate with people?”
There is one problem with that approach: Trying to realize all of your ideas is exhausting. Even in an arena like writing blog posts, where you can ship a lot and do it quickly, you’ll never be able to do everything, so no matter how hard you try, you’ll always come up short. And if you’re a designer, video maker, or data analyst? Forget about it. You’ll have to choose carefully from the start.
Once I accepted that I’d never be able to publish everything, most individual ideas seemed to matter a lot less. Now, it doesn’t matter whether I post this draft or that one. What matters is that posts go out every day. Ironically, this turned out to be a better filter for good ideas than hoping the market would decide for me. Whatever I can’t publish for a while, will I come back to it organically? Does it pop into my head again unannounced? If I forgot the idea as soon as I woke up the next morning, it can’t have been that important, can it?
Will I lose some good, perhaps even some great ideas by not scribbling every stray thought onto a piece of paper? Probably. But I will skip a lot more bad ones I’ll never have to think about again, let alone turn them into paper planes which’ll never take flight.
Don’t be afraid to let go of the unassessed. Important ideas will come back to you—and the ones you’re truly meant to share won’t leave you alone until destiny is satisfied.

This applies to more than just writing. If you forget to buy your partner a gift, that’s a problem. If you forget to send a thank-you email to a colleague, that’s also a problem. But if you forget to check out a new coffee shop that you only heard about once, that’s probably not a big deal.
The important things will come back to you. Trust that. Don’t stress about the little things.

Passion Seeps Through.original:
Weeb Jail is something else. It’s as if 13-year-old me had moved to Japan and started a Youtube channel. So, whenever the unnamed but self-proclaimed “King of Weeaboos” returns, I press play. This time it took nine months, but, as usual, WJ did not disappoint.
Until today, I had never heard of karuta before. 30 minutes later, I feel the incessant urge to learn and master the game. That’s because, as WJ explains in his mini-documentary about an anime, a competitive card game, and his own experience with both: “Passion is contagious. It doesn’t even matter what you’re passionate about. What matters is that you are. And sometimes, if that passion is great enough, it won’t even matter to you, either. What matters is it’s there.”
Weeb Jail, for example, was the only one passionate enough about Steins;Gate, one of my all-time favorite anime shows, to make a video analysis for every single episode. That’s how I found him and why I stuck with him. But he’s clearly also passionate about making videos, because whereas he usually sits in his room, this time, he filmed himself, the karuta players at a local club, even a whole music clip for the intro of his video. That, too, is contagious.
Passion seeps through, and while it’s inspiring when it rubs off enough to cause real change, even just witnessing it makes us feel alive. Get your dose of passion every day.

Passion seeps through. It’s not always obvious, but it’s always there. Look for it in others, and let it shine through your work.

Engaged.original:
The word “engaged” means a lot of things. For one, it means “busy.” “Occupied.” “Already in use.” By the time you agree to marry someone, that sure will be the case. You’ll already have seen your fair share of love. With each other. With the others. But now, you agree to hold out for someone special, and, in the meantime, no one else shall take that special place.
To engage also means to attract. To hire. To enter into combat with an enemy, even. Marriage will also be all of those. Sometimes, you’ll feel attracted to one another. At other times, you’ll be fighting. In any case, you’ve hired each other. “I want you to be my partner for life. No one else can do that job.” It’s a decision that needs settling into, but not one to take lightly.
There are, however, more interesting definitions still. Architecturally speaking, an engaged column is one attached to a wall. Ideally, that’s what your partner will be, won’t they? A forever-supporter to have your back so that, even if you crumble, you won’t fall completely.
In any well-oiled machine, meanwhile, all parts must be engaged. If the gears don’t interlock, the bearings don’t move, the screws don’t hold, the engine won’t go. The clutch must connect to the driveshaft. If it doesn’t, your horsepower will never make it onto the road. That, too, is engagement. To become two parts of one whole, a team that is better and can, ultimately, only function together.
In some ways, etymologically, we’ve come full circle. The original stem of the word “engagement” meant “to pawn,” “to pledge” something or, well, someone—usually oneself. Now, we live in a world where engagement is most commonly associated with large companies trying to hold our attention just long enough until they can sell it to the highest bidder. It’s a different kind of pawning, but pawned we are at the end —and we pay dearly to cover the interest.
In that sense, perhaps my favorite interpretation of the word is “involved.” To consistently give your partner the gift of your presence is, after all, a much more lasting commitment—and sometimes sacrifice—than however much money one might cough up for a ring. “Yes.” That’s the answer we’re all hoping for.  But not just, “Yes, I want to do the ceremony, have the party, wear the suit.” It’s “Yes, I want to be involved. Supporter or connector, entertainer or sparring partner, I’ll be here every day.” That’s worth a lot more than all the jewelry, process, and outward appearances. In fact, it might be the only thing that lasts—and to me, that’s what it means to be engaged.

The Kind of Letter You Want To Receive.original:
“Maybe we are both idiots?” The words were staring back at me from a postcard. The paper was printed in Italy, but it was written on in German—by a guy in Poland, naturally. My friend Robert—aka Multithink —truly lives up to his online alias.
Robert has sent postcards in Italian, German, English, Russian, Vietnamese, Czech, Persian, Japanese, Turkish, and Arabic. I told him what a brilliant idea and tradition that was, and, well, two weeks later, I check my mailbox, and…
Some of Robert’s postcards go to friends. Others to strangers halfway around the world. And whether it’s thinking through his words in another language or merely great effort on his part, he always manages to share a deeply personal message with the recipient.
In my case, Robert decided to discuss ideas. “Do you sometimes ask yourself where good ideas come from? Maybe, they appear from the void. Or you can only think of them in the shower, as the internet would have you believe. I believe good ideas are born when we come together.”
This is, of course, how Robert’s postcard habit was born, too. He wanted to connect with an online friend. His mom, rather, for she sent him good thoughts in a tough time. But she only spoke Italian. So Robert studied, scribbled, and hoped for the best —and his friend’s mom kept his letter for many years.
But it takes more than two people coming together for a good idea to blossom, Robert believes. “If we want crazy good ideas, we need at least one crazy person. Hence the million-dollar question: Who is the crazy one? You or me? Maybe we are both idiots?”
Most of my letters these days come from entities demanding money. Those usually don’t make me laugh out loud. Robert’s postcard, however, very much did. That ironic, innocent question, echoing into eternity—or perhaps it was simply the genius of his initiative.
Write more letters. Think multi. If you’re feeling a little crazy, maybe you’ll even try writing to someone in their own language—but most of all, write the kind of letter you, too, would actually want to receive.

 as in “maybe,” not as in “idiot,” of course. The question was in reference to a book I’d recommended to him, The War of Art. It’s Steven Pressfield’s take on overcoming creative resistance, and it’s a book I can read again and again. “I’m reading it for the third time,” I told him. “Maybe we are both idiots, reading the same book three times,” he thought. Or maybe we’re just stubborn. Maybe we just want to get better at our craft. Maybe we’re not idiots at all.
I’m sure there’s a lesson in here about how much you can say in how few words, but the real reason I’m telling you this story is that it’s the kind of letter you want to receive. The kind you can’t help but smile about. The kind that makes you think, “I’m glad I opened my mailbox today.”
In a world where the mailman mostly brings bills, advertisements, and other bad news, it’s easy to feel that checking your mailbox is a chore. But it shouldn’t be. That’s not what mail is for.
When I was younger, I used to send and receive postcards all the time. I had a map on which I marked all the places I’d been, and I’d always send a card back home. I also collected them from friends, family, and other people I knew. I must have 100 postcards and counting. Somewhere. Nowadays, I rarely send any. Maybe I should change that.
The last time I checked, it only cost 45 cents to send a postcard within Germany. That’s a bargain for a moment of joy. If you can make someone’s day for 45 cents plus five minutes of your time, why wouldn’t you?
I’m not saying you should send a postcard to everyone you know every day. That’s not feasible, and it’ll quickly get expensive. But every now and then, a handwritten note can go a long way. And if you’re not the recipient, it might as well be the sender.
The next time you open your mailbox and go, “Ugh, more boring mail,” ask yourself: “When’s the last time I sent something that wasn’t?” Chances are, you’re not the only one wishing for the kind of letter you want to receive.

Tainted Material.original:
Despite recently descaling our electric kettle, its filter kept clogging up. After each boil, the hot water would only drizzle out in spurts. “What’s with this thing?” I thought, “I just cleaned it!” I took out the filter at the spout, rubbed it, shook it, and put it back.
The situation improved slightly, yet two days later, I was back where I started. “Does it have to do with the steam that remains after each boil?” I wondered. “Have we been closing the lid, trapping the steam, and that calcifies the filter?” For days, I couldn’t figure it out.
I was just about to descale the whole device again out of desperation when, suddenly, it hit me: “What if it’s the water?” I checked our other filter —the one we run our water through before we boil it in the kettle—and sure enough, we hadn’t changed the cartridge in weeks. It was way past due. I switched it, tried again, and voilà! Who knew? You boil limescale-free water in your kettle, and your kettle stays limescale-free.
Our inclination is to blame first the tool, then ourselves —but when the raw material is tainted, the result can never be clean. Keep your inputs tidy, and all machines will run smoothly until the end.

The next time I used the kettle, the water was back to normal. “That’s weird,” I thought. “What did I do?” I realized I had taken out the filter twice, but the second time, I had turned it around. The side that was facing the spout was now facing the inside of the kettle. “Huh. Maybe that did the trick.”
I tried it again, and sure enough, the filter worked better when I turned it around. “But why?” I wondered. I took out the filter and looked at it. It was dirty. “Oh! The other side is dirty. That’s why it works better.” It seems the filter is made of two materials: a stainless steel mesh and a plastic frame. The plastic frame is the part that gets dirty, and the stainless steel mesh is the part that filters the water.
The plastic frame is a tainted material. It’s not part of the solution. It’s part of the problem. The plastic frame is there only to hold the mesh in place, but it also prevents the mesh from doing its job. The mesh can’t be removed from the plastic frame, so the only way to keep the kettle working is to turn the filter around every once in a while.
The next time you’re struggling with a tool, ask yourself: “Am I using tainted material?” If the answer is yes, you might be able to flip the problem on its head — and the result will be as clear as a cup of hot water.

I repeated this process several times, and it always helped a little, but never for long. Eventually, I realized that the particles in the filter were too fine to be removed by hand. I took the filter apart, and sure enough, I found sand. Not much, but enough to clog the fine mesh.
I rinsed the filter under running water, and it was back to its usual self. I’ve had to repeat the process several times since, and it’s taught me a valuable lesson: Sometimes, the source of tainted material is tainted material.
When a project goes wrong, you can try to fix it in different ways. You can make a small change to the final result, or you can adjust the process. You can change the process a little, or you can change it a lot. You can also scrap the project altogether, but that’s not the end of it.
If you decide to restart the project, you can begin from the same place you started the first time, or you can begin from a different place. You can use the same materials, or you can use different materials. You can even choose different people to work on the project, and you can change the timeline.
If you’re a creative, you’ll likely be familiar with this particular crossroads in the road: “Do I keep editing the video, or do I re-record it?” If you’re a manager, you’ll face a similar question: “Do I give the team more time, or do I give them a new deadline?”
The answer to these questions is not always obvious, and it’s rarely black and white. You can edit the video and re-record some scenes. You can give the team a new deadline but also a little more time. But when you’re stumped, when you’ve tried every trick in the book, and nothing seems to work, consider tainted material. Perhaps it’s time to throw out the sand, clean the filter, and start over.
It’s not an option we should turn to first, but it sure is liberating to remember it’s there.

What Do You Not Want To Do Today?.original:
We were sipping on preposterous, eight-euro tea in the Four Seasons lobby when my friend Michael walked me through his daily journaling prompts.
“So there’s, gratitude, self-reflection, some emotional check-ins, and of course a few productivity ones, too. ‘What do you want to do today?’ That sort of thing.” His next one jumped out at me: “Oh, and I also recently added one: ‘What do you not want to do today?’ You know, to avoid distractions.” It’s always the seemingly obvious things that hit you the most. “Wow! That’s a great question,” I said. “Brilliant!”
It makes sense to write a to-do list in the morning, of course. To ask, “What needs doing today? ” But with it, for most of us, comes the assumption that, naturally, we’ll then work on those items to the exclusion of all else—yet when do we ever? From fun but non-urgent tasks to the completely irrelevant, a million distractions regularly usurp the more important outcomes in our plans. What if we started paying attention to those instead of pretending we can magically keep them at bay by ignoring them?
“Let me not spend a whole hour watching movie trailers on Youtube again today.” “Finishing my drawing will have to wait until tomorrow.” “I know the boss asked me for it, but it didn’t seem like the competitor analysis was urgent. I think I can skip it for now.” Perhaps these insights are worth just as much as knowing where your time and effort should go to begin with.
What do you not want to do today? Try this question. See where it leads. Oh, and even if the prices are outrageous, having tea at the Four Seasons from time to time should not be the answer—because sometimes, new environments lead to new questions, and that’s always worth more than dollars.

We were sipping on preposterous, eight-euro tea in the Four Seasons lobby when my friend Michael walked me through his daily journaling prompts.
The first one? “What do you not want to do today?”
I thought it was brilliant. How many times have I gone to bed thinking, “I wish I hadn’t done that today?” A lot. But how often did I ask myself that question in advance? Never.
It’s a simple question, but it can lead to powerful answers. It’s also a question we rarely ask. We’re so busy trying to figure out what we want to do that we forget to consider what we don’t want to do.
The point of the question is not to make you feel bad for what you didn’t do. It’s to make you feel good for what you didn’t do.
If you don’t want to do something, don’t do it. That’s the whole point. You can either avoid it altogether or do it later. The important thing is to acknowledge it and make a conscious decision.
It’s okay to not want to do something. It’s okay to not want to do something that’s important. It’s okay to not want to do something that’s urgent. It’s okay to not want to do something that’s good for you.
The only thing that’s not okay is to not want to do something and then do it anyway. That’s how you end up feeling bad for what you didn’t do.
So ask yourself: What do you not want to do today? And then don’t do it.

I don’t want to answer 20 emails. I don’t want to think about the taxes. And I definitely don’t want to sit in front of my screen until 10 PM, which is what would happen if I didn’t consciously decide to stop doing things at some point.
“Wow. That’s a good question,” Michael said. “I’ll have to think about that one!”
If you’re an ambitious person, a creative, or an entrepreneur, you too are probably already overflowing with things you want to do. So instead of adding more fuel to the fire, why don’t you ask what you don’t want to do?
When you’re excited about your work, saying no is the hardest but most important thing you’ll do. It’s easy to get carried away, to spend all your time on something you love, and to forget there’s more to life than just that one thing. Sometimes, it takes a good question to remember.

The Perfect, Imperfect Filter.original:
In the two and a half hours we hung out, Michael and I talked about everything under the sun: work, blockchain, productivity, parenting, self-care, writing, creativity, and on and on. One particularly noteworthy topic? Note-taking.
Michael uses Obsidian, an advanced way to organize and link your thoughts. When he asked how I organize my ideas, I admitted my system was quite rudimentary. Apple Notes for administrative stuff and a basic structure, Evernote to save everything without immediate use, and then, well, a lot of writing drafts filled with notes. I did, however, explain my reason for never bothering to formalize my notes more: I believe the brain is the perfect filter.
When I write an already-long story, I don’t want to comb through every idea I’ve ever had to pick a few relevant examples to include. I’d rather just use what my brain comes up with in that moment. Sure, there’ll always be some recency bias, but often, when you think about a movie you watched last week, you’ll remember a similar one you watched many years ago. Your brain is already full of links. Why not trust them? It is very much imperfect, but this imperfection gives your creations a unique twist. An imprint only you could have made, thanks to whatever your mind delivered in that moment—and that’s beautiful.
Case in point: On the way home from my conversation with Michael, my brain was buzzing with inspiration. Had I taken notes during our conversation, I probably could have drafted a dozen blog posts on the spot. But I didn’t. I let everything simmer in my head, then picked one question from Michael that stood out to me. That became the next day’s post —and that, in turn, led me to this one. No elaborate system needed.
No matter what you do, your net will never be wide enough to catch all idea butterflies. Not all the great and extra shiny ones. Not all the normal ones. And not even all the small swarmers which you could release quickly and go watch them be on their way.
Don’t worry. That’s life. Catch what you can, and enjoy the rest as it flies by. You’ve already got the perfect, imperfect filter—all you have to do is trust it.

In the two and a half hours we hung out, Michael and I talked about everything under the sun: work, blockchain, productivity, parenting, self-care, writing, creativity, and on and on. One particularly noteworthy topic? Note-taking.
Michael is a big fan of Roam Research. He thinks it’s the best note-taking tool out there. I’m a big fan of Evernote. I think it’s the best note-taking tool out there. We debated for a good while. We both made good points. In the end, however, we agreed: There is no perfect note-taking tool. Not for everyone, and not at all times.
I’m an Evernote fan because it’s been around forever, and it’s just a simple, reliable, always-syncing note-taking tool. I like to keep my notes in folders, and I like that I can access them from any device at any time. Michael, meanwhile, prefers Roam because it allows him to link notes to one another and create a big web of ideas. He can see how his thinking is connected and how ideas relate to one another.
The truth is that both tools are great, and both tools are flawed. There is no perfect note-taking tool because there is no perfect note-taker. Everyone takes notes differently, and no tool can ever capture all the idiosyncrasies of human thinking in one system. The perfect note-taking tool would be a perfect AI that would read your mind and file away your thoughts in real-time. Until we have that, we’ll have to make do with what we have — and that’s perfectly fine.
The best you can do is to find the tool that works for you right now. That’ll be the perfect, imperfect filter. You’ll use it until it no longer works, and then you’ll switch to something else. That’s how life is. There is no perfect anything, and no perfect person, but there are perfect moments — and those are the ones we should savor.
Enjoy your note-taking tool. Enjoy your partner. Enjoy your job. Enjoy the moment. Don’t let the imperfections keep you from doing what you’re meant to do — and that’s to live life to the fullest.

I’m a big believer in note-taking. Always have been. I’ve taken notes in school, taken notes in college, and I take notes at work. I take notes when I read, and I take notes in meetings. I take notes from my own thoughts and ideas, and I take notes when I talk to people.
Michael, on the other hand, is a believer in “ the perfect, imperfect filter: ” the human brain. “I’ve never taken notes in my life, and I’ve done just fine,” he said. “Everything I need to remember, I remember. Everything else, I don’t.”
Michael is a smart guy. He has a PhD. He is a professor at a prestigious school. He has published a million papers. And he runs a company with thousands of employees. Clearly, his filter is working. If he had taken notes, he might have done better still. But he did extremely well regardless.
What I learned from this is that there are many ways to solve any one problem. Some people take notes. Some people don’t. Some people remember everything. Others don’t. Some people are visual learners. Others are more conceptual.
The only way to find out what works for you is to keep an open mind. Try different approaches. Listen to what other people do. What works for them may not work for you, but it’s good to know what’s out there. Keep trying until you find what fits, and then keep adapting as you go.
It’s okay to be different. Just because someone does something you don’t doesn’t make either one of you wrong. You’re two people, each with their own habits, beliefs, and attitudes. What you share is a problem, and how you choose to solve it is up to you.
The next time you catch yourself thinking, “I wish I could do that,” remember: You can’t — but you also don’t have to. You have your own way of doing things, and if it works for you, that’s all that matters.

If You Want To Break Something, Use a Ha.original:
The Green Hornet is a superhero who’s been reinterpreted many times since his invention in 1936. Similar to Batman, he’s a wealthy publisher who fights crime as a masked vigilante at night. In a 1966 TV show edition, his sidekick and loyal driver, Kato, received a significant upgraded to his previously only alluded to martial arts skills. Why? Bruce Lee played the part.
Despite the show’s brief, one-season run, many a young fan adored Kato’s cool moves in bringing down the bad guys. Plus, for once, it wasn’t just the main character dealing all the damage. With Lee’s height of only 1.72 m, in this case, it was literally “the little guy” providing inspiration to people all around the country.
One such inspired young girl, named Vicki, summoned her courage to send Bruce a fan letter. She asked him whether he used karate in the show and how she could best break a brick with her hand. In Letters of the Dragon, we can read Bruce’s response.
Always a teacher, Bruce first ensured his fan had all the facts: “Dear Vicki, the art I use on TV is not karate. It is the ancestor of karate and is known as gung fu, which is of Chinese origin (so is karate).” And then, instead of giving her action-hero platitudes, Bruce decided to continue to teach. In fact, the little piece of wisdom he shared next was sage advice I hope Vicki ended up remembering for the rest of her life: “Breaking boards and bricks are mere stunts and are not recommendable for anyone, especially a girl like you. Techniques are the main goal you should work at. If you want to break something, use a hammer.”
Watch a good kung fu movie. Most of the time, the master does nothing. They only fight when they have to. Similarly, Jet Li has never been in a real fight —and Bruce Lee did not smash bricks in his spare time.
If you want strength, accept. If you want inspiration, dive into a good story. Use that strength and inspiration to bring about real change. After all, more things in life need mending than tearing apart. But if you ever do want to break something, well, then just use a hammer—because even superheroes need efficiency.

Despite’t having much screen time, Kato was a hit. He was mysterious, smart, and, most importantly, a kick-ass fighter. As Kato starts to kick some serious butt, his boss asks him what he’s doing. Kato’s response is classic:
“If you want to break something, use a hammer.”
It’s a bit like the saying “if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” but with a twist: if you want to build a house, use a hammer. If you want to break something, use a hammer. In other words, don’t use a screwdriver when you need a hammer. Pick the right tool for the job.
The same applies to our lives. If you want to write a book, use a pen. If you want to build a company, use a computer. If you want to become a chef, use a knife. There are a million ways to spend your time, but only a few of them will lead you to your goals.
Don’t be like The Green Hornet, trying to fight with his bare hands. Be like Kato. Be the one who shows up with the hammer.

In a 1966 TV show edition, his sidekick and loyal driver, Kato, received a significant upgraded to his previously only alluded to martial arts skills. Why? Bruce Lee played the part.
As a result, Kato became a cult figure and Bruce Lee an international superstar. But what’s most interesting about this is how the show’s creators chose to portray Kato’s fighting skills. You might think they’d go to great lengths to explain them. To show the audience how he learned, where he learned, and how much. But they didn’t. They didn’t have to.

This is called ‘show, don’t tell.’ It’s a common principle in the arts, but it applies to life too. If you want to be a good writer, write. If you want to be a good singer, sing. And if you want to be a good friend, be there for your friends.
Whatever you want to be, be it. Don’t just talk about it. Life is not about the words. It’s about the actions.
The only time I will allow you to talk about something is when you don’t know what you want. “I want to be rich” is a fine thing to say, because it acknowledges you have no idea how to get there. You’re not sure if you want to be a writer, a singer, or a good friend. But if you keep saying it, maybe, one day, you’ll find out.
But if you already know you want to be a singer, then for god’s sake, sing. Don’t just talk about singing. Don’t just say you want to sing. Don’t just think about singing. Sing. Sing. Sing.
If you want to break something, use a hammer. And if you want to be something, then be it.

Working Titles.original:
Every time I see the words on the big screen again, I marvel at the brilliance behind the name: “a Working Title production.” Working Title is one of Britain’s most successful movie studios ever, the company behind films like Love Actually, Darkest Hour, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, among many others. Making their own name one that would forever remain in progress didn’t just make for great marketing. It’s also a good reminder there’s always work left to be done.
When I write, 99% of the time, I also do so under a working title. It helps in several ways. For one, there are now some words where there used to be none, making starting the actual draft a little less intimidating. For another, it’s a working title—if push came to shove, as a title, it would work. So if nothing else, I’ve already got a name under which I can ship the piece if need be. That’s reassuring. At the same time, it’s a working title—a title very much still in the works. I can change it any time. That, too, is reassuring—and thus the writer climbs the confidence ladder, one small step after the other.
There’ll always be exceptions, but however soon you can, give your work a title. It takes the pressure off in multiple ways and provides a target to aim at to boot. Who knows? Ship enough working titles, and maybe sometime, we’ll remember you as the Working Title of your field: always tinkering on another potential hit, yet never quite done after shipping the last one.

No Reaction Is a Good Reaction.original:
In a world where everyone’s brain is constantly overloaded to begin with, it’s merely the default. Who knows? Maybe people are quietly nodding along to your work. Sure, that’s not enough in the long run, but while you’re improving, it does just as well.
When we complain about how few responses our work elicits, we tend to believe the alternative is praise from lots of people. But what if it’s only criticism? Take any ride-hailing or food delivery service. How often do you give five stars? Once a year, maybe? But whenever the slightest detail is off, chances are, you’ll complain and try to get some of your money back.
It’s normal. Everyone does it. But it also means as a restaurant on a food delivery platform, you can be happy if one in ten interactions is a positive one—and the other nine don’t end in bad reviews. It’s a minefield of social feedback, and so every place with a five-star rating is akin to a miracle.
Wherever you happen to create, you’re already winning if the deck isn’t stacked against you. Silence can be frustrating, but if you consider it an upgrade from negativity, you can focus on its liberating qualities. You’ll only be funonymous for so long. Enjoy it—and don’t let a lack of explosions keep you from mixing more chemicals.

What Are We Doing?.original:
It’s a question that deserves asking. And often. Today at work, four people were discussing the specifics of a video I didn’t know we were creating, nor what for. So I asked: “What are we doing here?” No one had an answer, and if nothing else, it showed us: Perhaps we are trying to do too much.
My fiancée noted that the community team for her product didn’t seem to substantially increase the user numbers. I had a lucid moment and pointed out: “Your product has 1.8 million users. The community team consists of three people. If they give a talk to 1,000 people, and they all end up using it—which would be a tremendous result—you wouldn’t even see a blip in the metrics.” “Wow,” she said. “That is a good point!” I don’t know if “ grow the users ” is part of that team’s mandate. I’m sure it’s not the only one. But in any case, that team must keep asking: “What are we doing?”
I was out sick for a week, and when I came back, my team had started on a project I was supposed to lead. That’s totally fine, of course, but as a result, the target tone of the project shifted several times in two days. Do we want a technical primer? An extended marketing video? An educational mini-course? The first thing I had to do when I got back was ask: “What are we doing?” If multiple people are involved, working out the answer can take days—which makes it all the more important. There’s little worse than sprinting through a process no one feels they approved in hindsight.
The best questions are often the ones we daren’t ask because we think there must be an obvious answer we’re missing. Usually, we’re not, and other people have the same query on their mind. Even so, it is better to risk looking like a fool today than to guarantee we’ll look like one tomorrow. Have the courage to ask the simple questions again and again. Questions like, “What are we doing?”

Why can’t we just enjoy the little things?” We’ve been together for seven years, and in that time, we’ve had some great adventures, but we’ve also spent a lot of time at home, cooking, reading, watching movies, and just talking. Those times were some of our best times.
It’s easy to get carried away. To go, go, go. To do, do, do. But it’s rarely the doing that matters. It’s the being. The people we’re with. The memories we make. Those memories can be made in a million different ways, and not all of them require grand gestures.
Don’t forget to ask: What are we doing? You might not always get an answer, but you’ll always get a chance to reflect — and perhaps remember that, actually, what we’re doing is just fine.

Keep Your Cool.original:
Talking about not freaking out during major stock market declines in his 2017 annual shareholder letter, Warren Buffett suggested we remember a few select lines from a 19th-century poem by Rudyard Kipling, If :
“If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs… If you can wait and not be tired by waiting… If you can think – and not make thoughts your aim… If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you… Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it.”
It’s good advice even before it feels like the world is ending. When your team is freaking out about an imminent crisis, maintain your zen. When your results seem due but haven’t arrived yet, sit tight. When you’ve thought so much it feels like you’ve thought of everything, just stop thinking. And when few others have faith in you, remember your best reasons to have faith in yourself.
Keep your cool. The sun always rises.

You can choose to follow your heart. You can choose to ignore the noise. You can choose to not let others’ opinions drown out your inner voice. That’s what the poem is about. That’s what it’s always been about.

Are losing theirs and blaming it on you,

Improving Without Criticism.original:
George Lee may not have been part of Bruce Lee’s bloodline, but he was definitely family. As Bruce’s equipment manager—and, more importantly, maker —he forged dozens of specialized training items based on Bruce’s ideas and requests.
As a result of their close relationship, George received many letters from Bruce in his lifetime. Having read most of those letters, one pattern stands out to me: Not once does Bruce criticize George’s work. Whatever his next commission, however many tweaks he asks for, all you’ll ever read is praise for George’s creations. “Magnificent!” “Fantastic!” “Great!”
In one letter, Bruce yet again asks for changes to the latest devices. Here’s how it begins:
“George, Remember the kicking and punching padded boards you made for me—well, after using them for a while I’ve come to many improvements. When you have time, can you make an extra kicking board and punching board for me? Your kicking board is tops for kicking, no heavy bag can replace it. The accompanying sheets will describe the added improvements.”
Can you see it? Not one word of objection. Only praise —and some ideas for the next iteration. The message is clear: It’s enough to try again. Harsh words, denunciation—we don’t need those to get better. “This was a good attempt, but we can still do better. Let’s try one more time with some twists.” These two sentences can fuel a lifetime of effortless, joyful learning. Bruce was the living embodiment of this attitude. It’s worth emulating.
As long as you still want to improve, look back without judgement, then begin the next round. Life is one long game, and it’s ours to win—if only we keep leveling up.

George said he had a good memory. “But how do you remember the mistakes?” Bruce asked. “If you don’t write down your mistakes, you can’t correct them.”
George shrugged. “You’re right. I’ll start writing things down.” Bruce smiled and left. The next day, he returned with a gift: a little book, titled “George’s Little Green Book.” “This is where you write down your mistakes,” Bruce said.
George was happy to receive the gift, but he didn’t expect what came next: Bruce handed him a second book. “This is where you write down my mistakes,” he said. “When I make a mistake, I want you to write it down in this book.”
George was stunned. “Bruce, why do you want me to write down your mistakes?”
“Because I don’t want you to make the same mistakes I make,” Bruce said. “I want you to be better than me.”
George was speechless. “I don’t know what to say.”
Bruce smiled. “Then don’t say anything. Just write.”
We can’t always offer criticism in the moment, but that doesn’t mean we can’t offer it at all. Don’t wait for the perfect moment. Make the moment perfect. It’s never too late to hand someone a little green book.
Even better, however, is to ask them for one. “Here’s where I’ll write down my mistakes. Where’s the one where you write down mine?”
Improvement is a two-way street, and there’s no reason why we can’t both benefit from each other’s mistakes.

Are You Paid Enough To Worry?.original:
My fiancée recently asked me this. I was nervous about a variety of projects going past their deadlines given some reshuffling in our planning at work and me being out sick for a week.
The more I thought about it, the more I realized the projects veering off course was due to external factors. A request from a senior leader here, a life event there. Plus, given my junior rank in the firm, the best I could likely do was to form alternative solutions, present them, and let my boss decide. That’s exactly what I ended up doing, and, as usual, it all turned out fine.
When a ship gets hit by a cannonball from the enemy’s fleet, it is not the oarsmen’s job to bring the vessel back on track. Only the captain has enough visibility to call the next maneuver.
Hierarchy aside, however, I think the truth of the matter is this: You’re never paid enough to worry. What’s a CEO’s salary compared to the company’s market capitalization? 0.01%? Ultimately, even the person who all fingers point to in the end is but a small fish in a vast ocean.
At the end of the day, none of us are paid to sit there in anxiety. We are paid to show up, do our best, solve problems, and try again tomorrow. As long as you do that, you’ll be fine at any job —and if ever you’re not, a million more of them awaits.

“I’m not sure I’ll be able to get everything done on time. I’m really worried about it.”
“Do you get paid enough to worry about it?”
I thought about it for a moment. I get paid enough to show up and do my best. That’s it. That’s all any job can ask of you.
If you do your best, you can’t fail. You can’t control the outcome, but you can control your effort. The outcome is what you get paid for. The effort is what you control.
The outcome is not worth worrying about. You can’t change it. You can only change your effort. And if you give your best effort, you can be proud of it regardless of the outcome.
The only thing worth worrying about is whether you’re giving your best effort. If you’re not, you can try harder. If you are, there’s no point in worrying.
If you’re not happy with the outcome, you can always get a different job. You can’t control what people think of you, but you can control what you think of yourself. And if you think you’re doing your best, that’s enough.
So, are you paid enough to worry? Probably not. Because worrying is not part of the job. It’s a distraction. A distraction from doing your best. And if you’re not doing your best, you’re not doing your job.
So don’t worry. Just do your best. And be proud of it.

When she asked me, I thought about it, and I realized: “Actually, I am. I’m doing fine. I should stop worrying.”
When you’re starting out as a freelancer, entrepreneur, or solo creator, the answer to this question is always “No.” You’re not getting paid enough to worry.
You’re not getting paid at all, and you should be worrying about how to fix that. You’re getting paid $10 an hour to write crappy articles, and you should be worrying about how to find better work. You’re getting paid $500 for a logo design, and you should be worrying about how to score a client who’ll pay you $5,000.
When you’re still struggling to make ends meet, the answer is always “No.” You need to worry about making more money. You need to worry about diversifying your income. You need to worry about how to make it through the dip until the next, more rewarding project comes along.
But if you’re already making enough, the answer is always “Yes.” You’re paid enough to worry. You should be worrying about how to do better work, not more of it. You should be worrying about how to do the best work you can possibly do in the time that you have.
You’re paid enough to worry about how you can deliver the best possible value to your customers, audience, and fans. You should be worrying about how to make your work more fun. You should be worrying about how to enjoy the process, not how to extract more dollars from it.
The answer to this question will change many times throughout your life and career. What’s important is that you ask it. “Am I paid enough to worry?”
When you’re not, go out and get yourself some more money. When you are, go out and do the best work you can.

Working for the Cat.original:
After weeks of back and forth around a joint presentation, the CEO of the company we were in talks with left. Suddenly, there’s a new boss, a new team, and the whole process starts from scratch. I smiled when I saw the email. I don’t think my slides will go to waste. They can be amusing, the tides of time and business.
In German, when we do work that ends up being futile, we say it’s “for the cat.” The expression might go back to a fable about a blacksmith who, willing to accept any payment, tries to feed his cat with the mere “Thanks!” from his customers. Soon, the cat starves, and the blacksmith is forced to charge fixed prices like everyone else.
Frustration is the easy choice when we fear our work might have been for the cat, but the truth is we rarely know in the moment. It’s too soon to tell. Sometimes, working for the cat can be a blessing. What if the project just didn’t sit right? When it feels off from the beginning, perhaps our starving cat took a bullet in our stead.
When you’re happy to be here, ultimately, nothing is for the cat. You show up, try to help out, and whoever is the recipient of your generosity will be glad to receive it at the time. Sometimes in life, we get something for nothing—so at other times, we must do something for nothing in return. Trust fate to figure it out for you, and, in the meantime, don’t worry if no one thanks you for it.

The only one who was sad was the cat. For weeks, I had been working on the presentation, which meant I had been working for the cat. Now, I had to do other things, and the cat was left with nothing to do. I think she was bored. She kept following me around the house, meowing and trying to get my attention. “What are you doing? Why aren’t you working on that presentation? Why don’t you have time for me?”
It’s funny how we can project our own feelings on others. Of course, the cat didn’t care about the presentation. She only cared about the attention I was giving her while working on it. I’m sure she was happy to have me back. But it’s also true that, sometimes, we work for the cat. We work for the reward, for the money, or for the praise.
There’s nothing wrong with working for the cat. We all do it at times. Just don’t forget to work for yourself. To work on what’s important to you. Because even if you can’t feel it, you are always working for someone.

Knowing Too Much and Too Little.original:
The more time he spends wandering through the Aiel Waste, a barren, desert landscape in the Wheel of Time universe, the more “Dragon Reborn” Rand al’Thor understands the extent of his powers. Powerful magic that’s bound to corrupt him, strength to withstand even strong enemies’ attacks, and unreliable but enlightening visions of the future—such are the burdens of the chosen one.
As Rand and his fellowship are guided to an unknown location by one of the many Aiel clans, he overhears the name of their destination: Rhuidean. “That’s where you’re taking us!” Rand says, pointing at Rhuarc, the clan’s chief. “I know there’s a trial for me there!”
Rhuarc only sighs and shakes his head. “You know too much—and too little,” he tells Rand. It’s true. Thanks to his visions, Rand knows more about what’s coming than he should, and it puts him in danger. But he also knows less than he would need to know in order for his information about the future to be actually useful—and that, too, puts him in danger.
Our thirst for knowledge is everlasting. Often, however, the little extra we fight so hard for does us more harm than good. Most of the time, it’s enough to trust that, right now, we have everything we need. Face trials as you meet them, and reap the rewards as they fall. What you know is just enough, and the chosen one always makes it through the day.

As he continues to learn about his abilities, however, Rand also realizes how much he doesn’t know. “I have to know more,” he tells his friend Mat. “I have to learn…”
“Learn what?” Mat says. “How to fly? How to be safe from Aes Sedai and the Forsaken? How to win the Last Battle? Light, Rand, you are the Dragon Reborn! You are what you are. Learn to live with it!”
It’s true. Rand is the Dragon Reborn, and there’s nothing he can do to change that. But it’s also true that the more he learns, the better he can handle this fact—and all the responsibilities that come with it.
It’s a classic case of knowing too much and too little at the same time, and we all face it. The more we know, the more we realize we don’t know. The more we understand, the more we see what we’ve misunderstood. And the more we do, the more we’ll see how much we have yet to do.
In that sense, we are all the Dragon Reborn. We have to learn to live with what we are, but we also have to keep learning in order to do so. It’s a never-ending cycle, and while we can’t do anything to stop it, we can choose to accept it.
Don’t worry about knowing too much and too little. Just keep learning, and you’ll always know enough to do what’s right.

Using Your Judgment.original:
In early 1965, Bruce Lee’s father died. He was summoned to Hong Kong to attend the funeral and deal with the estate.
The young Lee family didn’t have much money at the time. Bruce was 24 years old. He and his wife Linda had only married the previous August, and their son Brandon was merely a few weeks old. They hadn’t even gone on a honeymoon yet, nor had they been able to afford “proper” wedding rings.
In Hong Kong, however, many goods were cheaper than in the United States. Perhaps for this reason, perhaps to distract himself or, as we all sometimes do, to spite his challenging finances, Bruce spent a good deal of his month-long trip shopping for gifts for his wife and family.
He scouted for a diamond ring for Linda. He worked on getting her a wig made of real human hair, a hot item in fashion at the time. Lee even thought of his mother-in-law. However, since long-distance phone calls were expensive, Lee’s communication with his family happened mostly via letters, and that made aligning everyone’s requests with the right appointment at the right vendor a challenge.
But, as ever, Lee was not discouraged. In one letter, he told Linda: “I have a purse for your mother and if financial situation allows I might be able to pick up more stuffs for her. I’ll try but you know the U.S. Customs, not to mention money problems. I’ll use my judgment.”
“I’ll use my judgment.” When’s the last time you heard that phrase? Have you ever? And, more importantly, did you trust whoever said it to do so? Here’s a man writing to his family thousands of miles away, saying, “I know money is tight right now, but I still want to treat you and make the most of this opportunity for it. So don’t worry. I won’t go crazy. I’ve got this.” Of course, back in the day, Linda had little choice but to trust her husband—yet I’d like to think she would have done so regardless.
“I’ll use my judgment.” The phrase reminded me how little trust we often extend to one another these days—and how little confidence we usually have in our own ability to make sound decisions. But even 60 years after Bruce’s trip, there’s still plenty of need for both in the world.
Yesterday, I watched Pat Flynn complete a Pokémon card collecting challenge. His goal was to obtain a full set of over 250 cards in a single day during a convention. As always, Pat traded and received help from many people along the way. At one point, he gave a 10-year-old kid $400—a literal Mount Dollar-est for a child of his age—to go and restock his trade binder so he could make more deals. “I trust you!” he told the young boy. What a vote of confidence! Only a short while later, the kid returns with a big stack of great cards, which Pat can immediately swap with some other folks for more of the Pokémon he needs to complete his challenge.
In many ways, our access to infinite, real-time information has made us hypersensitive. We tend towards distrust, worry, and micromanagement. But just because we can see everything, everywhere, all at once, that doesn’t mean it’s all relevant to us. In fact, a man without a smartphone who doesn’t do long-distance phone calls and mostly writes letters to communicate can, even today, go through life without major complications. And if that’s not inspiration enough, empowering our kids to become emotionally self-sufficient adults should definitely do the trick.
Money, fame, cool hobbies and good deals, even life itself—it all comes and goes. Use your judgment, and you’ll be fine. I have complete faith in you.

While in Hong Kong, Lee was asked to audition for a role in a TV show. He gave an impressive performance, and the producers offered him the lead role. The show would have been a hit, and Lee would have become a star. But he turned it down and returned to the US.
The reason? “Using his judgment,” his wife Linda wrote in her book Bruce Lee: The Man Only I Knew. “He had to be himself, and it was impossible to be himself in a commercial world.”
It was a decision that would cost him a lot of money, fame, and potentially even his life. But it was the right decision, and Lee would never have forgiven himself for not making it.
Using your judgment is hard. It means saying no when you want to say yes. It means taking the path less traveled. It means leaving money, fame, and comfort behind in order to do the right thing.
But using your judgment is the only way to be yourself. It’s the only way to live a life that’s true to your values. And it’s the only way to find peace and happiness.
So when you’re faced with a difficult decision, remember: using your judgment is always the right thing to do.
Using Your Judgment.ckpt_1628:
In early 1965, Bruce Lee’s father died. He was summoned to Hong Kong to attend the funeral and deal with the estate.
A few days before his return to the United States, Lee was called into his brother’s office. The family lawyer was there, and he presented Lee with a choice: “Do you want to take over your father’s entertainment business, or do you want to inherit all the money?”
Lee asked for a moment to think, and then he went outside. He walked around the block. After a few minutes, he returned and said: “I want to take over my father’s business.” The lawyer was stunned. “Are you sure? That’s a lot of responsibility. The money is just money. You can do whatever you want with it.”
But Lee was sure, and he explained: “I want to take over my father’s business, because I want to use my judgment. I don’t want to live off my father’s money. I want to live off the work that I do.”
When Lee got back to America, he did not immediately shut down his father’s business. Instead, he started a kung fu school in Seattle. Eventually, however, he would close all his schools and pursue acting full time. He would use his judgment, and, in doing so, he would become a legend.
It’s easy to outsource your decisions. To let other people run the show. “I’m not sure about this project. I’ll just do what my boss says.” “I don’t want to choose between these two people. I’ll just marry whoever asks me first.” “I have no idea where to invest. I’ll just give all my money to this fund.”
Sometimes, deferring is the right choice. We can’t think of everything, and we can’t be experts in every field. But life consists entirely of decisions. From the moment we wake up to the moment we fall asleep, we choose what to do, what to think, what to say, and how to act. If we abdicate that responsibility for too long, we’ll wake up one day and find we’ve barely lived at all. We’ll have outsourced our lives right under our own noses.
The only way to truly be alive is to use your judgment. To decide, and act, and live. To try your best, make mistakes, and get up again the next day. Life is short. Don’t wait for it to pass you by.
